Parents of Michigan students with disabilities demand special education reforms
articles.description: More than 75 people attended a meeting Monday night focused on what the state can do to improve special education. Many shared personal stories of their students.
articles.content: More than 75 people attend a state meeting about special education Parents raised concerns about students receiving specialized services, communication with local schools and student discipline Attendees told Bridge they hope state officials take their concerns seriously and make changes SAGINAW — Dozens of Michigan parents and advocates gathered Monday to demand that local schools and state officials provide more support for students with disabilities. More than 75 people packed a State Board of Education Special Education Committee meeting in Saginaw. It was the committee’s first public meeting outside of Lansing since the state board formed the bipartisan group in June and charged it with finding ways to improve services for students with disabilities.“We acknowledge that we are in a tough place,” State Board of Education president Pamela Pugh, a Democrat from Saginaw, told the audience. “We acknowledge that we do not have all the answers. We acknowledge that this process is something that we set out to do, not even knowing which direction to go in, but knowing that we needed to continue to hear from parents.”Parents shared stories of students with disabilities not receiving enough specialized services to learn in their classrooms and instances where parents had to battle their local schools. Terricina Jackson, an advocate in Saginaw and parent of a 9-year-old son with autism, said she hopes “the state holds the administrators and the district responsible for the violation of children’s rights, the implementation of IEPs (individualized education programs), the data that is not being provided to families.” Related: Michigan wants to scrap rarely used special ed rule. Child advocates fear harm Report: Michigan must overhaul ‘inequitable’ way it funds special education A renewed push to ban seclusion, reduce restraint in Michigan schools Michigan fight over special ed services lingers, years after COVID shutdown “I want the board to hold these schools accountable, the ISD accountable for the lack that we are all experiencing. I’m not sure that’s going to happen. “ Terricina Jackson, an advocate and parent of a 9-year-old with autism, told Bridge she hopes state officials hold local districts accountable for their actions. (Isabel Lohman/ Bridge Michigan) Jackson said Monday’s meeting involved “a bunch of photo opps. I think that they allowed us to express our concern because they know that families need to be heard, but actually implementing, I’ve not seen anybody do that in five years.” Attendees told Bridge they want schools to provide support for students and for the state to hold schools accountable for their actions. Sarah Earle, a parent of a 14-year-old, told Bridge she hopes her family’s and others’ concerns are heard and “that change is made” across the state. “These kids deserve the very best just like everybody else.” Attendees shared experiences in small groups with their discussions recorded on AI tools. The state plans to compile responses from multiple meetings. Donate In one small group, participants discussed students needing one-on-one paraprofessionals, changes to state teacher credentials, and concerns that students are losing out on key help that would allow them to learn. “Parents should not have to reach a breaking point to get their children help,” said Jennifer Gruesbeck of Saginaw township during the public comment portion of the meeting. “We should not have to become experts in special education, constantly advocate, document every incident, attend endless meetings, put our jobs in jeopardy, and fight for basic services just to ensure our children have access to an education.” Small groups discuss their concerns during a breakout session at the Michigan Department of Education’s Special Education Committee meeting in Saginaw on Monday, Nov. 9. (Courtesy of the Michigan Department of Education) Some traveled far to share their experience. Carrie Dickerson, a parent and advocate, said she travelled two hours to attend the meeting. “While efforts to travel the state are appreciated, many families cannot make a trip like this.” Dickerson said. “Parents of children with disabilities often face significant barriers, including work schedules, caregiving responsibilities, transportation challenges, and disability-related needs of their own or their children.” The committee plans to hold meetings in Oakland, Grand Traverse and Marquette counties in the future, according to a news release. The dates for these meetings have not yet been publicly released. Pugh said the committee also plans to hold virtual sessions. There were 226,800 Michigan students receiving special education last school year in Michigan public, private or homeschool settings. They’re part of a system some say is filled with problems. Schools continue to face high special education teacher shortages, and as of last year, Michigan had one of the nation’s highest rates of special education drop outs. Christopher Earle and Sarah Earle attended the State Board of Education Special Education Committee Monday, Nov. 9 with hopes state officials will change education for their 14-year-old son and other students with disabilities. (Isabel Lohman/Bridge Michigan) Michigan reimburses local districts for a percentage of the cost of providing special ed services and transportation. That’s in addition to a per-pupil foundation allowance from the state’s School Aid Fund. Last year, advocates called for the state to move toward a weighted funding model that provides more state money for students with the highest needs., arguing the current system is inequitable.Meanwhile, parents and advocates have raised concerns about the state’s complaint process which allows a parent to file a free complaint against their local district. A 2025 Bridge examination of state records found that since 2018, state investigations stemming from parent complaints had jumped 21%, while the overall population of special education students increased just 3.6%. Advocates previously told Bridge the system was stacked against parents — making them fight for services that are supposed to be guaranteed by law. Kourtney Sabourin, a parent of an 11-year-old with autism, told Bridge she has filed four state complaints and “every time I’ve been dissatisfied.” She said districts know they “are going to get a slap on the hand” by the state if they violate rules, but “they’re not afraid of anything and students continue to suffer.” The meeting on Monday comes as the Michigan Department of Education analyzes public comment over a set of changes it’s proposing to special education rules. One contentious idea is to scrap the so-called “stay put” provision. Currently, when a parent or guardian files a special education complaint with the state, the department can require that the student remain in their current classroom or specialized program while it investigates. But MDE says the stay-put provision applies to legal proceedings rather than departmental investigations and that it has only been invoked once in the 47-year history of the state complaint process. It says the change aligns with federal disability law. The Autism Alliance of Michigan and other student advocacy groups are opposed to the proposal State Superintendent Glenn Maleyko, who attended Monday’s meeting, said that since he started a listening tour in February, special education is the top concern. “We know it’s very important,” Maleyko said. “It’s probably one of the more challenging areas of education, but we really need to work together.”

articles.title: U-M evaluating potential of finding indigenous remains at planned data center site
articles.description: The archeological review comes after a warning that the Huron River region is “highly archaeologically sensitive.”
articles.content: (Rob Hess / Michigan Public)The University of Michigan said it is working with an archeologist to evaluate the potential that indigenous artifacts or human remains could be discovered on the site of its proposed hyperscale data center in Ypsilanti Township.The archeological review comes after a warning by the State Historic Preservation Office that the area surrounding the Huron River is “highly archaeologically sensitive.”U-M’s proposed data center is situated within that region. But the project site has not been specifically assessed by the office, according to a spokesperson.Scott Slagor, cultural resource protection manager at the Historic Preservation Office, informed the university in an email that the proposed location of the data center, as well as the fact that construction is set to occur on an undeveloped parcel, increases the likelihood of an archeological discovery on the site.“This risk includes burials,” the Slagor wrote, explaining that an adjacent property includes “a recorded cemetery.”“You absolutely do not want to hit remains during construction,” he wrote.U-M selected the 144-acre Ypsilanti Township parcel in August, amidst pushback from residents. The university has said the data center will support research “to advance science and education.” It will operate in partnership with the Los Alamos National Laboratory, which specializes in nuclear weapons research.Slagor’s recommendations, which were framed as general guidance for initiating an assessment, came in a September email exchange with U-M’s project director, Rob Green. The emails were provided to Michigan Public by Doug Winters, an attorney for Ypsilanti Township, and confirmed by a Historic Preservation Office spokesperson.The exchange began with Green seeking advice from Slagor on how to research the archeological history of the U-M property.“Through our community engagement, we have received some comments claiming there might be Native American burial grounds on the property,” Green wrote, noting that “we have not been able to find any direct evidence to support this claim.”The Historic Preservation Office manages Michigan’s list of archeological sites to help ensure their preservation. Archeological data maintained by the agency can only be shared with federally qualified archeologists.Slagor advised that the university consult with a qualified archeologist to “to conduct an archaeological assessment” and “advise you on the path forward for the property.” Slagor also recommended the university reach out to the Tribal Historic Preservation Offices of nearby tribes.A U-M spokesperson declined an interview request and directed Michigan Public to a statement from October 30.“The University is grateful for the cooperation and recommendations provided following preliminary discussion with SHPO representatives,” the statement reads. “In accordance with their recommendation, the university is engaging a Federally Registered Archeologist to conduct an official consultation with SHPO. We are reaching out to the appropriate Tribal Nations to ensure the project is proceeding with respect to the community.”According to an spokesperson for the office, the emails obtained by Michigan Public represent the extent of current communication between U-M and the agency.The U-M statement also noted that the university has not yet broken ground on the site and that non-archeological surveys found “no evidence of archeological artifacts or culturally-sensitive materials found at the project site.”Winters, the Ypsilanti Township attorney, told Michigan Public that he did not trust U-M to conduct a careful assessment before beginning construction.“We've known for many, many years this property, adjacent to the banks of the Huron River, was home to Native American tribes for centuries,” Winters said. “This is not news to U of M, but they were not going to voluntarily come forward until we pressed the issue.”In October, the Ypsilanti Township Board of Trustees and the United Tribes of Michigan both passed resolutions urging the university to hold off on construction until it completed detailed archaeological assessments.Editor's note: The University of Michigan holds Michigan Public’s broadcast license.

Detroit Regional Chamber urges Whitmer to join Trump-backed tax credit opposed by teachers union
articles.description: The state attorney general says she has "grave concerns" the program would violate the Michigan Constitution.
articles.content: (Courtesy / Grand Rapids Public Schools )A prominent business group wants Governor Gretchen Whitmer to opt Michigan into a federal education program that's opposed by the state’s largest teachers union.The Detroit Regional Chamber sent a letter urging Whitmer to join the Federal Education Freedom Tax Credit. The program allows people to make a $1,700 donation to a Scholarship Granting Organization who – in turn – gives out scholarships to students.More than 30 states have opted into the program so far.The scholarships can be used for things like books and tutoring. It can also be used for private school tuition – which is driving the hesitancy to adopt the tax credit by some Democrat-led states.Chamber CEO Sandy Baruah says the political climate isn’t helping either.“We know that there's some unnecessary controversy around this, just because it is a Trump administration initiative, but we think this is a good one, and I think this supports education,” Baruah said.The Michigan Constitution bans public money from going toward private schools.Michigan Education Association spokesman Thomas Morgan said it’s another “voucher scheme.”“The program was created to weaken public education and divert billions of dollars to private and religious schools and the for-profit companies that service them,” Morgan said.In 2000, Michigan voters rejected a proposal that would have established a state-funded voucher program.Last month, Whitmer and four other Democratic governors sent a letter to the U.S. Department of Treasury for more information on the program.In an op-ed for the Detroit Free Press, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel panned the program.“I have grave concerns about whether the voucher program violates the Michigan Constitution,” Nessel wrote.Baruah wasn’t sure about the specifics of this federal program running afoul of state law. He said with Michigan being one of the worst states for childhood literacy something needs to change.“We should be turning over every stone that improves education for children in the state of Michigan.”For the MEA, Whitmer allowing the program to start in the state would be a betrayal.“Opting Michigan into this federal voucher scheme at the end of her term would drown out much of the great work that Governor Whitmer has helped accomplish on behalf of Michigan students and schools and educators,” Morgan said.

articles.title: What could China get from Jensen Huang?

articles.content: It’s difficult to overstate Nvidia’s power in today’s AI landscape. The company’s chips are the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built, and demand has consistently outpaced supply for years. Nvidia has also been an influential investor in a wide range of up-and-coming AI companies in recent years, with about $99 billion worth of equity investments in frontier AI labs, neoclouds, infrastructure companies, and more. Its chief executive has even become close with President Donald Trump. This is why, as both cofounder and longtime CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry. Huang is in hot water after news broke of his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen) is an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud provider and a top Nvidia customer. Questions are swirling around how the affair may have influenced Huang’s reported push to sell advanced chips to China — and potentially even influenced President Trump’s own decisions surrounding AI export controls. US officials believe the Megaspeed executive is a foreign intelligence asset that has funneled information straight to the Chinese government, per The New York Times — in particular, officials reportedly believe that Megaspeed is related to a convoluted web of Chinese companies working together to access chips in bulk and perhaps even illegally get some of those chips into China. Alibaba is reportedly one of Megaspeed’s top customers. “It’s not entirely surprising that the CEO of arguably one of the most important, if not the most important, AI chip companies is the target of some sort of intelligence-gathering from countries like China,” Hanna Dohmen, a senior research analyst at CSET, said in an interview with The Verge, adding that an alleged spy would potentially be interested in “better understanding what the US government is thinking on export controls,” as well as gathering information on Huang’s conversations with the Trump administration, attempting to influence policy, and gathering information on trade secrets like “who’s buying Nvidia’s chips, who’s getting them first, what’s coming next in terms of AI chips.” Megaspeed’s sister company, headquartered in Malaysia, spent $4.8 billion or more on Nvidia chips and technology between June 2024 and February 2026, the Times reported, citing trade records from trade platform ImportGenius. The transaction sizes were outside the norm for a small company, particularly when Nvidia chips are so difficult to get. Nvidia spokespeople had said Huang’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive was strictly business. Their interactions were described as “not unusual or unexpected” in statements to the press. Nvidia’s line was, “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job.” But at some point, their relationship became personal. In June 2024, just before Megaspeed became an Nvidia customer, photos show the two with other AI executives at a bar in Taipei after a local trade show; the following year, they reportedly had a business dinner in Taipei with others as well. But in private, according to US officials cited by the Times, the two’s relationship raised alarm bells for the US government — they had reportedly been surveilling the Megaspeed executive for months, if not longer, and that’s how it came out that she was in close contact with Huang. The revelation is particularly concerning because of Huang’s lobbying role. He’d been trying to convince the Trump administration and Congress to loosen export controls for sending advanced semiconductors to China, ostensibly so that Nvidia could sell more chips. We now know this was happening around the same time that Huang was spotted at the Taiwan dinner with Alice Huang in May 2025, according to Culper Research, which shorted Nvidia’s stock earlier this year. That dinner occurred shortly after Nvidia had shared the Trump administration’s new restrictions on its China-specific H20 chips in April. Just a couple months after the Taiwan dinner, Huang reportedly met with Trump in the Oval Office in July 2025 to plead his case for loosening export restrictions on Nvidia’s advanced semiconductors. Days later, the company announced that the administration had blessed sales of its H20 chips to China. Huang had argued that spreading American chips to China would help establish US technology as the standard, rather than allowing for Chinese chips to grow, according to The New York Times. After setbacks earlier in the second Trump term in export policy to China, Huang began speaking with then-White House AI czar David Sacks in 2025, who became the key advocate for Nvidia’s view that selling American chips to China would be beneficial, the Times reported. By October 2025, Huang was lobbying Trump to allow Nvidia to sell more advanced chips to China, ahead of Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, per the Times; but after Trump considered the proposal, he ultimately decided not to move forward. (That same month, Huang hired an external PR firm known for handling sex scandals, Wired reported.) Months later, in December 2025, Trump changed course slightly, allowing Nvidia to sell H20 chips to a greenlit list of “approved customers” in China, with the US government taking a 25 percent cut of those sales. The same rules would apply to other US chipmakers, he wrote on Truth Social at the time. CSET’s Dohmen said that during the past two years, the US has seen a light loosening of AI export control regulations under the Trump administration, driven partly by Huang’s own lobbying. But it’s important to note, she said, that “even without any kind of intelligence operations from the Chinese side, it is in Nvidia’s interest and in Jensen Huang’s interest to lobby for looser export control restrictions.” Any restrictions by definition stifle Nvidia’s business expansion and cut off potential sales to help it grow its already stunning market cap — which is currently about $4.25 trillion, second only to Apple. Huang’s relationship with Trump is also particularly relevant here. The president lavished praise on Huang during a speech last year, saying that until recently, he hadn’t even heard of Nvidia, and then he wanted to break it up. But after meeting Huang, he said, he understood why it would be difficult to re-create the company he’d built. More recently, Huang put Trump on speakerphone when the president called him during an appearance onstage at the All-In Summit, publicly displaying his close access to the Oval Office. This past spring, a classified memo — the writing of which was overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, per the Times — circulated among Trump administration officials ahead of the president’s trip to China in May, warning of the Megaspeed executive’s alleged involvement in surveillance on behalf of China’s Ministry of State Security. Her reported goal was to learn about advanced AI chips in the US and try to influence them being made available to China on a large scale. Asked if he had known about the memo reviewed by Rubio at a press briefing on Monday, Trump said, “I’d certainly check with the intelligence people. It could have been mentioned. Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.” Earlier in the briefing, he said he was unaware of the alleged spy connection ahead of his trip to China. Huang was initially left off the list of executives joining Trump on the trip, but the president later asked him to join. Trump had been briefed about a year ago that US intelligence believed the Megaspeed executive to be a China intelligence operative, according to the Times, and that she had a close relationship with a US citizen who turned out to be Nvidia’s CEO. At the time, he reportedly chose not to take action. So far, the allegations haven’t affected Huang’s future at Nvidia. He’ll continue to lead the company during the investigation. Trump has also stood by him since news broke of the affair, telling reporters this past weekend, “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.” On Sunday, Huang wrote an internal memo to Nvidia employees — some of which are his own family members — writing, “I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” He then addressed Nvidia’s board, partners, and shareholders, adding that he is “fully committed” to leading the company and “will work to earn back your confidence.” This weekend, Nvidia’s board of directors launched an independent investigation into the national security allegations. Huang will not have control over the participants in the investigation, and Nvidia said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello wrote in a note on Monday that Morningstar “can’t rule out the investigation fading away and Nvidia returning to business as usual,” particularly since Huang is the “only CEO the company has ever known.” There’s also the fact that Huang’s Nvidia struck deals in August with six large financial institutions to provide more than $500 billion in financing for the buildout of AI data centers and other infrastructure, and as the US-China AI race intensifies, those are high-stakes agreements. “It’s unclear to us what these partnerships and financing deals would look like with a different Nvidia CEO,” Colello wrote. “Costs of capital may rise for future investments if perhaps the most prominent CEO in the AI landscape is no longer orchestrating such deals.” Morningstar still maintained a very high uncertainty rating for the company, with Colello writing that it’s possible US approval of Nvidia to sell H20 chips to China will be revoked and that the company could ostensibly be sanctioned as well. Trump told reporters on Sunday that Huang should remain CEO of Nvidia and that he would “certainly take him” on his next trip to China. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump told reporters. “He dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else.”

articles.title: The US Senate’s 11 Democratic freshmen arrive at the Capitol
articles.description: WASHINGTON — Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer Monday welcomed 11 newly elected Senate Democrats at the U.S. Capitol, following midterm elections in which his party flipped both chambers in Congress. “Last week the American people put Donald Trump and the GOP on blast,” Schumer, a New York Democrat, said on the Senate floor. “Americans pulverized […]
articles.content: U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., center, poses for a photo with newly elected Democratic senators in his office in the U.S Capitol on Nov. 9, 2026 in Washington, D.C. From left to right: Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio, James Talarico of Texas, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, Josh Turek of Iowa, Roy Cooper of North Carolina, Juliana Stratton of Illinois, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, Annie Andrews of South Carolina, Troy Jackson of Maine, Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Adam Hamilton of Kansas. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)WASHINGTON — Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer Monday welcomed 11 newly elected Senate Democrats at the U.S. Capitol, following midterm elections in which his party flipped both chambers in Congress. “Last week the American people put Donald Trump and the GOP on blast,” Schumer, a New York Democrat, said on the Senate floor. “Americans pulverized the red wall and for good reason. Americans want a government that recognizes and responds to their needs and Democrats are ready to deliver.” Joining Schumer for a brief press event in his office were Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, Roy Cooper of North Carolina, James Talarico of Texas, Juliana Stratton of Illinois, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, Annie Andrews of South Carolina, Josh Turek of Iowa, Adam Hamilton of Kansas and Troy Jackson of Maine. While Schumer is currently the Senate Democratic leader, he’ll have to run again next month to keep his leadership position. Several of the incoming Senate class also broke barriers. Pappas will be the first openly gay elected senator, El-Sayed is the first Muslim senator and Minnesota voters made Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan the first Native American woman senator. She could be joined by Alaska Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, an Alaska Native whose Senate race is still too close to call. By the 120th Congress in January, Democrats will have 54 senators, potentially 56 if Peltola and Mississippi Democratic candidate Scott Colom win their races, in which votes are still being counted. Colom could become the first Black senator from the state since the Reconstruction era if he defeats GOP incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

articles.title: Permitting overhaul advances in US Senate with tepid bipartisan support
articles.description: A proposal to overhaul the federal process for permits to construct energy projects passed a procedural hurdle in the U.S. Senate on Monday, though several Democratic supporters said the legislation needed more work. The Senate voted, 73-25, to advance what’s known as the permitting reform bill, despite opposition from some corners of the environmental advocacy world […]
articles.content: The U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C., on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)A proposal to overhaul the federal process for permits to construct energy projects passed a procedural hurdle in the U.S. Senate on Monday, though several Democratic supporters said the legislation needed more work. The Senate voted, 73-25, to advance what’s known as the permitting reform bill, despite opposition from some corners of the environmental advocacy world who are influential with Democrats. Several Democratic members said they would be pursuing major changes through the amendment process. The measure is sponsored by the bipartisan leaders of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee — led by West Virginia Republican Shelley Moore Capito as chair, with Rhode Island’s Sheldon Whitehouse the top Democrat — and the Senate Energy Committee’s Chair Mike Lee of Utah and ranking Democrat Martin Heinrich of New Mexico. The loudest opponents of the bill are environmental groups, and their Democratic champions in Congress, that say the bill’s promise to promote federal permitting for renewable energy production and transmission projects is outweighed by the advantages it would provide fossil fuel production. “We support the elements of the legislation that help accelerate needed transmission, clean energy deployment, and grid modernization,” Natural Resources Defense Council CEO Manish Bapna said in a Sunday statement. “But the current package goes too far in weakening essential environmental safeguards and public participation requirements.” Bapna said the group understood compromise was crucial to any kind of permitting reform bill, but that the current legislation, an updated version of which the sponsors released Saturday, still fell short. NRDC would be “willing to assist” in making further changes to the measure, he added. Oregon Sen. Jeff Merkley, a Democrat, similarly said Monday he could not yet support the bill, which he said had not been adequately vetted by either chamber of Congress, but he said he shared some of its objectives and hoped to improve it in coming days. “Permitting reform for electrical transmission lines is essential,” he wrote. “But the current bill raises too many serious issues that require more deliberation. I will vote against the bill before us today, but I look forward to working with my colleagues to get permitting reform right.” Democrats also raised issues with provisions they say would weaken tribal power to weigh in on proposed projects. Nevada Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto said ahead of the Monday vote she would support the procedural measure, but would vote against final passage if tribal issues are not addressed. “Clean, reliable electricity in this country should be cheap and accessible – and permitting reform is the best way to deliver for the American people,” she said. “But I cannot ignore the concerns that Tribes in Nevada have with this bill text… If Title III stays in this bill, I will not vote for final passage.”

articles.title: Incoming chair of US Senate panel will seek healthcare overhaul, but unclear on details
articles.description: WASHINGTON — Oregon Democratic U.S. Sen. Ron Wyden plans to press for “the boldest” healthcare bill possible after he takes over as Finance Committee chairman next year, but he didn’t commit to Medicare for All, a longstanding policy goal for progressives, during a briefing Monday. Wyden told reporters in the Capitol that while he supports […]
articles.content: Oregon Democratic U.S. Sen. Ron Wyden speaks with reporters in the Senate Daily Press Gallery on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — Oregon Democratic U.S. Sen. Ron Wyden plans to press for “the boldest” healthcare bill possible after he takes over as Finance Committee chairman next year, but he didn’t commit to Medicare for All, a longstanding policy goal for progressives, during a briefing Monday. Wyden told reporters in the Capitol that while he supports legislation that would eliminate private health insurance companies and put all Americans on a Medicare-like health program, he needed time to discuss legislation with his colleagues. “I’m sure that when I get out and talk to my colleagues, there’s going to be differing views on the issue, different opinions,” he said. Wyden added he believes the country’s health insurance network is “broken” and a “mess” that’s in need of significant overhaul. But he declined to say exactly when or how the committee would change the system. “It’s a jerry-built kind of creature that defies common sense,” he said. “So what I’m going to do when I talk to the senators is I’m going to push for the boldest, best bill possible. And I think senators are going to do it because I think they recognize that healthcare is far and away the most important issue.” Separately, Wyden said he was “certainly looking at” a bill from Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders that would require Medicare to cover vision, hearing and dental care. Wyden declined to directly answer a question from States Newsroom about whether he can accomplish his policy goals while a rule remains in place that requires at least 60 senators vote to advance bills. The hurdle, known as the legislative filibuster, forces bipartisanship in the upper chamber, but could very well block Democrats from passing many of the changes they called for during the midterm campaign. Tariffs and oversight In addition to healthcare, Wyden said he plans to focus his chairmanship on taxes, trade and oversight. Wyden said he would like to permanently extend the child tax credit, a change he believes could garner President Donald Trump’s support. “Yes, unless the president wants to be against kids,” he said. “Sometimes he’s against things that I didn’t expect. But we’re going to push hard.” Wyden said he hopes to overturn the tariffs that Trump has placed on Canada by building a coalition large enough to override a veto, which would require broadly bipartisan votes in each chamber of Congress. “We’re going to push, you know, very hard to build a coalition that can handle a veto because this is Trump,” he said. “Trump’s wheelhouse has always been about this for reasons that are so perverse I can’t even, you know, kind of spell them out in plain English. But we’re going to push this very hard, and I think we’re going to have a good shot at a very strong vote and influence when we try to get this to actually change.” Wyden said he planned to advocate for a bill he’s proposed that would require billionaires “to pay a tax like everybody else.” When it comes to the committee’s oversight and investigative roles, Wyden said he planned to look into the banks that had Jeffrey Epstein as a client. “I feel very strongly about this because we’ve got three Wall Street banks who, if they had done nothing, folks, nothing except follow the law for years on end, we could have stopped Epstein cold,” he said. On healthcare, Wyden said he planned to investigate “big pharma and big insurance very closely.” The committee’s lawyers are also looking into a way to eliminate a deal Trump struck with his own administration to exempt himself from any future IRS audits. “We’re gonna try and get rid of it. And I’ve got my lawyers checking it out and I’ll have some more to say about it down the road,” he said. “But I mean, the proposition that the president of the United States doesn’t get subject to what everybody else gets is preposterous, and I’m going to do everything I can to change it. And we’re looking into what the tools and options are.”

articles.description: The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services would oversee the grants that could be funded by $170 million the state is set to get from a settlement with Meta.
articles.content: Social media companies including Meta, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, are facing a wave of lawsuits claiming the apps are harmful to kids.(Dustin Dwyer / Michigan Public )Some Michigan lawmakers are working to spend the state’s share of a multi-state settlement with Facebook’s parent company.Michigan is set to receive over $170 million as part of the agreement with Meta over the threats social media pose to kids. That would be spread out over time.The bills would create a new Social Media Settlement Fund to handle that money. The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services would then oversee the grants that the money could be spent on.State Rep. Julie Rogers (D-Kalamazoo) is a cosponsor on the bipartisan package.“We are hopeful that setting up the fund and designating some buckets that it could go into would shore up youth mental health, perhaps help with after school programs, crisis intervention programs and various things that would support their mental wellbeing,” Rogers said.Since the money isn’t all coming at once, Rogers worries lawmakers could be tempted to spend it outside of its intended purposes. That’s especially as Michigan could face some tough budget years ahead with changing federal policies.“There will continue to be cost shifting from the federal government down to states, and so I don’t want this new fund to be basically the Legislature’s piggy bank for anything under the sun,” Rogers said.The bills are coming late in the legislative term. That means it could be next year, when the next state Legislature takes over, before they move.Rogers said she and her co-sponsor, Rep. Mike Mueller (R-Linden), at least wanted to start the conversation.“I think also when you’ve introduced bills, it does get people talking and so it’s kind of putting a lens and shining a light on this issue and the settlement money and we’re hoping we can protect it for its intended purpose and use,” Rogers said.She’s joining the state Senate next term. Mueller is keeping his seat in the state House of Representatives.

articles.title: Mamdani can’t be president – but he still wants to be involved in the 2028 race
articles.content: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is jumping into the 2028 planning. Ed Reed/Mayoral Photography Office Although New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani can never be president, he clearly intends to be involved in the race – confirming a report from Axios that he has had conversations with labor union leaders about potential left-wing and labor-aligned Democratic candidates for the 2028 presidential race. He acknowledged his meetings with labor leaders at an unrelated press conference in Manhattan on Monday morning, while not revealing much about what was discussed or his preferences for an eventual Democratic nominee for president. Instead, Mamdani emphasized the importance labor has in shaping priorities for 2028. “I had sought and continue to meet with labor leaders precisely because they have been on the front lines of delivering for those working people and the importance of ensuring that the crises that affects working people are at the centerpiece of any of the politics that comes from now until 2028,” Mamdani said, when asked about his conversations regarding the 2028 presidential race. One top labor leader in the city, Hotel and Gaming Trades Council President Rich Maroko, welcomed the mayor’s interest. “Wherever we can find common ground on endorsements, we obviously want to,” Maroko said in a statement to City & State. “He’s done an incredible job of choosing candidates who share our commitment to labor and understanding the priorities of our members, and because of that, I expect there to be more opportunities where we can be aligned in the future." Though HTC supported Andrew Cuomo in the 2025 mayoral primary, Mamdani earned their support for the general election and he’s built a close relationship with the union since. Mamdani wouldn’t be the first mayor to get involved in a presidential election. Former New York City mayor Bill de Blasio attempted to host a presidential forum for candidates in 2015 before making his own failed run for the 2020 Democratic nomination. “I don’t think that there’s a tension in helping to elect Democrats and also in ensuring that we as Democrats are accountable to the very reason that working people have entrusted their faith in us once again,” Mamdani said Monday. Some think Mamdani is well positioned. “If Mandani were to choose to be very involved and play a kingmaker sort of role, he has the credibility now to do it,” said Democratic strategist Trip Yang, who did work for a pro-Mamdani super PAC in 2025. “He’s proven in his first year he can govern in New York. And he’s proven that his endorsement carries weight in New York.” Mamdani, who was born in Uganda and became a U.S. citizen in 2018, is barred from running for president himself. But Yang said that fact has given him “freedom” to get involved in other ways, including by speaking with potential candidates. It’s no secret Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are close political allies, but he’s met at least one other rumored candidate too. Rep. Ro Khanna of California, a progressive whose allies have urged him to run, recently visited City Hall for a closed-door meeting with Mamdani. But Mamdani, who has so far avoided much politicking beyond New York since stepping into City Hall, is likely keen to not be seen playing kingmaker over keeping his focus on New York City. “He really likes to be seen doing direct work and he does not like to be seen, kind of playing politics and whatnot,” Democratic consultant Ryan Adams said. Mamdani might not be the deciding factor in who makes it out of a primary for the Democratic nomination, but some still think he could be influential. “He’s become the avatar of what the Dems can be to a lot of people,” Adams said. “I hear folks all over the country saying things like ‘Mamdani is my mayor,’ which is weird to hear from a woman in Omaha.” Discussing the presidential race is another shift for Mamdani. He was heavily involved in several Democratic primary races in New York City and in Gov. Kathy Hochul’s reelection, but has largely stayed away from elections outside New York. In one exception, Mamdani attended a Brooklyn fundraiser in early October for Michigan’s now Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed. Update: The article was updated with a comment from Hotel and Gaming Trades Council President Rich Maroko. NEXT STORY: A guide to New York Republicans’ infighting

Judge sets summer 2028 trial for the man accused of killing Charlie Kirk
articles.description: Judge sets summer 2028 trial for the man accused of killing Charlie Kirk AP News MICHAEL RUIZ: Tyler Robinson judge to give long-awaited trial date ruling in assassination of Charlie Kirk Fox News Charlie Kirk murder suspect Tyler Robinson faces 2028 trial USA Today Judge sets trial date for Charlie Kirk’s accused killer for summer 2028 CNN Charlie Kirk's accused killer set to stand trial for aggravated murder in Jun
articles.content: PROVO, Utah (AP) — The man accused of assassinating conservative activist Charlie Kirk will stand trial in the summer of 2028, a Utah judge ruled Monday. Attorneys for defendant Tyler Robinson, 23, proposed a trial starting in 2029. But District Judge Tony Graf faced pressure from Kirk’s family and supporters, including President Donald Trump, to speed up court proceedings that already have lasted more than a year. Robinson has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in the killing of Kirk, 31, as the activist spoke to several thousand people at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025. Robinson could face the death penalty if convicted. Graf allocated 105 days for the trial, beginning with jury selection on June 21, 2028. He said the dates balance Robinson’s right to prepare his defense with the rights of Kirk’s widow, Erika Kirk, to a speedy resolution. Erika Kirk’s attorney disagreed with the schedule but said there is no choice but to accept it. “A trial in the summer of 2028, three years after Charlie’s assassination, does not feel very speedy to the Kirk family,” attorney Jeffrey Neiman told the judge. He had argued the trial should start next October. In a statement after Monday’s hearing, the Kirk family characterized Graf’s decision as a “delay” and said, “every additional day without justice prolongs our family’s pain.” Robinson’s defense team declined to comment after the hearing. The defendant turned himself in a day after the shooting. His lawyers have not offered alternative theories for Kirk’s death. Prosecutors had said they could be ready for trial by October 2027. Rather than hold the proceedings during the Thanksgiving and Christmas holidays, they proposed a January 2028 start date. Kirk helped galvanize young voters around Trump during the 2024 election. Trump weighed in on the trial in a social media post last month, saying Robinson should be tried “within a month.” The Republican president criticized Graf, a former prosecutor appointed judge last year, for “taking forever to ask questions that people already know the answer to.” Utah County prosecutors allege Robinson targeted Kirk for his political beliefs. They say a bullet found in the rifle used to kill Kirk was engraved with the words “Hey Facist! CATCH!” and that Robinson wrote in a text message about Kirk: “I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can’t be negotiated out.” Robinson’s attorneys said in court documents that they must sift through tens of thousands of files turned over by prosecutors. They plan to conduct extensive investigations into Robinson’s life in search of mitigating factors that could influence his sentence if convicted. Defense attorneys have said they will conduct surveys to see if it’s possible to seat an impartial jury in Utah County. Depending on the results, they may ask to hold the trial elsewhere. The judge said he will hear arguments about the venue next December. Associated Press journalist Matthew Brown contributed from Billings, Montana.

Hotel giant Wyndham exposed customer data after app security lapse
articles.description: Exclusive: Wyndham left a hardcoded credential in its customer app, allowing anyone to access customer data. The hotel giant wouldn't say if it has the ability to check for any past unauthorized access.
articles.content: Hotel and resort giant Wyndham has acknowledged a cybersecurity incident after a good-faith security researcher discovered a bug that allowed anyone to access customers’ personal information. Security researcher Robert Wiggins at What Security exclusively told TechCrunch that he found a password inside the source code of Wyndham’s Android app, which granted access to an internal company database, hosted by tech company Salesforce. Wiggins told TechCrunch that the credential exposed personal information including customer names, email addresses, and Wyndham member numbers. The database also stores customer login tokens (called JWTs) that keep customers logged-in to their apps without having to repeatedly enter their own passwords. The database also contained Wyndham files and documents. According to Wiggins, the database had millions of entries, but he was unable to determine an accurate number of exposed customer records. Wyndham touts some 129 million enrolled rewards members. The researcher said Wyndham has no way to report security flaws, and asked for TechCrunch’s help in alerting the company. Soon after TechCrunch made contact with Wyndham’s cybersecurity staff, the exposed credential was revoked, preventing any further access to the database. “Our team has taken steps to address the issue,” a Wyndham spokesperson told TechCrunch. “Our security teams have no evidence of any unauthorized access,” the statement added, without providing any further details about the claim. Wyndham’s spokesperson would not say, when asked, whether the company had the technical means, such as server logs, to determine if anyone had access to the customer database prior to Wiggins’ discovery. TechCrunch also asked Wyndham whether it planned to notify customers whose information was exposed, or disclose the incident to U.S. regulators, such as filing a notice with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, as public companies are required to do for material cybersecurity incidents. Wyndham would not say. Wyndham’s spokesperson also would not say for how long the password was embedded in its customer app, or how Wyndham plans to ship a long-term fix for the app. App and software developers generally avoid including passwords or credentials in publicly released software and apps — a process known as “hardcoding” — as anyone with a copy of the software can extract the password and use it to access its associated server or database. Given the simplicity with which credentials can be abused by anyone, many cases of hardcoded credentials are automatically scored with a maximum vulnerability severity rating. For Wiggins, this is his second public discovery of hardcoded credentials in two weeks, after finding a near-identical vulnerability in Applebee’s app that exposed customer data. Wiggins relied on AI tools for both discoveries, which make it easier to identify simple security weaknesses, such as hardcoded credentials, by scouring thousands of lines of decompiled app code every second. When asked about Wyndham’s response, Wiggins told TechCrunch that he was glad the company fixed the issue, but noted that without visibility into any past activity, someone with malicious intent could have leaked large amounts of customers’ personal information. The company would not say whether it planned to set up a vulnerability disclosure program to allow outside security researchers and hackers to privately report security vulnerabilities. Michael Francess, Wyndham’s cybersecurity director who responded to the incident, told TechCrunch that researchers can alert [email protected] with details of potential security issues. The company’s spokesperson would not say whether it plans to change its website to allow researchers to alert the company. This is the latest known security incident at Wyndham in recent years. In 2024, a security researcher found several Wyndham hotel check-in desks were running remote-access spyware that was leaking screenshots of guest records and booking information to the open web. Soon after our reporting, the spyware app found on the hotel computers, called pcTattletale, was hacked and its banks of customer data stolen, forcing the company’s owner, Bryan Fleming, to shut down the company. Fleming, a former resident of Michigan, was later arrested by federal authorities and convicted of making, selling, and advertising unlawful spyware. For East Lansing Band Students, the Lessons Go Beyond Music
articles.description: Unlike other school subjects, technology can't provide shortcuts for band students. Struggling and eventually figuring it out is good for students, teachers say.
articles.content: David Larzelere and Holly Thornton manage classrooms of more than 70 students, helping young musicians turn dissonance into harmony while teaching them skills and lessons that extend far beyond the band room. Larzelere is an East Lansing High School alumnus — class of 1995 — and is in his 17th year of teaching at ELHS. Thornton taught for eight years in Okemos before becoming the band teacher at MacDonald Middle School four years ago. Together, they create spaces for students seeking community and a shared passion for music. In a joint interview with East Lansing Info, the two spoke about the programs they lead, the students they teach and the rewards of helping young musicians discover their potential. For both, a career in education seemed almost preordained. “I come from a long line of teachers in my family,” Larzelere said. “Both my grandparents were teachers. My mom was a teacher. My aunt was a teacher. And so that was something that was kind of in my blood. When I graduated from high school, I really was more focused on being a performer. I really wanted to be a professional trumpet player.” An impactful student teaching experience, however, helped him discover what he called “a better path.” Thornton said she always knew she would become a teacher, but it was her own music teacher who inspired her to pursue music education. She wanted to create that same experience for other children. While Larzelere began playing the piano before dabbling in trumpet and saxophone, Thornton fell in love with the French horn and had no reason to look elsewhere. Both inherited strong music programs, which they’ve had opportunities to make their own. Despite their shared commitment to education, the two acknowledge that their classrooms operate quite differently from those of colleagues who teach math, science or social studies. Thornton said band instruction is teacher-led about 99% of the time, whereas other classrooms might alternate between whole-group instruction, individual work and small-group activities. “If we’re not leading the class or facilitating [or] playing together, we really can’t all learn at the same time,” she said. “It’s just too noisy and too chaotic, so it’s very teacher-led. It’s a little more responsive and adaptable, but has the benefit of being a bit more customizable.” Unlike teachers working through a set curriculum, Thornton said she doesn’t necessarily know how long it will take students to master a particular piece of music. “We just want to perform at a high level and give kids a great experience,” she said. “But it means that we’re sort of cultivating the curriculum as we go, always adapting and modifying to the students who are in front of us and to what they can do, and what music we’re preparing for the performance schedule, as well.” And while band requires discipline and dedication, neither teacher believes students need to demonstrate musical aptitude before joining. Thornton said students aren’t required to pass an audition or test to participate. Teachers might help determine which instrument is best suited for a student, but they don’t turn children away based on their abilities. “We’re certainly willing to give every kid a chance who has the desire to want to learn to be a musician,” Larzelere said. “For a student who’s starting band [class] and just wants to get in there as a beginner,” Thornton added, “they just need to care and try. They just want to try and do the thing because it’s not an easy task to learn how to read music and play an instrument. It’s hard for kids to tolerate being bad at something, and to keep trying and persevere and push through. And that growth is one of the best parts about my job, seeing them go from no concept of how to do it to being able to play a whole song, or a whole melody, and play in front of the class.” Larzelere said band is one of the few remaining places where students can’t rely on technology, instant gratification or shortcuts to achieve success. “There’s no app,” he said. “You just gotta put in the work, put in the time and keep trying your best.” He said students who are successful in band often demonstrate the same skills that help them succeed elsewhere in school. “They can sit and listen to a teacher for five minutes, and then you say, ‘hey, can you do this,’ and they do that, and they have the executive skills to kind of function in a classroom.” But learning those skills, and developing the confidence to use them, doesn’t happen overnight. “There’s just something really valuable about making kids do something hard,” Larzelere said. “I think when you put kids in a situation that’s challenging and then give them support so that they can be successful, to me, that’s how you build self confidence for a student and how you’re giving them skills. There’s always going to be hard [times] in life, and if you can teach them how to get through those hard things, that is going to then help them as they develop into human beings. “Giving them the skills and the coping mechanisms to get through situations like that, I think, is invaluable.” Thornton sees those lessons unfold in her classroom, sometimes in the smallest moments. She said that no matter how well she’s teaching, there will always be a student struggling to understand something. But watching that student finally succeed is among the most rewarding parts of her job. “When someone is kind of struggling, struggling, and then they figure it out, that first time a beginner trumpet player gets their G out, that first time they can play the line and everybody claps for them because they really finally did it, and they’ve tried a bunch of times in a row,” she said. “The struggle is worth it. Like, I will often say to kids, it’s not easy, but it’s always worth it.” Support outside the classroom can also make a significant difference. Thornton said parents who encourage their children’s musical pursuits, help them obtain instruments and remind them to practice play an important role in their success. “It certainly helps to have somebody who’s going to rent you an instrument and to remind you to practice,” she said. “I myself have two kids who are taking piano lessons, and I struggle to get them to practice sometimes. So we know that that’s real. We’re all busy. There’s a lot of activities.” For families unable to afford rental instruments, Thornton said the program provides assistance to ensure that students who want to participate have the opportunity. Beyond the music itself, both teachers see band class as a place where students develop relationships, find community and discover a sense of belonging. “Band and music is a place where kids belong, where they have a community, and where they kind of find their own growth and confidence in connection with others,” Thornton said. Those connections can last well beyond graduation. Both teachers said they stay in touch with former students. Larzelere said he keeps up with graduates through Facebook and enjoys seeing former ELHS musicians perform in college marching bands. “I think I have three [former students] right now that are actually teaching music and I have one student who is in a graduate school for performance,” he said, “and he will be a professional bassoon player. He’s an outstanding musician.” The teachers credit the East Lansing community for helping sustain the district’s strong music programs. “The East Lansing community has always been supportive of the arts program,” Larzelere said. “[Like] budget cuts, I’ve been here 17 years and it’s never even in the back of my mind that this community is not going to be supportive of our music program and performing arts programs in East Lansing.” The East Lansing Band and Orchestra Parent Association, a booster organization, raises funds and provides volunteers to support the programs. Both teachers said that support reflects a broader appreciation for music and the arts throughout the district. “It’s one of the cooler things about this district, though, that it is so collaborative,” Thornton said. “I was just explaining this to my student teacher today, that it’s nice that we’re not positioned in opposition to each other, that it really is instrumental music, and just trying to support each other. We’re just celebrating music and kids who want to.” Do you have a question that you would like ELi to investigate? Just click here! articles.title: The race is on to sue Nvidia
articles.description: Nvidia’s stock slid more than 4% after its board opened an investigation into Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, and one securities law expert says the company’s earlier insistence that it was all “normal” could turn into a very expensive problem.
articles.content: Nvidia’s stock slid more than 4% on Monday, the first trading day after its board said it would investigate CEO Jensen Huang over his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive U.S. intelligence believes was spying for China. Securities lawyers were already moving. At least four firms, including Schall, Brown & Schwartz and Levi & Korsinsky, announced investigations Monday into whether Nvidia misled investors. Robert Bartlett, a Stanford Law professor and securities law expert, expects them to have plenty of company. “I would definitely wager that there’ll be a filing,” Bartlett said in an interview Monday morning, adding that he wouldn’t be surprised if a case had been filed by the end of the day. Plaintiffs’ lawyers have good reasons to be first in line; under federal securities law, the first complaint triggers a public notice, and investors then have 60 days to ask the court to be named lead plaintiff. A firm that files early gets a head start on signing up investors with large losses, as well as on shaping the story of the case. Bartlett was right, in fact. A case surfaced Monday afternoon in the Northern District of California, where Nvidia is headquartered. Rosen Law Firm, a New York-based plaintiffs’ firm that specializes in securities class actions, filed it on behalf of Mark Kistenmacher, a retail investor who made seven purchases totaling roughly $20,500 this year, according to a schedule attached to the complaint. (Rosen was lead counsel in a $250 million settlement with Alibaba and ranks among the most active filers of such cases.) The proposed class covers anyone who bought Nvidia securities between Oct. 9, 2025, and Nov. 8, 2026, and the suit names both Nvidia and Huang. The complaint accuses them of misleading investors about Huang’s ties to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center outfit where Alice Huang was considered a top exec, and it points to three statements as proof: Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo’s late-October claim that Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected,” the company’s even earlier claim that it found “no evidence of diversion” of its chips, and Jensen Huang’s Oct. 30 comment to Bloomberg that Nvidia’s dealings with Megaspeed were “normal and not unusual.” All three were false or misleading, the suit says, because Huang was having an affair with Alice Huang. Kistenmacher is asking for unspecified damages, interest and attorneys’ fees, and he wants a jury trial. While much remains unknown, the legal theory here doesn’t depend on anything the board’s investigation may turn up about Huang’s private life. When The New York Times first reported on Huang’s ties to Alice Huang last month, Rizzo really did tell the Times that the relationship was “not unusual or unexpected.” Rizzo separately told another outlet, The Hill, that “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” Of course, the world now knows that was not true. Worse, the Times reports that U.S. intelligence had been monitoring Alice Huang for more than a year. From a securities perspective, Bartlett said, the company’s earlier statement was “clearly a misleading statement.” And because Huang is CEO, Bartlett said, “his knowledge gets imputed to the company.” In other words, Nvidia is treated as having known what its chief executive knew. The Kistenmacher complaint makes the same argument. Bartlett predicted a “classic fraud on the market” claim, in which investors argue they paid prices that reflected false or incomplete public information, and lost money when the truth emerged. This early lawsuit relies on that theory, and Monday’s drop of $7.97 per share, or 4.27%, gives the attorneys involved a lot to work with. Damages in such cases are tied to the stock’s decline, and Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world, so you can imagine a settlement could prove exceedingly expensive. That means a large payment from the company and its directors-and-officers insurers, but typically no personal consequences for the CEO or the board. It is also a civil matter, so Huang isn’t facing prison over it. The irony, as Bartlett noted, is that the suit is brought in the name of Nvidia’s shareholders, and shareholders ultimately pay for the settlement, directly or through insurance premiums. Bartlett sorted Nvidia’s wider exposure into buckets. The first is the securities fraud claim, which is the clearest immediate problem for the company and potentially for Huang. The second is governance: what the board knew and when. It’s possible directors were kept in the dark, but the board also has oversight duties, and once the Times began reporting on the Megaspeed connection, the company should have had reporting lines to bring a critical risk like this to directors. If it didn’t, or if directors didn’t act, board-level liability is possible. A third category, one that would change everything, would arise only if the board’s investigation finds Huang knew about the intelligence connection. That would be “a whole other ball game,” as Bartlett said. (The board said in a statement to the public Sunday that it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.) There’s also the question of government action. The SEC can seek an officer-and-director bar for intentional securities-fraud violations, which Bartlett said is technically on the table. But he doubts the current SEC under Chairman Paul Atkins would have the appetite, given President Trump’s support for Huang. A roughly two-year clock after discovery of the facts would leave room for a future administration to act, but the window would be tight, and Bartlett posited that’s pretty unlikely when asked about it. It’s worth underscoring that neither law firm announcements nor this newly filed complaint is a sign of a strong case. Plaintiffs’ firms are quick to publish these notices when they see an opportunity. Which firm winds up leading the case is decided later by the court, and that decision usually depends on which investor has suffered the biggest loss. Kistenmacher said in his filing that he’s willing to serve as lead plaintiff, but the court will ultimately choose among the competing investors. No doubt they’ll materialize soon. articles.title: Democrats flip Georgia state House, giving them new control of at least 12 legislative chambers
articles.description: Democrats flip Georgia state House, giving them new control of at least 12 legislative chambers AP News Democrats officially win control of Georgia state House with slim majority Georgia Recorder Georgia Republicans lost power in a rout. Now what? The Atlanta Journal-Constitution Midterm election upsets give Democrats narrow majority in Georgia House for first time in decades CBS News VIEWPOINT: Looking at the afterm
articles.content: Democrats have taken control of the state House in Georgia after also gaining the governor’s office in last week’s midterm election, giving the party control of each for the first time in more than 20 years. The flip gives Democrats control of at least 12 new legislative chambers across the U.S. after their major gains at all levels. It’s the biggest gain for either party in a single election since the Republicans took the majority in 20 chambers in 2010 amid the Great Recession and the rise of the conservative tea party movement. After officials are sworn in later this year and in early 2027, Democrats will have trifectas — control of both legislative chambers and the governor’s office — in at least six states where they’re currently sharing power with Republicans. The party running a state government can have a major impact on issues including tax bills, how data center development goes and who qualifies for Medicaid health insurance. The Associated Press, which has been calling elections since 1848, on Monday determined the outcome of enough Georgia races to declare Democrats had won the lower chamber. The news organization has not yet determined who will control the state Senate in North Carolina or either chamber in Alaska. Republicans have controlled the House in Georgia since 2005 and both the Senate and governor’s office since 2003. Democrats have made gains. In 2020, for instance, Joe Biden narrowly won a plurality in the presidential election there and Democrats prevailed in both U.S. Senate elections. Donald Trump won there in both 2016 and 2024. This year, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governorship and Democrats took control of a House in which Republicans had a comfortable 99-80 majority heading into the election. As of Monday, Democrats had won 91 House seats and Republicans 86. Three had not been called — including one where the state’s secretary of state is investigating the late upload of a memory card containing nearly 400 votes. While the split government will likely block Democrats from passing some laws, it does open many topics to negotiations. In North Carolina, Democrats have taken hold of the House and kept the office of governor, where Josh Stein’s term has two more years. As of Monday, the AP hadn’t called one race in the Senate. If the GOP holds it, the party would have a 26-24 majority. A Democratic victory would mean a tie, and Lt. Gov. Rachel Hunt, a Democrat, would hold the tiebreaking vote. Both legislative chambers in Alaska currently are controlled by multiparty coalitions. With several races not called, it’s unclear how that will shake out for 2027. The AP has also not called the race for governor between Democrat Jonathan Kreiss‑Tomkins and Republican Bernadette Wilson. Currently, there are Republican governors in 26 states and Democratic governors in 24. Democrats will have at least 28 of those jobs next year, with the race in Kansas also remaining to be called. Democrats gained control of four more state Senates in Arizona, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, bringing the total they lead to 24. They’ll have the majority in at least 27 lower chambers, up from 19, after flips in Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Texas and Wisconsin. Election gains in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin will give Democrats trifectas in all those states. This article has been corrected to show that Democrats gained control of the state Senate in Arizona, not Nevada.

articles.title: Pope urges Argentina to protect the vulnerable from Milei’s austerity measures
articles.description: Pope urges Argentina to protect the vulnerable from Milei’s austerity measures AP News In Argentina, Pope Leo Walks in the Giant Shadow of Francis The New York Times Pope urges Argentines to follow model of saints during Mass in the ‘land of saints’ The Hill Pope Leo urges Argentinians to proclaim Christ with joy Vatican News A Missionary Pope Faces a Chain Saw-Wielding Populist in Argentina WSJ
articles.content: BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — Pope Leo XIV delivered a sweeping tribute to the dignity of workers before Argentina’s labor and business leaders Monday in what critics of Argentine President Javier Milei took as a rebuke to his libertarian agenda, capping a day that began at a disability home struggling under his government’s spending cuts. The two politically charged stops bookended Leo’s first Mass in Argentina, which the Vatican said drew an estimated 2.5 million people — the largest crowd of his papacy. His visit has electrified this predominantly Catholic country that had not hosted a papal visit in nearly four decades. Leo’s Argentine predecessor, Pope Francis, never once returned home during his 12-year papacy, a decision widely attributed to his wariness of being pulled into his nation’s deep political divide. Leo, an American with no such personal stake, waded into the fray Monday, channeling Francis with a subtle but unmistakable reminder of Catholic social teaching. The hall erupted when he invoked Francis’ famous “three Ts” of social justice: “tierra, techo y trabajo,” or land, housing and work. “To deprive a person of work is not simply to deny that person an income,” Leo said at the Catholic University of Argentina. “It severely wounds their dignity, deprives them of the ability to contribute to society and plunges them into social exclusion.” The audience brought together union leaders who have staged general strikes against Milei and industrialists battered by cheap imports since his government scrapped trade barriers. Also in attendance were informal workers, whose share of the labor force has climbed from 41% when Milei took office to 45%, as mass layoffs and a sputtering economy have wiped out formal jobs. Most poignantly, there were the “cartoneros,” the Argentine trash pickers and recyclers who had a pride of place during Francis’ papacy. Opposition leaders heard a pope taking Milei to task. “Let them listen to him, those who have closed their ears,” said Buenos Aires province Gov. Axel Kicillof, the most powerful elected figure in the left-leaning Peronist opposition. Milei has praised the pope’s message while steering clear of its substance. He called Leo’s speech to Argentine officials on Sunday, which defended pensioners and public universities squeezed by his cuts, “outstanding,” with “many elements of great value.” He declined to elaborate, saying he did not want to “fall into the mud of using the speech politically.” Union leaders said Leo’s speech amounted to vindication of their fight. “At a time when we Argentines are living through such an assault on our living conditions, which are deteriorating day by day, it is a breath of encouragement to keep resisting, to keep fighting,” said Hugo Godoy, secretary-general of the Autonomous Argentine Workers’ Central, one of the country’s main labor federations. But Leo’s itinerary spoke for itself. His first stop Monday was the Cottolengo Don Orione, a sprawling “city of charity” south of Buenos Aires that houses more than 400 people with disabilities. Residents and staff wept as he arrived, and he embraced people in wheelchairs. He told them their lives were a blessing, not a burden. “A nation’s progress is also measured by how it welcomes all people with disabilities and particular needs,” he said. Milei’s government has withheld much of the funding for disability care despite a law Congress passed over his veto last year to restore it, prompting protests from Argentina’s Catholic bishops. As the cash-strapped home drew international attention ahead of Leo’s visit, authorities paid it about $535,000 for medicine, diapers and food, covering four of the 12 months it is owed, said Fernando Montero, who oversees its disability services. The Senate is due to consider legislation in the coming days that would earmark money for disability benefits in next year’s budget. “The people here deserve this grace,” said Kuyen Rolon Rey, a volunteer. “Choosing such a small place, but big if measured with love, makes us very happy.” Leo used the speech at the Catholic University to push back on core tenets of Milei’s libertarian creed, insisting that private property is “always subject to a social mortgage.” “Wherever the domination of a few becomes the rule, work is turned into the exploitation of all components of the work community, and workers end up being valued solely for their efficiency,” Leo said. For many in the room, that described life under Milei. “We are going through times when work is seen as an expense or a loss, as though people forget that behind every worker there is a family and human beings who feel, live and think,” Sabrina Soledad Sapone, a union delegate, told the pope at the gathering. Leo hailed labor unions, which have led the fight against Milei’s free-market overhaul, as “indispensable institutions when they defend those who have no voice.” He also defended informal workers’ movements, which Milei’s government has barred from distributing welfare payments alleging that they foster dependency on the state. Waste pickers, farmers and artisans “do not passively wait for state assistance,” Leo said. “They organize themselves from the grassroots to build community-based solutions.” Leo — who took his name partly in response to the AI revolution — warned that “artificial intelligence and unregulated automation can put countless jobs at risk,” and called on governments to shield workers just as Milei, who opposes regulating the technology, courts billions of dollars in AI investment. On a day when Leo was clearly honoring the social justice legacy of Francis, the American pope paid spiritual homage to his predecessor by praying before a plaque in his honor in his former cathedral, surrounded by children. Thousands arrived at midnight to claim a spot at the Monumento a los Españoles, where St. John Paul II celebrated Argentina’s last papal Mass in 1987. The government declared a national holiday so people could attend. Milei and his sister, Karina Milei, the secretary-general of the presidency, sat in the VIP seats. In his homily, Leo said Argentine families face joblessness, violence and addiction but remain the bedrock of society. “Do not give in to those who dismiss the Christian family as outdated,” he said. “On the contrary, today more than ever, it remains a pillar amid the many insecurities of our time.” Isabel Martín, 73, who came with her parish group, said she was praying for Leo to “touch the heart” of Milei, whose spending cuts have also hit pensioners hard. “The pope was very specific in his message yesterday,” she said, referring to Leo’s inaugural speech with Milei. “The weakest cannot be the ones carrying the burden of the adjustment, especially poor retirees. If anyone can make him reconsider, it’s the pope.” Argentina’s minimum pension is about $300, roughly a quarter of what an older adult needs to cover medicine, housing and food. Leo’s message also resonated with younger Argentines, who have shown the sharpest decline in Catholic practice of any age group. Margarita Lanús, who turned 16 on Monday, shared a birthday cake on the sidewalk with her family while waiting for the Mass. “I really like that he says things as they are,” she said. “He goes straight to the point.” Associated Press religion coverage receives support through the AP’s collaboration with The Conversation US, with funding from Lilly Endowment Inc.
