articles.title: FDA Approves First Factor Xla Inhibitor to Help Prevent Stroke in Certain Adults at High Risk
articles.description: FDA today approved Sunharbo (asundexian) 50 mg tablets, the first factor XIa (FXIa) inhibitor for use in combination with antiplatelet therapy to reduce the risk of stroke in adults following a recent mild-to-moderate non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or a high-risk transient ischemic attack.
articles.content: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved Sunharbo (asundexian) 50 mg tablets, the first factor XIa (FXIa) inhibitor for use in combination with antiplatelet therapy to reduce the risk of stroke in adults following a recent mild-to-moderate non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke (a stroke caused by a clot that did not originate in the heart) or a high-risk transient ischemic attack (TIA), often called a “mini-stroke.” “Stroke is a leading cause of disability and death in the United States, and survivors are at risk of having another stroke,” said Hylton V. Joffe, M.D., MMSc, Director of the Office of Cardiology, Hematology, Endocrinology, and Nephrology in the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. “Today’s approval represents a meaningful advance for patients and health care providers seeking a new option for secondary stroke prevention.” The effectiveness of Sunharbo was demonstrated in the OCEANIC-STROKE study, a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 study that enrolled 12,327 adults. Participants had a recent non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke (NIH Stroke Scale ≤15) or high-risk TIA and were randomly assigned to Sunharbo or placebo within 72 hours of symptom onset. Both groups also received antiplatelet therapy. Sunharbo 50 mg once daily significantly reduced the risk of ischemic stroke by 26% compared to placebo over a median treatment of 14.2 months. The overall rate of major bleeding was similar between the Sunharbo and placebo groups but was increased with Sunharbo in patients older than 75 years and during the first 90 days of treatment. Gastrointestinal bleeding occurred more commonly with Sunharbo compared to placebo. The most frequently reported adverse reaction (occurring in 3% or greater of Sunharbo-treated patients) was diarrhea. Concomitant use with medicines that are combined P-gp and strong CYP3A4 inducers (such as carbamazepine) is not recommended because these medicines may decrease Sunharbo’s effectiveness. Sunharbo is not recommended in patients with moderate or severe hepatic impairment. Sunharbo should be withheld at least 24 hours before elective surgery or invasive procedures and for at least 24 hours after thrombolysis for acute ischemic stroke. Sunharbo is not approved for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation. The FDA granted Sunharbo Fast Track and Priority Review designations. The approval was granted to Bayer HealthCare Pharmaceuticals Inc., Whippany, N.J. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products.

Ohio State suspends fraternity while investigating a video showing men engulfed in flames
articles.description: Ohio State suspends fraternity while investigating a video showing men engulfed in flames AP News Video shows men on fire at OSU fraternity event WSYX Ohio State University investigating fraternity after video appears to show two people on fire NBC News Ohio State students voice concern after fraternity suspended 10TV Men Set on Fire at Ohio State University Receiving Treatment for Burns Firehouse.com
articles.content: COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — A fraternity at Ohio State University has been temporarily suspended while authorities investigate a video that appears to show two panicked men engulfed in flames. A video shared on social media shows a large group of people standing outside, many wearing the school’s red and white colors, laughing and shouting while a man sits on the ground with his sweatpants on fire. He then lunges at a second person and tackles him. The second man’s clothing also catches fire, and they both roll on the ground removing their clothes as several onlookers intervene. One appears to be holding a small fire extinguisher. University spokesperson Benjamin Johnson said the school has placed Sigma Alpha Epsilon fraternity on interim suspension while it investigates, and has referred the matter to university and Columbus police. The university did not say how the fraternity is linked to the event, whether the burned men are students or what condition they were in Monday. “The university is aware of this extremely concerning incident, and the individuals in question are receiving medical care,” Johnson said in a statement. “Ohio State is committed to a safe and healthy environment and expects students and student organizations to uphold that commitment and the university’s values.” Columbus Police Sgt. Joe Albert said it appears the matter took place on Saturday. Police did not receive any calls for service at the location, but someone called police Sunday evening reporting that the video was circulating online, he said. Steve Mitchell, CEO of Sigma Alpha Epsilon, said behavior that violates its high standards has no place in its organization and it will take appropriate action to hold those responsible accountable based on the investigation. “We take this matter seriously and are actively investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident while working closely with university officials and local law enforcement,” he said in a statement. More than 60,000 students are enrolled at the university. The episode comes as fraternities are back in the national spotlight in the wake of a former Cornell University student’s lawsuit saying she was gang raped at a fraternity party in 2024. Ramer reported from Concord, New Hampshire.

articles.title: Q&A: Michigan’s next House speaker wants ‘transformational’ change
articles.description: Democrat Ranjeev Puri, the next speaker of the Michigan House, wants to enact bold policies but to bring ‘normalcy’ back to Lansing. Here’s what he told us.
articles.content: State Rep. Ranjeev Puri, the current House minority leader and Canton Democrat, will be the state House Speaker next term As speaker, Puri says he hopes to ‘return some normalcy’ to the chamber after a historically unproductive session House Democrats will have a 63-seat majority starting in 2027, their largest margin in decades LANSING — Michigan Democrats, who won full control of the Legislature in last week’s election, have a “mandate” to try to lower costs and grow the state’s population, according to incoming House Speaker Ranjeev Puri. “I don’t want to see us focus on who’s playing in what sport, or who’s using which restroom — I want us to start tackling why our household median income in Michigan is lagging behind our peer states, why our population growth is still not where it needs to be,” Puri told Bridge Michigan in an interview. “That is a sign of success, of what these two years could be.” Related: Democrats take full control of Michigan government. What to expect Michigan Dems flip three US House seats as Huizenga, Barrett fall Michigan election firsts: Muslim, LGBTQ, Democratic socialist wins The 42-year-old Canton Township Democrat will lead a 63-47 seat House majority next term, the party’s largest since 1964. Democrats ousted 10 incumbents in last week’s election, and colleagues quickly selected Puri to serve as the 80th speaker for the two-year session that begins in January. Coupled with a 23-15 majority in the Senate and incoming Gov. Jocelyn Benson, Democrats will once again enjoy full control of Lansing. Puri was part of the 2023-24 Democratic trifecta, which was the party’s first in 40 years. That session began with a flurry of activity, but Democrats crashed and burned in their final weeks as narrow margins, caucus infighting and a Republican walk-out ground the Legislature to a halt. This time around, Puri says he has a better idea on how to lead the caucus, and what Democrats’ resounding victory up and down the ballot on Nov. 3 means for Michigan. Topics are already being floated: Affordable housing, accessible healthcare, improving the state’s education system. But both Puri and Senate Majority Leader-elect Darrin Camilleri, D-Trenton, have so far been tight-lipped about what they might tackle first, particularly given budget pressures due to state and federal tax changes.Donate “These are going to be big discussions” among legislative Democrats and Benson, Camilleri told Bridge in a separate interview. “I mean, we’ve got to get on the same page, and I’m confident that we will. But these are discussions that we all need to start having.” Puri, the son of Indian immigrants, is the first Sikh American to serve in the Michigan Legislature, let alone as speaker. He worked in the auto industry, and on President Barack Obama’s campaigns, before running for office himself and has served as House minority leader the past two years. He’ll replace outgoing House Speaker Matt Hall, who won re-election last week but will not lead his caucus next term. Bridge spoke with Puri about how he plans to lead the Michigan House and what he hopes to accomplish over the next two years. The following questions and answers have been edited for clarity. Bridge: When we talked before the election, you kept a lot of policy priorities close to the chest and said you wanted to see your membership first. Now that the dust is settled, what can we expect out of House Democrats next term? Puri: It’s still kind of being fleshed out. I think a couple things are clear: One charge upfront here is to return some normalcy to this institution. It has been weaponized and led by just political divisiveness in terms of all aspects of it for the last two years, and that’s just not how the institution has been designed to work. HOW THE HOUSE FLIPPED Michigan House Democrats flipped 11 Republican-held seats in the 2026 midterm election, outing 10 incumbents in the process to give the party one of its largest chamber majorities since the 1960s. Those races include: House District 27: Democrat and former state Rep. Jaime Churches beat incumbent state Rep. Rylee Linting, R-Wyandotte, by 1,641 votes according to unofficial totals. House District 28: Democrat Sherry Berecz beat incumbent state Rep. Jamie Thompson, R-Brownstown, by 724 votes according to unofficial totals. House District 44: Democrat and former state Rep. Jim Haadsma beat incumbent state Rep. Steve Frisbie, R-Battle Creek, by 2,301 votes according to unofficial totals. House District 46: Democrat Jan Maino beat incumbent state Rep. Kathy Schmaltz, R-Jackson, by 2,829 votes according to unofficial totals. House District 54: Democrat Sarah Pounds beat Republican Roman Gaskey for a seat currently held by state Rep. Donni Steele, who did not seek reelection and instead successfully ran for state Senate. Pounds beat Gaskey by 2,823 votes according to unofficial totals. House District 55: Democrat Alex Hawkins beat incumbent state Rep. Mark Tisdel, R-Rochester Hills, by 1,728 votes according to unofficial totals. House District 57: Democrat Tom Turner beat incumbent state Rep. Tom Kuhn, R-Troy, by 292 votes according to unofficial totals. House District 58: Democrat Katrina Manetta beat incumbent state Rep. Ron Robinson, R-Utica, by 2,109 votes according to unofficial totals. House District 68: Democrat Matt Schlinker beat incumbent state Rep. David Martin, R-Davison, by 1,274 votes according to unofficial totals. House District 86: Democrat Joseph McClusky beat incumbent state Rep. Nancy DeBoer, R-Holland, by 1,604 votes according to unofficial totals. House District 109: Democrat Anna Aho Rink beat incumbent state Rep. Karl Bohnak, R-Deerton, by 3,202 votes according to unofficial totals. The institution is not a place in which you enact policy only for the people that vote for you. It has been designed to make sure that we’re doing the people’s business, making sure that we’re making people’s lives better… kind of returning to the norm of how (the Legislature) is supposed to run, and expanding the funnel of not artificially creating rules that it’s going to be the least productive legislature of all time — again, just unnecessary. I guess I shouldn’t say it that way. It’s just a stark contrast to just how I envision leading the institution. How do you see yourself leading the House? Puri: We’re going to be charged with enacting whatever policies we can at the state level to hopefully supplement the work that these newfound majorities, Democratic majorities, at the federal level can do to kind of thwart these failed economic policies (of the Trump administration). So, I think that will be kind of a big part of our agenda. I have 26 new members coming in. My approach to leadership has always been decentralized. I’m not someone that has to make everything about me. And, in that same vein, I made a kind of pledge to these new members that they’re going to have an equal share in the kind of agenda that we craft. And so, I didn’t really focus beyond Nov. 3 for the last three, six, nine months. I mean my mind, my team, all of our resources were laser focused on delivering, winning, as most seats as we possibly could on Nov. 3. I am thrilled with that outcome, and now we shift that focus to crafting an agenda that is going to meet this moment, that is going to be something that — again, all members of our caucus can have a role in making sure that their perspectives are shared. And then we’re going to do that work, obviously, alongside the new Democratic trifecta of Governor Benson, Lieutenant Governor Brinks and Senate Majority Leader-elect Camilleri. The last time Democrats controlled the state Legislature and governor’s office, it ended pretty badly in the state House. What did you learn from that experience that you’re taking into this upcoming term? Puri: I learned that we needed to flip more seats, which is why we were focused on Nov. 3. Eleven red-to-blue (district) flips is the most since 1964, I’m being told — and we have a sizable majority now. And, the reality is that every term is different, right? Like, the politics, the need, the problems, challenges that are facing a state, the political environment, it all shifts so much from term to term — I mean, four years ago seems like a completely different political environment. I think the benefit that we do have is that I, one, have 26 members coming in, which leads to a sizable majority for us — and then for our returning members, we have members in their second, third, fourth and fifth terms, and so there’s just a lot of perspectives, experience and know-how of the institution and how it works. And so my charge, my job as speaker and leader of the caucus, is to make sure that …all those perspectives are brought together to enact a robust agenda that is going to actually start tackling transformational policies that can really improve the trajectory of our state. I don’t want to see us focus on who’s playing in what sport, or who’s using which restroom — I want us to start tackling why our household median income in Michigan is lagging behind our peer states, why our population growth is still not where it needs to be. That is a sign of success, of what these two years could be. Gov.-elect Benson has already identified early priorities for her administration, including passage of a Michigan-specific Voting Rights Act and voluntarily opening up her office to public records requests through the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). Are those priorities the House will see through? Puri: The Voting Rights Act remains a priority for the House Democrats. …We haven’t gotten into individual policies yet as a caucus. We plan to have a lot of forums to be able to do that over the next couple months, in terms of retreats and offsites and all sorts of just creating an environment for all those perspectives to be shared. On the question about FOIA, obviously, I think government works best when we are enacting policy that leads to more transparency and anti-corruption, and so (I) look forward to working with the governor and the Senate on just open records legislation. But you know the logistics of FOIA, and the framework for 110 elected officials, is very different from the governor and for one office. articles.title: Michigan can reap billions by expanding trails and greenways, study finds
articles.description: Greenways and trails have become more popular in promoting community connectivity and ecotourism, but the network should be expanded in Michigan and the Great Lakes region, recent study says.
articles.content: LANSING — Greenways and trails have become more popular in promoting community connectivity and ecotourism, but the network should be expanded in Michigan and the Great Lakes region, said a recent study. Trails primarily in Southeast Michigan currently connect 45 communities, and the Great Lakes Way project is pushing to increase the number of usable greenways and sustain funding for such efforts. The study examined the Great Lakes Way, which connects people to natural resources and expands ecotourism with trails. It estimated potential economic benefits of $3.75 billion to $5 billion annually by fostering connected trail tourism and expanding ecotourism in the region. It appeared in the journal Eco-Tourism and Sustainable Development. Involved in the project are the Great Lakes Institute for Environmental Research in Windsor, Ontario, and the PEA Group headquartered in Auburn Hills. PEA Group is a collective of engineers, surveyors and landscape architects who work to revitalize communities in Michigan, bordering states and Ontario. As of now, there are 160 miles of greenways and 156 miles of “blueways”— watertrails — in the project. Around 65% of trail miles are usable, said John Hartig, a coauthor of the study and science-policy advisor for the International Association of Great Lakes Research and Great Lakes Institute for Environmental Research. Related: Bridge readers list Au Sable among Michigan’s best rivers. Who else won? Michigan communities invest millions in their rivers. Will it bring returns? 10 years after Michigan took over Belle Isle, Detroit takes stock Petoskey committed to saving access to ‘Miracle Mile’ trail section E-motos, sometimes mistaken for e-bikes, causing trouble on Michigan trails The original question, Hartig said, was “What if they were to connect a region with an interconnected set of greenways from Port Huron to Toledo, Ohio? It was a tall order, but that is the Great Lakes Way.” It is “the trail of trails,” he said. Hartig said the project grew from a two-decade-long greenways initiative but communities could not reach their funding goals and projects fell through. After these concerns were addressed by the Community Foundation for Southeast Michigan, $25 million was raised to help match greenways grants.Donate The Detroit Greenways Coalition has been an active member of the project’s advisory committee, said Todd Scott, its executive director. The Detroit Riverwalk between Gabriel Richard Park and Ralph Wilson Park, west of downtown, sits across the river from Windsor, Ontario. (Ella Miller/Bridge Michigan) “Our biggest concern is that it wouldn’t be designed to the best,” Scott said. “It would be easy for communities to take the easier route and do something that’s not really appropriate for a facility like this, like having bikes on sidewalks.” According to the project’s 2021-24 progress report, initiatives involved St. Clair County’s Bridge to Bay Trail, the Downriver Linked Greenways, the Huron Waterloo Pathway Initiative, the Detroit Riverfront Conservancy and its Detroit Riverwalk, the Upper Peninsula’s Iron Belle Trail, Detroit’s Joe Louis Greenway and Monroe County’s Cornerstone Trail, among others. For example, there is trail work being done on the Joe Louis Greenway, which connects Dearborn, Hamtramck and Highland Park and links them to larger trail systems that crisscross the state, according to the city of Detroit website. Hartig said the project’s planned water trails have all been completed, including the Detroit Heritage River Water Trail and the River Raisin Water Trail. Walkers enjoying the Joe Louis Greenway in Detroit. (Courtesy of the City of Detroit) However, Scott said he doesn’t consider the water trails to be 100% completed. “It needs to be done right,” Scott said. “Some things still still need more work before we would consider them to be done. For example, it would be great to have more camping facilities and bathrooms along the route.” According to Michigan Trails Magazine, the almost 5-mile Detroit Riverwalk between Gabriel Richard Park and Ralph Wilson Park west of downtown, was named “Best Riverwalk in America” by USA Today for multiple years. The Gordie Howe International Bridge, uniting Canada and the United States through a multimodal byway — a scenic or historic “byway” road for tourism, safety and economic development — opened last summer. “It has been unbelievably great how that turned out, and the amount of usage is insane,” Scott said. “It is double the expectations of what the Windsor Detroit Bridge Authority thought it would be, and it has caused tremendous economic activity on both sides of the river.” While many projects aren’t fully complete, communities are already seeing benefits of their connectivity. Hartig said the bridge, as a toll-free trail for pedestrians and cyclists, “is an opportunity to expand and foster cross-boundary trail tourism and travel. The bridge is a tourist attraction now.” Organized by the Waterfront Regeneration Trust, the first Great Waterfront Trail Adventure in August was a multi‑day cycling tour from Windsor, across the Gordie Howe International Bridge for the first time. “Canadians came over and visited, and what an amazing experience they had,” Hartig said. “It is bridge-building and trail-building – creating a bridge between cultures and communities of our two countries.” Scott said, “It’s going to be interesting to see how cycle tourism grows and how Detroit businesses take advantage of that.” “There’s a little humble bar near the base of the bridge, and I stopped in the week before the pathway opened and said, ‘How are you guys prepared for this pathway’ and the people who will come off it to the bar? And when the bridge opened, they ran out of food.” At the same time, Scott said some communities are uninterested and don’t see participation as a priority and that has been a concern. Hartig said the eight Great Lakes states have been exploring a trail to mirror Canada’s Great Lakes Waterfront Trail that would be built over time on the foundation of existing, planned and complete trails. “It started small, in metropolitan Detroit,” Hartig said. “But, right now the big thing is the other states in the Great Lakes started noticing what we are doing, and they said, ‘Why can’t we extend the Great Lakes Way further?’” Hartig said buying into the project because the trails make communities attractive places to live, work and play, and be sustainable. Hartig said the Great Lakes Way adds value for urban and rural communities. “We brought Canadian cyclists into Detroit for a day. They learned about Detroit, got coffee and soon enough will be staying overnight in hotels and Airbnbs,” he said.

articles.title: DCU shake-up: James Gunn and Peter Safran out post-merger
articles.description: Producer and former Kevin Feige protege Jeremy Latcham will replace Gunn and Safran.
articles.content: It's barely been two months since the controversial Paramount and Warner Bros. merger, and we've already got a shockingly unexpected ouster: Co-CEOs of the rebooted DC Universe, James Gunn and Peter Safran, are stepping down from that role despite the Hollywood rumor mill assuming that the duo would be safe. It's unclear whether the pair chose to resign or were forced out, or what will happen to their planned slate of projects beyond 2028's Superman: Man of Tomorrow, which is in post-production. Producer Jeremy Latcham—a protege of Marvel's Kevin Feige who worked with Gunn on Guardians of the Galaxy among other MCU films—will replace them. Per Gunn and Safran's joint statement: Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision. In that time, we helped restore Superman to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with Peacemaker, Creature Commandos, Lanterns and Clayface. We’re immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with. We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter. We’re excited to return to what drew us to this job in the first place, which is telling the stories we love, including the next chapter of Clark and Lex’s journey in Man of Tomorrow. DCU fans are mourning the news and what it could mean for the franchise. My feelings are mixed. On the one hand, I'm on record that I’ve found the rebooted DC Universe films released thus far to be enjoyable but rather forgettable, even when the positives outweigh the negatives. (I have yet to see Clayface, which debuted to good reviews and a solid box office showing.) But HBO has done right by the DCU: I loved both seasons of Peacemaker; Lanterns is a shining beacon of what is possible when someone is allowed to get really creative within the genre; and I'm very much looking forward to next year's Jimmy Olsen (Skylar Gisondo) series The People v. Gorilla Grodd—described as a “mockumentary crime comedy superhero series.”Read full article Comments

articles.title: Voters approve housing bond measures but reject easing lot-size and environmental rules
articles.description: Voters in California, Hawaii and Rhode Island gave the go-ahead last week for bond measures aimed at boosting the housing supply and homeownership. But a California measure to cut back on the state’s decades-old environmental law to spur housing development and a Massachusetts proposal to loosen minimum lot-size rules both failed. Massachusetts’ Question 7, a […]
articles.content: A room inside a 25-unit complex under construction in Central Falls, Rhode Island, in 2024. Rhode Island was one of four states with housing measures on the ballot last week. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Voters in California, Hawaii and Rhode Island gave the go-ahead last week for bond measures aimed at boosting the housing supply and homeownership. But a California measure to cut back on the state’s decades-old environmental law to spur housing development and a Massachusetts proposal to loosen minimum lot-size rules both failed. Massachusetts’ Question 7, a ballot measure that would have overridden local zoning rules and allowed single-family homes on smaller lots, suffered defeat at the ballot box by fewer than 33,000 votes or 1.2 percentage points. The proposal would have allowed single-family homes to be built on lots of 5,000 square feet or more if they had at least 50 feet of street frontage and access to public water and sewer services. Zoning policies for single-family homes currently are set by local governments, not the state, and many require lot sizes of 40,000 square feet or more. In California, Proposition 45 to shorten and streamline the permitting and environmental review process for several types of projects, including housing, under the state’s 50-year-old environmental law fell with nearly 56% of voters in opposition. But California voters approved two measures to allow the state to issue bonds intended to boost housing. Proposition 1, to allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing, passed with roughly 61% of the vote. It will dedicate $10 billion for housing programs and $1.25 billion for veterans’ home loans. The Legislative Analyst’s Office says the bond would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units. Proposition 37, to authorize the state to issue up to $25 billion in bonds to create a down payment assistance program, passed with about 62% of the vote. Each loan would cover up to 17% of the home price. Qualified buyers are defined as those who have been a California resident for at least a year, plan to occupy the home, earn less than 200% of the area median income and can pay at least 3% down. In Rhode Island, more than 61% of voters approved a $120 million bond to fund the construction and development of housing projects in the state. At least $25 million must go toward producing housing intended for homeownership, and up to $10 million may support public housing development. Hawaii voters by nearly 62% approved a new constitutional amendment allowing counties to use special bonds to pay for infrastructure such as roads, water and sewer systems in designated areas. Those bonds would be repaid through future growth in property tax revenue in those districts rather than through an increase in the property tax rate. articles.title: Feds award $10B to states in second year of rural health grants
articles.description: Federal officials on Monday announced $10 billion in awards across all 50 states in the second year of the Rural Health Transformation Fund, grants created by Congress to bolster rural health in response to concerns about Medicaid cuts. Texas received the largest grant for the 2027 fiscal year — almost $282 million — followed by […]
articles.content: Federal officials announced rural health grants to states. (Photo by David DeWitt/Ohio Capital Journal)Federal officials on Monday announced $10 billion in awards across all 50 states in the second year of the Rural Health Transformation Fund, grants created by Congress to bolster rural health in response to concerns about Medicaid cuts. Texas received the largest grant for the 2027 fiscal year — almost $282 million — followed by Alaska, Montana, California and Oklahoma. The five-year fund is providing $50 billion in grants meant to address rural healthcare access and health improvement, with $10 billion available each year until 2030. Congress created the program in response to concern from rural health care providers — as well as lawmakers on both sides of the aisle — about the effects of sweeping Medicaid cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that President Donald Trump signed last year. Rural areas are expected to lose about $137 billion, according to health research organization, KFF. Half of the annual funding is distributed equally among states, with each receiving $100 million in “baseline” funds. The other half is calculated based on a state’s rural population and healthcare facilities, as well as specific initiatives detailed in the applications, among other factors. States applied for and developed their own programs, using the money toward focus areas ranging from maternal and behavioral health, preventive health and chronic disease management, access to care and the rural healthcare workforce, and tech and health equipment investments. All 50 states submitted annual reports documenting their progress from the first year. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said it reviewed the reports as part of determining each state’s award for this year. “States have already put these resources to work bringing better care closer to home for their rural communities, and CMS looks forward to helping them build on that progress in the coming year,” agency Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz said in a news release. States must use the grants to test out and grow approaches toward making programs sustainable after the fund’s five years have ended, the agency said. Rural healthcare leaders have said the infusion of federal dollars is welcome but won’t be enough to offset Medicaid cuts. Democrats, who won the majority in both the U.S. House and Senate in this month’s midterm elections, are aiming to push for a repeal of the law, which would still need Trump’s signature. articles.title: Sheffield unveils Detroit land bank reforms to tackle resident frustrations
articles.description: The plan centers on a resident-first approach to strengthen land bank buyer protections through property tours and other support in renovating severely distressed properties.
articles.content: Detroit Free Press is a partner and shares a reporter with BridgeDetroit. Stories shared are not under a paywall. Detroit Free Press Detroiters who are frustrated with the process of obtaining land bank properties may find relief through a new initiative aiming to ease access to land and home ownership. Mayor Mary Sheffield and Detroit Land Bank Authority Director Tammy Daniels on Nov. 9 announced a plan to boost transparency, access and accelerate the development and renovation process for land bank homes, which residents have long complained about while Sheffield was a City Council member. City officials and community members announced and celebrated the plan outside of a Dexter-Linwood home, one of dozens that will be restored to serve as temporary housing for Detroiters experiencing housing instability. “I heard, firsthand, from Detroiters who wanted to purchase a land bank property, fix up a home, or invest in their neighborhoods. But they oftentimes felt frustrated throughout the process. They wanted greater access to properties, they wanted clearer answers, and they wanted a partner who would help them navigate the process more easily,” Sheffield said. “Our residents deserve a land bank that is transparent, that is accessible, and focused on neighborhood stability.” Daniels said the plan centers on a resident-first approach that strengthens the land bank’s buyer protections through property tours and other support to help buyers understand how to renovate severely distressed properties. Daniels also highlighted the property at 2626 Webb St. in Detroit, where officials stood, as an example of restoring distressed property, which is one of the goals of the land bank. “This is what returning property to productive use can look like. A beautifully renovated property that no longer is a blight on the community, but also an asset to those who are in need of assistance,” Daniels said. Detroit Land Bank Authority CEO Tammy Daniels speaks at a Nov. 9, 2026, news conference in Detroit. Credit: City of Detroit Flickr The reforms come as the City Council in recent years has debated the land bank’s relevance. In December, the council renewed a one-year operating agreement with the DLBA after spending much of 2025 considering significant changes proposed by Council Member Mary Waters. Sheffield had publicly considered rolling some functions of the land bank under the city’s housing department. As a council member, she sought clearer processes and improved customer service in response to resident complaints. Unlike some others, Sheffield did not advocate to dismantle the land bank, but said it needed major improvements. Focus on buyer protection The first part of the plan involves thorough vetting of potential buyers to certify they have the financial means and providing free tours of properties for buyers to gauge the needed rehab work. It also includes a $1.5 million grant program to help buyers complete the renovations and bring their properties into compliance, and a separate $1.5 million emergency resource assistance program to help occupants of land bank-owned properties complete the Occupied Buy Back program, which provides residents a pathway to homeownership. Increased access Sheffield mandated that any city-imposed holds on 7,500 land bank properties be released and made available for sale. The move is expected to address frustrations over unavailable properties being withheld from sale to residents for potential larger developments, according to the city. The land bank will also provide a new tracking tool showing its 56,000 parcels, including the available properties, land being held from sale and the reason for the holds. Detroit officials on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, unveiled a series of reforms to improve access to Detroit Land Bank Authority properties, increase transparency, enhance customer service and expand investment opportunities. Credit: City of Detroit Flickr Revamped customer service The land bank is creating a new field office at Butzel Family Recreation Center to expand access to programs, a 72-hour turnaround standard for customer service requests and a new after-hours customer service resource for prospective buyers and current clients. Simplifying programs Small-scale beautification project purchases, such as community gardens and green spaces, will be directed through the DLBA website, as opposed to requiring the process to be handled in person for residents, block clubs and community groups. The Nuisance Abatement Program will move to a referral-only model and the land bank will no longer survey neighborhoods for troubled properties, according to the city. The program will only accept and review referrals from residents and from city departments, registered community groups and from City Council. The revamped vetting process will include a referral for housing assistance if occupants are found in a vacant property. The Nuisance Abatement Program will not apply to occupied homes. Priority areas and homelessness prevention The land bank will commit $6 million to restore 75 homes to provide temporary supportive housing for residents in need of housing stability.In partnership with the Homeless Action Network of Detroit, which acts as the city’s Continuum of Care, the land bank will create more than 170 beds for Detroit’s housing insecure residents. “Today marks a commitment to ending homelessness in the city of Detroit. This is something that is innovative. I have not seen this in all my time working in the homeless response system, so I am just elated that we will have people, men, women and children who will be able to call this home, not a shelter, but they will be able to call this home,” said Tasha Gray, executive director of the Homeless Action Network of Detroit. Dana Afana is the Detroit City Hall reporter for the Free Press. Contact: dafana@freepress.com. Follow her: @DanaAfana.

articles.title: Incoming House Speaker Puri: Diversity is the new Democratic caucus’ greatest strength
articles.description: Democrats were elected last week to control both the state House and Senate, and with it will come a diversity of thought on big policy ideas and approaches to wielding power — which could pose a challenge for the party’s incoming House Speaker-elect Ranjeev Puri of Canton. Puri was officially elected speaker late last week […]
articles.content: State Rep. Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) speaks to supporters in Detroit after Democrats retook the majority on the Michigan House and retained control of the Senate. Puri is likely to be the next Speaker of the House. Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Democrats were elected last week to control both the state House and Senate, and with it will come a diversity of thought on big policy ideas and approaches to wielding power — which could pose a challenge for the party’s incoming House Speaker-elect Ranjeev Puri of Canton. Puri was officially elected speaker late last week as new members of the House Democratic caucus met for the first time and selected its leaders for the 2027-28 legislative session. The Nov. 3 election saw the Democrats expand their majority in the state Senate, while Democrats took back control of the House from Republicans, led by outgoing Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township). In an interview with Michigan Advance, Puri said he welcomed the challenge to bring together the new coalition of recently elected lawmakers, and relished their unique perspectives. Puri added that he views the management of their competing interests as a party as more of an honor than a chore. Puri elected House Speaker as Democrats prepare to take control of state government “It doesn’t always have to be about me,” Puri said. “I’m going to foster an environment, especially over the next couple of months here, between now and the first day of session, to make sure we have the right dialogue and the right forums for people to express their perspectives and for us to kind of naturally and organically have those debates and deliberations internally.” Puri said that those efforts would help his caucus reach “a robust agenda that’s going to meet the needs of our caucus and this moment.” The moment, as it stands, has given the state’s Democrats — and the party nationwide — a mandate to bring forth real change after a disjointed eight years of President Donald Trump in the Oval Office, Republican control of Congress over the last few years and with the GOP leading the agenda in the state House. Puri said he would be the type of leader that will listen to his caucus, and approach his members’ individual policy aims on level ground. “I’m hoping there’s no one coming into these conversations thinking that everyone agrees with them,” Puri said. “This is just going to be the kind of healthy debate that is imperative to a functional democracy. That is going to be the work that we do internally.” That doesn’t mean there isn’t room for big swings and home run shots in Puri’s new House majority — quite the contrary. The incoming speaker said his approach would be to dream large and tackle tough issues that could lead to transformational laws and regulations. “If we do that correctly, it is going to transcend some of those divides within my own party, those that exist along partisan lines, and in terms of real systemic problems, challenges that are facing our state,” Puri said. “Our median household income is not growing and is falling behind our peer states. Our population growth is still not where it needs to be. The more time we can spend tackling those larger issues, the better our governance will be.” That’s where the incoming Democratic caucus’s diversity will shine, Puri said, while reiterating that his “decision-making process doesn’t always have to be about me.” Michigan House Speaker-elect Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) speaks to members of the news media on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, outside of the House chamber in Lansing, Mich. Puri donned a baseball cap with the word “Immigrant” on it during the press conference; he will be the first South Asian American to serve as the chamber’s speaker, as well as its first Sikh speaker of the House. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance) Part of that comes from his close ties to his district, and his family, and his focus on not being a creature of Lansing every day of the week. “I don’t think that this maybe sets me apart, but I’m rooted as the father of four young kids, and doing what I can to chart our state on a path to achieve the most success that it can,” he said. “But at the end of the day, I’ve never spent a night in Lansing. I come home every day, and it’s a promise I made to my family — that I’m either going to be home for dinner or home for breakfast. When I come home, I’m not a representative or leader or speaker, or anything; I’m just Dad. That’s my north star and if I ever lose that north star, that would be when I know that my time has come.” One big change that Puri hopes to implement immediately is a shift in decorum of how the speaker handles disputes within his caucus. Hall was replaced last week as caucus leader, with the House GOP tapping state Rep. Tom Kunse (R-Clare) instead. Kunse promised to lead the caucus with a steady hand and with a commitment to nip disagreements with Puri in the bud behind closed doors, and not on social media or in the public view. He also vowed to do the same for disagreements within his own caucus. Gongwer News Service reported that much of the reason why Hall was not reelected as caucus leader had to do with how he wielded power as speaker. Gongwer noted that Hall had scuttled bills in committees if their respective chairs had somehow crossed him, threatened committee assignments for rank-and-file members and pushed easy win legislation to the negotiating table for larger caucus priorities — including as leverage during fraught budget battles. That made it difficult for Hall to maintain his grip on the caucus. Return of the trifecta: Michigan Democrats reclaim full control of state government The current speaker was not the only one who faced some dysfunction as the House majority leader in recent years, however; former House Speaker Joe Tate (D-Detroit) lost control of his caucus during its lame duck session of 2024, which saw obstructionism from Hall’s incoming caucus but also some key defections in the Democratic majority, mainly in the form of state. Rep. Karen Whitsett (D-Detroit), that blunted its session-end priorities. Each of those experiences have given Puri some pause over how he intends to run the speaker’s office for the next two years. “I can’t speak to the former speakers or impugn their motives, or to what happened and didn’t happen behind the scenes,” he said. “What I can tell you about myself is that I generally tend to be a little more decentralized than most preceding me. It’s really important to me to make sure we are uplifting the perspectives of my membership. I have 26 new members, and a 63-member caucus, that are going to represent a vast array of perspectives that are far different than just what I see in my own House district. I take that very seriously.” Another change that will mark Puri’s time as a speaker: “shying away from the politicalness that has been used by House leadership over the last couple of years to kind of lead on every issue. “If we can spend less time talking about who’s playing in what sport and more time about how we can improve the lives of every Michigander, in terms of household median income and job growth, I think that would be a successful use of these next two years,” Puri said.

The masculinity midterms
articles.description: This story was originally reported by Grace Panetta of The 19th. Meet Grace and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy. In April, Republican Rep. Tony Gonzales of Texas resigned after being accused of having improper relationships with staff, including a former staffer who died by suicide. The Republican who ran to […]
articles.content: (Sarah Porter for The 19th; Getty Images) This story was originally reported by Grace Panetta of The 19th. Meet Grace and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy. In April, Republican Rep. Tony Gonzales of Texas resigned after being accused of having improper relationships with staff, including a former staffer who died by suicide. The Republican who ran to replace him, gun influencer Brandon Herrera, known online as “the AK Guy,” had a long history of using profane and misogynistic language to denigrate women. The district had gone for President Donald Trump by 15 points in 2024. But on Tuesday, Democrat Katy Padilla Stout flipped the seat, which stretches along the U.S.-Mexico border from El Paso to San Antonio. Padilla Stout, a former child welfare attorney and teacher, will be the first Latina to represent the district. Padilla Stout’s win came amid a bipartisan reckoning over sexual misconduct spurred by the release of the Epstein files. In Ohio, Democrat Brian Poindexter defeated Rep. Max Miller, who had been accused of domestic violence by his ex-wife; he denied the allegations. In North Carolina, Democrat Jamie Ager flipped a seat held by Rep. Chuck Edwards, who dropped his reelection bid and was censured after a House Ethics investigation into his inappropriate relationships with young staff. Rep. Jimmy Gomez of California, also under a House Ethics probe over alleged relationships with staff, lost to progressive Angela Gonzales-Torres. Voters’ frustration with high prices and anger at the Trump administration’s policies drove Democrats’ tsunami-level victories Tuesday, flipping control of both the House and the U.S. Senate. But the results also show that voters were fed up with misbehaving men of both parties. The release of the files connected to the late disgraced sex offender Jeffrey Epstein became a major campaign issue for Democrats, who connected the Epstein files to corruption. And many Democratic men became more comfortable leaning into their own masculinity on the campaign trail. Voters also largely weren’t swayed by Republicans’ efforts to make the election a referendum on the narrow conception of gender they put forth with attacks on transgender people and a pugilistic, machismo-laden vision of masculinity rooted in muscles and high testosterone. The conservative ideal of masculinity was perhaps best encapsulated by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s state of the force address in September, where he declared the department would no longer be the “woke” or “weak” department with a Dr. Seuss-ian definition: “No fatties. No trannies. No beardos. No weirdos. No wimps. No radicals.” He went on to declare: “The ideological clowns are out. The patriotic cowboys are in — with testosterone testing on top.” Trump’s closing message of the 2026 midterm elections also focused on how people presented themselves and conventional ideas of attractiveness as opposed to what voters really cared about: He kept telling voters to look at people’s asses. He most frequently lauded the derrière of GOP Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio, who lost his race on Tuesday notwithstanding, and said rapper and recent MAGA convert Nicki Minaj had “a beautiful ass” at a rally in Michigan. At first blush, this election cycle might not seem very gendered, especially compared with recent midterm cycles. In 2022, outrage over the Supreme Court overturning a right to abortion helped Democrats to a better-than-expected performance, and 2018 took place in the wake of the #MeToo movement and Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s confirmation to the Supreme Court. But in the past couple of years, both political parties have been reorganizing around the axis of gender, the driving force shaping so much of American life and American politics. If politics flows downstream from culture, consider two of the bestselling and most talked-about books of the year: Caro Claire Burke’s “Yesteryear,” a novel about a tradwife influencer who wakes up in 1855, and Belle Burden’s memoir “Strangers: A Memoir of Marriage,” a real-life cautionary tale from a woman whose identity and financial independence were subsumed by a husband who cheated on and then abruptly left her. The ideal of the “Pilates girl” jumped from the manosphere to mainstream reality TV shows like “Love Is Blind” and “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives.” Discussions of what it means to be a “girl’s girl” also dominated culture and reality television. Discussions of motherhood and postpartum psychosis swept the headlines during the trial to determine whether Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy was criminally responsible for killing her three children. Then, a nationwide discussion about sexual assault on college campuses was reignited when a former Cornell student filed an explosive lawsuit against the university, and seven men she accused of raping her at a fraternity house in 2024. This was also the year of tradwives and girlbosses, looksmaxxing and framemogging, alphas and betas — and a UFC fight on the White House lawn. That “Freedom 250” fight was a moment much hyped by Trump, who won a second term after being found liable for sexual abuse and campaigned on an aggressive, ascendent vision of masculinity. He appointed several men accused of sexual misconduct to his Cabinet, including Hegseth and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The right declared a total cultural victory after Trump’s win in 2024, viewing the result as a repudiation of “wokeness” and the start of a golden, seed-oil-free age of hotness, glistening with the sheen of beef tallow skincare products. And even though the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement, which helped elect Trump and elevate Kennedy to his Cabinet, was led by women concerned about food quality and safety, Kennedy has spent much of his time focused on boosting testosterone and combating erectile dysfunction. The obsession with hormones bled into the Texas Senate race, where much of Republicans’ messaging was to alternatively accuse Democratic Senator-elect James Talarico of being “low T,” or low in testosterone, and gay or transgender. On the left, Democrats largely eschewed the explicit appeals to identity politics and social justice-laden language that defined their party’s messaging in the first Trump term, a period some dubbed “Woke 1.0.” In a sign of how much Trump has reoriented American politics around image, Democrats have also leaned into hotness and thirst to boost support for candidates like Michigan Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and Montana Rep.-elect Sam Forstag. Democrats also made a play to win the men, especially young men, who shifted right in 2024, by showing that their party can be masculine too. Candidates like El-Sayed, Montana independent Senate candidate Seth Bodnar and Indiana Democratic Secretary of State-elect Beau Bayh ran ads featuring them lifting weights, shooting guns or both. Former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed speaks at an election night watch party in Detroit, Mich., on Aug. 4, 2026. The Democratic primary for U.S. Senate was too close to call at the time he spoke. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance) No Democrat ran on masculinity more than El-Sayed, a weightlifting, rock climbing public health expert who sought to undercut his opponents’ machismo at every turn. In September, he accused Vice President JD Vance of having a fake beard and challenged him to a weight-lifting contest. He argued against data centers by saying it wasn’t worth building more of them so Republican nominee Mike Rogers “can make AI videos of himself looking swole.” When Rogers accused El-Sayed of being anti-football, he challenged him to a game: “Since you’re too afraid to debate me, how about you ‘hold me accountable’ on a football field instead. Tackle, no pads like we used to play when we were kids. I’d be happy to show you [how] much I love football.” And El-Sayed closed out his campaign by challenging yet another Cabinet member’s athleticism. “Pete Hegseth, everybody knows that guy from the locker room,” he said in an interview with comedian Hasan Minhaj. “You know he would have rode the pine. He probably got to start two games his entire career playing whatever sport he was, and it made his life, and his parents came and cheered so hard for him.” Hegseth’s father, Brian Hegseth, jumped in to his son’s defense, accusing El-Sayed of having “little man syndrome” in a post on X. “Proud to say, as Pete’s dad, he was an absolute star on the court in HS. Captain, all-conference, all-state player…earned!,” he wrote. “We parents cheered him on, yes. That’s what families do-support each other. #Envy makes him bitter.” El-Sayed won his race by 7 percentage points as Democrats held all the statewide offices on the ballot in Michigan and are on track to flip three U.S. House seats. A faction led by Vance that has been encouraging young people, especially young women, to get married and have children younger as a solution to falling birthrates was also met with skepticism from many on the right. Five days before the 2026 midterms, Vance held a Fox News town hall at Texas Christian University to turn out young voters, many of whom backed Trump in 2024 but are feeling squeezed by the economy, see milestones like homeownership as increasingly out of reach and, in many cases, are disillusioned with politics. Kate White, a senior at the university and vice president of the organization’s Turning Point USA chapter, began her question to Vance by noting that the right pushes “the constant message” to young people to get married and have as many children as possible. It’s a call to action that she said “doesn’t acknowledge” how expensive it is for young people like her to afford homes and start families. “And so my question is, how does the right and yourself expect us to start families young when the average price of a home in America now costs more than $415,000, which just feels out of reach for us?” she asked. “First of all, thank you for the question and thanks for the support,” Vance responded. “I want to point out that I think that I’ve been asked four or five questions by my count, and I’ve only been asked one question about Jon Husted’s ass, and it was by Jesse Watters,” the Fox News host. Vance did go on to answer the question in earnest, blaming low housing supply on immigrants, an argument economists say is unfounded, and high home prices on Wall Street investors. Those arguments fell flat with voters in Texas, where Democrats swept every statewide office in a historic rout for the GOP: both Talarico and Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa flipped Tarrant County, which includes Fort Worth, and nationwide exit polls indicate young voters swung left. The struggles of young men were a major fixation of politicians, pundits and think-tankers across the political spectrum — though that concern and curiosity has largely not extended to young women, who face many of the same economic headwinds as young men but vote much more reliably Democratic. The 2024 election unleashed a torrent of antipathy toward working women, with some connecting the Elon Musk-led so-called Department of Government Efficiency and its sweeping cuts to the federal workforce to wanting to punish “girlbosses” and busybody “HR ladies.” But cracks in that coalition didn’t take long to appear. Some Vance-backed proposals, like redirecting childcare subsidies intended for lower-income working parents to married, stay-at-home parents, rankled others on the right who oppose government intervention in family policy. And several right-wing commentators were furious at Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton for a tweet celebrating women accounting for the vast majority of the job growth since early 2025 — never mind that the majority of working women are not corporate “girlbosses” but work in healthcare, education and food service jobs. articles.description: Arrests for low-level offenses, including vagrancy and drug possession, increased nationwide in 2025, even as violent crime continued to decline, according to a new analysis of federal data. The analysis, which was released in late October by the criminal justice advocacy organization FWD.us, found that arrests for vagrancy, an offense often associated with homelessness, rose […]
articles.content: A homeless encampment under a bridge includes a tent and bags of belongings in Paterson, N.J. Arrests for vagrancy, an offense often associated with homelessness, rose 44% between 2024 and 2025, according to a new analysis by advocacy group FWD.us. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Arrests for low-level offenses, including vagrancy and drug possession, increased nationwide in 2025, even as violent crime continued to decline, according to a new analysis of federal data. The analysis, which was released in late October by the criminal justice advocacy organization FWD.us, found that arrests for vagrancy, an offense often associated with homelessness, rose 44% between 2024 and 2025, while arrests for marijuana possession increased 6% and possession of other drugs rose 3%. Arrests for immigration violations nearly tripled, rising 188% between 2024 and 2025, amid President Donald Trump’s crackdown on illegal immigration. The increase continued into 2026, with an average of 36,093 arrests per month through July — nearly four times the monthly average in 2024, according to the report. The findings point to a shift toward more aggressive enforcement of lower-level offenses, particularly in states that have rolled back major changes to their criminal legal systems in recent years, according to the analysis. Voters in nearly a dozen states also backed tougher approaches to crime in this year’s midterm elections, approving statewide ballot measures that impose stricter penalties for certain offenses or tighten bail restrictions. “There is at this point plenty of time to choose a different path from this one and to kind of redirect ourselves,” said Zoë Towns, the executive director of FWD.us. The increases in arrests for low-level offenses also come as arrests for more serious offenses, including homicide, robbery and burglary, continue to decline, mirroring broader national crime trends. Some of the sharpest increases in arrests for low-level offenses were concentrated in a handful of states. Arizona, California, Hawaii and Nevada accounted for more than half of the nationwide increase in vagrancy arrests. FWD.us linked the trend in part to the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in City of Grants Pass v. Johnson, which gave local governments greater latitude to enforce restrictions on sleeping outdoors. Meanwhile, California and Oregon, which rolled back portions of earlier progressive drug policy changes in 2024, experienced increases in arrests for drug possession offenses other than marijuana. Those arrests rose 24% in California and 39% in Oregon. In 2025, Black people were arrested for marijuana possession at more than four times the rate of white people. From 2024 to 2025, arrests of Black people rose nearly 10%, accounting for 83% of the national increase and 45% of all marijuana arrests in 2025. But the analysis does not establish that the policy changes caused every increase in arrests or determine whether greater enforcement improved public safety. The organization warned that continued growth in low-level arrests could reverse years of progress in reducing incarceration and racial disparities, particularly as states reconsider criminal justice policies amid ongoing debates over crime and public safety. articles.title: WATCH LIVE: Tyler Robinson judge to give trial date ruling in assassination of Charlie Kirk
articles.content: Tyler Robinson will stand trial in the summer of 2028 for the shooting of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, a Utah judge ruled Monday.Attorneys for defendant Tyler Robinson, 23, proposed a trial starting in 2029. But District Judge Tony Graf faced pressure from Kirk's family and supporters, including President Donald Trump, to speed up court proceedings that already have lasted more than a year.Graf allocated 105 days for the proceedings, beginning with jury selection on June 21, 2028. He said the dates balance Robinson's right to prepare his defense with the rights of Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, to a speedy resolution.Erika Kirk's attorney disagreed with the schedule but said there is no choice but to accept it."A trial in the summer of 2028, three years after Charlie's assassination, does not feel very speedy to the Kirk family," attorney Jeffrey Neiman said. He had argued the trial should start next October.In a statement after Monday's hearing, the Kirk family called Graf's decision a "delay" and said, "every additional day without justice prolongs our family's pain."Robinson's defense team declined to comment after the hearing.Robinson has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in the killing of Kirk, 31, as the activist spoke to several thousand people at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025. The defendant turned himself in a day after the shooting. His lawyers have not offered alternative theories for Kirk's death.Robinson could be eligible for the death penalty if convicted.Prosecutors had said they could be ready by October 2027. Rather than hold the proceedings during the Thanksgiving and Christmas holidays, they proposed the trial begin in January 2028.Kirk helped galvanize young voters around Trump during the 2024 election. Trump weighed in on the trial in a social media post last month, saying Robinson should be tried "within a month." The Republican president criticized Graf, a former prosecutor appointed judge last year, for "taking forever to ask questions that people already know the answer to."Utah County prosecutors allege Robinson targeted Kirk for his political beliefs. They say a bullet found in the rifle used to kill Kirk was engraved with the words "Hey Facist! CATCH!" and that Robinson wrote in a text message about Kirk: "I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can't be negotiated out."Robinson's attorneys said in court filings this week that they must sift through tens of thousands of files turned over by prosecutors. They plan to conduct extensive investigations into Robinson's life in search of mitigating factors that could influence his sentence if convicted, and to devote "substantial time" to issues such as jury selection.

articles.title: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
articles.description: "*sshole" poses a serious threat to Internet security.
articles.content: Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting. The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real. Attackers conducting "mature intrusions" Security firm Greynoise said Monday that honeypots it maintains in Southeast Asia have come under attack by a group it’s tracking as GT10. The group conducted “mature intrusions" into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign. A backdoor the group is using in the attacks contains Chinese language comments and appears to be generated with the use of AI.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Anthropic must face lawsuit over Claude subscription marketing
articles.content: Anthropic must face a proposed class action claiming it oversold its Claude Max subscriptions, after a federal judge in San Francisco found its "5x or 20x more usage than Pro" marketing plausibly misleading [1]. Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California granted in part and denied in part Anthropic's motion to dismiss on Friday, Nov. 6, in Kahn v. Anthropic PBC, No. 3:26-cv-05763 [1]. Courthouse News first reported the ruling, according to The Next Web [3]. Plaintiffs Karl Kahn and Solomon Smith say the multipliers on the $100 Max 5x and $200 Max 20x plans apply per five-hour session, while weekly limits are not 5x or 20x higher. Their complaint calculates that on Claude's Sonnet 4 model, Max 5x users get 3.5 times Pro's weekly usage and Max 20x users 6 times [1]. Anthropic argued that reasonable buyers would understand "more usage" as per session, pointing to its help pages. Tse noted that the per-session disclosure sits "two hyperlinks away from the primary sales pages" and outside the sales funnel, and that given the monthly billing cycle consumers can reasonably infer a promise of 5x or 20x more usage per month [1]. He also rejected Anthropic's argument that a Claude subscription is not a "service" under California's Consumers Legal Remedies Act, finding Claude Code plausibly is one [1]. The breach of contract and negligent misrepresentation claims survive, as does Smith's CLRA claim; Smith is a computer-science student, and "educational use is plainly not commercial use," Tse wrote, quoting the plaintiffs [1]. Kahn's CLRA claim was dismissed because he had not shown he uses Claude for personal rather than commercial purposes [1]. The UCL and FAL claims fell because both plaintiffs still subscribe, so they lack standing to seek an injunction, and they did not explain why damages would be an inadequate remedy [1]. Tse also dismissed a claim over Anthropic tightening usage limits during billing cycles, finding its terms of service reserve the right to change capacity limits [1]. The amended complaint is due Dec. 2; if the plaintiffs do not amend, Anthropic must answer by Dec. 16 [1]. Anthropic's amended S-1, filed Nov. 2, says the company "is subject to several putative class action complaints alleging that it markets and sells subscription plans for Claude through false, misleading, and deceptive advertising practices," that the matters are generally in early stages, and that it intends to defend itself vigorously [2]. A risk factor adds that changes to usage limits "have resulted, and could in the future result, in claims that our disclosures regarding model access or capabilities were inadequate or misleading" [2]. articles.title: Anthropic releases new Mythos and Fable models amid RSI concerns
articles.description: Anthropic says the new models "show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision," as well as in communicating more clearly with users.
articles.content: Anthropic released new versions of its most advanced models on Monday, with the launch of Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2. The company says the new models “show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision” and communicate more clearly with users. Notably, Anthropic is lowering the cost of Fable from $10 to $8 per million input tokens. As a result, Fable 5.2 is now cheaper than its primary competitor GPT-6 Astra. Anthropic says that the new version of Fable will return responses 30% faster across effort levels. Faster inference serving is available for double the price. Fable 5.2 is also compatible with zero data retention (ZDR) policies through the Enterprise Frontier Safeguards system, long a sticking point for many enterprise clients. It’s Anthropic’s first model release since the arrival of a third-party report from the assessment group METR, which suggested the lab might be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) — or the ability for AI models to carry on model training independently. The METR report found internal models were speeding up Anthropic’s AI progress by roughly 2x, although many uncertainties remain. Still, Anthropic’s release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. “Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow.” Anthropic maintains that the new version of Mythos does not have the ability to act covertly against its user, a verdict that’s detailed further in Mythos 5.2’s system card. “Claude Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities than prior Claude models on several of our evaluations, particularly when its reasoning is hidden from the monitor,” the system card reads. “That said, we believe that low levels of absolute performance on our new covert evaluations support claims that rely on detection of harmful actions in high-stakes situations.” Fable 5.2 has been available to select parties in pre-release for some time, and Anthropic says the model has already “solved two open problems in theoretical physics, formalized Fermat’s Last Theorem, and supported numerous other research projects.” Also on Monday, AI startup Physical Superintelligence announced a new proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture, a pivotal step in setting theoretical limits for quantum computing. Notably, the lab said the result was achieved by running “a non-public Anthropic model” within PSI’s own system. Anthropic did not confirm or deny whether Fable 5.2 was the model in question. articles.content: After publishing a support article in early September outlining usage limits for some Apple Intelligence features, the company has updated Logic Pro with an option to “Buy More Usage” for a one-time purchase price of $49.99, as spotted by 9to5Mac. It has a built-in AI assistant to do things like “start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.” These Intelligence Usage Packs, as Apple calls them, will allow users to continue accessing certain Apple Intelligence features that have usage limits because they rely on cloud-based AI models from OpenAI or Google Gemini. The Usage Packs can only be used by the Apple Account that purchased them (Family Sharing isn’t supported) and, as Apple explains on its website, any unused additional usage will roll over from month to month, but will expire 12 months after it was purchased. For Logic Pro, Apple says the usage limit is “impacted by the complexity of conversations you have with the assistant.” Users finding themselves running out of access can find the option to buy an Intelligence Usage Pack in the Intelligence Features > Show Usage section of the app’s main menu. Currently, only Logic Pro has the option to buy more usage, but it’s expected to be added to other Apple Creator Studio apps this month, including Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Motion, plus Pages, Keynote, and Numbers that are getting access to Apple’s AI chatbot.

articles.description: With Michigan set to receive a sizable amount as part of a settlement agreement between 50 states and territories and Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, two state lawmakers are looking to use those funds to bolster Michigan’s youth mental health efforts. In August, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel announced the state would […]
articles.content: Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey MonitorWith Michigan set to receive a sizable amount as part of a settlement agreement between 50 states and territories and Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, two state lawmakers are looking to use those funds to bolster Michigan’s youth mental health efforts. In August, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel announced the state would receive at least $171 million, following allegations that Meta had intentionally designed its apps with addictive features, harming young people and misleading the public about the safety of its platforms. To ensure the settlement funds are reinvested in youth mental health efforts, state Reps. Julie Rogers (D-Kalamazoo) and Mike Mueller (R-Linden) have proposed legislation to create the Youth Social Media Settlement Fund within the Michigan Department of Treasury. “For years, parents, educators and health professionals have raised concerns about the toll social media can take on our children’s mental health,” Rogers said in a statement. “Now, these companies are facing legal consequences, and Michigan stands to recover millions of dollars. We have a responsibility to make sure that money goes toward helping our young people, giving them the care, support and opportunities they need to lead healthy lives.” If House Bills 6463 and 6464, sponsored by Rogers and Mueller, are signed into law, this new trust fund would receive money from social media-related lawsuits and settlements. The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services would use that fund to distribute grants for youth mental health services, crisis intervention, after-school programs, mentoring and other evidence-based programs. The package also includes statewide planning and annual reporting requirements to ensure the funds are used as the Legislature intended. “The funds made available through this settlement should be invested in solutions that address the growing mental health challenges facing our communities,” Mueller said in a statement. “As technology continues to rapidly evolve, we must ensure our efforts keep pace with the challenges our children face and provide them with the resources and support they need to thrive.”
