articles.content: Ross Douthat speaking with President Trump in the Oval Office in Trump's first interview since the 2026 midterm elections. (Photo courtesy "60 Minutes"/CBS News)WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said in an interview that aired Sunday his mass deportation campaign, which helped propel his return to the Oval Office, had gone too far and potentially led to Republicans losing the U.S. House and Senate in the midterm elections. “I think it might be too tough, yeah,” Trump said in the interview with Ross Douthat of “60 Minutes”. “And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough.” He added that he thinks his immigration crackdown “both helped and hurt” him in the midterm elections. “When you go into a hotel and you say, ‘Let me see your pass,’ and you have a woman that’s worked there as a, you know, as a maid, as a cleaner, as a this, as a that, as a waitress, a lotta good things, great job, and all of a sudden, they’re being taken out of the country, it’s tough,” Trump said. “It’s a tough thing.” The president’s description of his mass deportation campaign was in stark contrast with his decision to elevate Stephen Miller, the main architect of his immigration crackdown, to White House chief of staff — the first major shakeup since the midterm elections. Trump added that he is willing to work with Democrats on legislation to provide legal status for immigrants who work in certain sectors, such as hospitality. The Trump administration has carried out one of the largest de-legalization efforts in recent history, stripping more than 1 million immigrants of their humanitarian and temporary legal statuses. Trump said that he believes Democrats would be interested in addressing long-term immigrants in the country, but he did not specify which lawmakers were interested in a deal. “I think that’s something that’s actually doable,” Trump said of working with Democrats on immigration policy. Miller backlash It’s unclear how any dealmaking with Democrats will proceed with Miller, who was behind efforts to strip millions of legal immigrants of their Temporary Protected Status as well as the effort to redefine the constitutional right to birthright citizenship, leading White House staff. Trade associations representing businesses in hospitality, agriculture and construction have said the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown has harmed their businesses and the broader economy. They also slammed the president’s decision to promote Miller. “One of the main reasons why the Republicans lost the midterm elections was in big part because of Stephen Miller’s cruelty on immigration policies,” Benny Melendez, vice chair of the South Texas Builders Association, said in a statement. “I don’t understand why Trump would appoint him as Chief of Staff for the White House. It seems like they now want to lose the White House in the 2028 election.”

articles.title: Trump’s DOJ ends California suit over suspected noncitizen voters after midterm losses
articles.description: The U.S. Department of Justice is dismissing a lawsuit that tried to force California to set aside the ballots of suspected noncitizen voters, marking the formal end of the Trump administration’s most aggressive effort to control vote counting in the lead-up to the midterm elections. The Justice Department filed a notice in court Friday night […]
articles.content: San Francisco sheriffs walk past voting booths at City Hall on Nov. 3, 2026 in San Francisco, California. (Photo by Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images)The U.S. Department of Justice is dismissing a lawsuit that tried to force California to set aside the ballots of suspected noncitizen voters, marking the formal end of the Trump administration’s most aggressive effort to control vote counting in the lead-up to the midterm elections. The Justice Department filed a notice in court Friday night that it was abandoning the lawsuit. The decision ended what had been a dramatic weeks-long battle between the federal government and state and local election officials over control of California’s elections. The filing came less than a week after the U.S. Supreme Court, hours before Election Day, ruled against an emergency request by the Justice Department — and after Republicans suffered crushing electoral losses nationwide. President Donald Trump will enter the final two years of his term facing a Congress controlled by Democrats. Ballots from 20,000 people The DOJ had asked the Supreme Court to stop election officials from processing and counting ballots from roughly 20,000 people the Trump administration suspected were noncitizens. The justices instead quickly rejected the request in a one-sentence order. While the Supreme Court rebuffed the Justice Department, a federal judge in California had scheduled a hearing for Nov. 13 that would have given the Trump administration another chance at an order requiring election officials to set aside the ballots. The hearing, which may have included witnesses, would have potentially revealed new information about how the list was developed. California election officials had heavily criticized the accuracy of the list, which was compiled by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. In the Friday court filing, Assistant U.S. Attorney Julie A. Hamill wrote that the Justice Department was dropping the lawsuit because by Nov. 13, ballots from individuals on the list would be “commingled” with other ballots. “There is then no way to get the challenged ballots segregated,” Hamill wrote. Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wrote on social media that the Justice Department’s efforts “to restore confidence and integrity in elections continue.” “We will pursue every civil and criminal remedy to ensure only eligible American citizens vote in American elections,” Essayli wrote. Californians defend ‘well-defined standards’ Dean Logan, the top election official in Los Angeles County, which had been sued by the Justice Department, in a statement said he welcomed the dismissal of the lawsuit. As Los Angeles County’s registrar-recorder/county clerk, Logan’s office had warned that setting aside the ballots could throw the election into chaos and effectively halt ballot counting. Lawyers for California and Los Angeles County had emphasized during the lawsuit that noncitizen voting is illegal under state law and the state takes preventive measures. Voters must sign their ballot envelopes and those signatures are checked by election workers. Voters must also attest under penalty of perjury that they are U.S. citizens. “At each stage of this election, and in response to the Department of Justice, we have been clear that state and federal law sets well-defined standards for verifying and challenging voter eligibility,” Logan said. The lawsuit against California had been one in a series of steps taken by the Trump administration ahead of Election Day aimed at asserting power over elections, which are run by states under the U.S. Constitution. Homeland Security has arrested dozens of noncitizens over alleged election crimes in recent weeks. And DHS conducted election-related field operations that were temporarily paused by a federal judge over concerns that they were intimidating naturalized citizens. The Justice Department sent federal grand jury subpoenas to election officials in Los Angeles County and raised the prospect that election officials would face prosecution if they tabulated the ballots of noncitizens. A federal judge issued an order prohibiting the DOJ from threatening election workers, but the order was paused by the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals. Legal action in more states The Justice Department preemptively sued Alaska over the certification of its U.S. Senate race. Trump said he ordered the action, angry that the ballot included a candidate with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. A federal judge tossed the lawsuit. As of Monday, the race remained too close to call, with Democrat Mary Peltola holding a lead of a few hundred votes. The DOJ also demanded Washington state set aside the ballots of about 400 people it alleged were suspected noncitizens. A federal judge issued an order preventing the DOJ from forcing the state to comply.

articles.description: "Do not ask again" prompt leads to passwords, API keys, and more being shared.
articles.content: Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That's the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets, including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories. The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the "Yes, and don't ask again" option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local ".claude/settings.local.json" file on the user's computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it. This isn't really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user's local machine (assuming that machine doesn't become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer's global .gitignore list, which usually prevents it from being shared publicly.Read full article Comments

articles.description: Anthropic bought billions of dollars' worth of natural gas turbines in a deal that could give it buyer's remorse.
articles.content: AI’s power crunch has become so acute that Anthropic, a company that has generally avoided buying physical infrastructure, is spending $3.4 billion on natural gas turbines. The AI company, which is planning to go public this year, is buying Caterpillar generators that equipment supplier OnePWR had originally ordered, according to a Financial Times report. The generators are capable of producing up to 1.7 gigawatts of electricity. Historically, Anthropic has preferred to rent rather than buy. The company disclosed in its S-1 filing in May that it is paying SpaceX subsidiary xAI $1.25 billion per month through May 2029 to use xAI’s computing power. “We expect to enter into additional similar services contracts,” Anthropic stated in the filing, meaning more deals to rent computing power. But as demand for compute ramps up, the market for power has also grown increasingly uncertain, which may have forced its hand. The backlog for natural gas turbines stretches into the early 2030s, and queues to connect to the electrical grid can be just as long. Anthropic’s purchase looks like a last resort. According to the report, OnePWR ordered the turbines a couple years ago but couldn’t find financing to complete the purchase. Anthropic had planned to buy them from OnePWR but instead went directly to Caterpillar, the manufacturer. It’s not clear why OnePWR was unable to secure financing despite Anthropic’s apparent interest as a customer. Whatever the case, Anthropic likely wanted to keep the generating capacity to itself rather than give a competitor an opportunity to snap it up. AI companies have been ramping up their purchases of natural gas equipment and supplies in recent years. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta have all announced plans to build massive natural gas power plants to power their data centers on-site, rather than drawing from the public grid. The binge has given a second wind to fracking, the drilling method used to extract natural gas from underground rock. And if the buildout proceeds as planned, U.S. data centers alone could consume more natural gas than Germany and Japan combined by 2035. The reliance on natural gas also exposes hyperscalers to price fluctuations. One analyst expects that prices could more than triple by the end of the decade in some markets. articles.title: Democrat Ana Aho Rink to represent Marquette, Ishpeming, Munising in Michigan's 109th House district
articles.description: Ana Aho Rink, a physician assistant who once worked at Planned Parenthood, was elected to represent Michigan's 109th House district, which includes Marquette.
articles.content: Rep. Ana Aho Rink speaks with April Baer via Zoom. ( Michigan Public)Republicans swept the state House seats in the Upper Peninsula back in 2024 — including the often Democratic stronghold of Marquette. In this year's midterm election, Anna Aho Rink flipped that seat back to blue.Rink is a physician assistant who once worked at the only Planned Parenthood clinic in the U.P. The clinic has since closed. Rink will represent Michigan's 109th House district, which includes Marquette, Ishpeming, Munising, Negaunee, and Norway.On Wednesday, Nov. 4, Rink spoke with Stateside's April Baer about what the win means for her region. Scroll up to listen to a recording of the interview, or read the transcript below.April Baer: Do you mind telling us a little bit about how you came to get into politics?Anna Aho Rink: I've been a physician assistant for over 20 years. Nearly 17 of those years was working at the Planned Parenthood office in my hometown of Marquette, Michigan. That had been really a dream job caring for my community, and not just my community. There is such a lack of reproductive health care resources throughout the entire Upper Peninsula, and even into northern Wisconsin. I cared for patients from all over this whole giant landmass. And in April of 2025, due to Trump budget cuts to Medicaid reimbursement, Title X funding for Planned Parenthood offices, my office was forced to close. And just like that, we lost significant access to care. Really, really necessary and life-saving care here in the U.P.. I had already been struggling and hustling, trying to make connections for people, and get them the healthcare services they needed in a rural area, but as well as in a situation where healthcare is becoming increasingly expensive and harder to access, and people's insurance plans are covering less and less. And really, when my office closed, that was kind of the last straw. I was like, "Okay, how much can I continue to hustle from the ground level, and continue to see folks have their rug swept out from underneath them, and people that care trying to pick up the pieces repeatedly, when truly it is policy being made in Lansing and Washington that is not working for us."AB: I just wonder if you have any observations for us about how reproductive care has changed in the U.P.? You mentioned the fact that there are big cuts to Medicaid that go far beyond reproductive care. What does health care access look like in your community right now?AAR: It's a struggle across the Upper Peninsula for folks to access the care they need. And we are short on providers. Our rural hospital systems are struggling to keep their doors open. And every day people wonder, "Hey, will I still be able to stay with this provider? Or will I be forced to travel hours to see someone to get the care that I need?"But especially with regard to reproductive health care, when my office closed, immediately the community I work in or live in rallied and created a new system, reproductive health resources for the Upper Peninsula. And it is a nonprofit organization that helps to connect people with providers that they can see, resources in terms of like monetary funds that they can access to get care, who safely can provide reproductive health care around the Upper Peninsula. So people know where to access, places to go, since they don't have that kind of central hub that we had before. But certainly having policy at the state level to help facilitate additional care and resources, including mental health care, family medicine across the board, so all people's needs can be met — that is important work that needs to be done. And again, we've seen so much support on the local level, but we need support at the state and federal levels as well in order to make sure our neighbors are being cared for the way they deserve.AB: Access to health care in the U.P. is not a new issue. It's something that a lot of voters have grappled with over a long time. I was curious about what other issues, as you were out on the campaign trail, what kinds of issues people talked to you about that you think really influenced the vote this year?AAR: First and foremost, affordability. Cost of gas, cost of food, housing prices, rent, mortgages, property taxes — all the things that we're doing to just kind of make it day to day. And it was interesting as the campaign progressed on over the course of the summer, I had a lot of people saying, "Oh, we are barely keeping our heads above water. We are really, really struggling to make ends meet at the end of the month." And within the past few weeks, I have spoken to more and more people that have said, "We're really just straight up underwater now. We're not able to pay all of our bills. We didn't make our mortgage payment this month. We've been rationing medications for six months already." The fact that that is the prevailing message that I've heard over and over again really highlights how much people are struggling here, and certainly was reflected in the election results that we saw.AB: What is the first thing that you think you want to take on when you get to Lansing? What's at the top of your to do list?AAR: So there are some energy bills and pension bills that have kind of been left by the wayside that really have folks hurting specifically in my district and have left this little era of uncertainty around those occupations and our energy prices. And so getting those shored up, and dealt with, and out of the way is going to be, I think, huge and has to be top of mind for folks. Putting in caps on prescription drugs such as insulin, and inhalers, emergency medications, life saving medications. That is really crucial. The number of people I've spoken with over the past few months knocking doors that are rationing their insulin, people that have straight up gone without all of their inhalers for their COPD and are really, really struggling because their insurance isn't covering them. That is absolutely unacceptable. We need to do better. And so those things are top of mind. And then, you know, healthcare is my background. And so really working to make sure we maintain access for our rural communities. We need to prioritize that, and we need to make sure that people have insurance and the support that they need in order to be able to pay for that access.AB: Anna, you'll be coming to Lansing as the only U.P. House member who's a Democrat. Are there some issues that you think you could find common ground on with some other folks who may be from other parts of the region that you think you might be able to make an impact on?AAR: 100%. I mean, the thing that is special about Yoopers is that, first and foremost, we care about other Yoopers. And so that is such an easy starting point to find common ground on. All of us know how much people are struggling to pay their bills right now. And so it will be, I think, a really, really great starting point to capture, you know, how can we do the best for our areas? We know that there is a lot of need around emergency services - rural emergency services - here. And so I'm looking forward to partnering with other lawmakers in the U.P. to work on policy changes for that, to help support our rural communities.AB: I want to come back around to something that you mentioned earlier, and that's that a significant portion of the pressure on health care costs as we experience them in Michigan, has to do with things happening within the federal government: cuts to Medicaid, different kind of changes in policies that affect how the state structures its piece of the health care system. What reason do we have to think that what the composition of Lansing looks like might make a difference in how the federal government addresses these kinds of issues in ways that that might change things?AAR: Well, as we experience more and more states having to sort of take things into their own hands, so to speak, to restructure their health care systems, and we see states kind of working together to collaborate and work to create health care systems that actually work for the people that live here, there is going to be ever-increasing pressure on Washington to take care of the whole country. But in the meantime, there is not time to wait. We cannot wait for them. We cannot wait for their policy. We need action now. We need to take care of our people now. We have to figure it out.____________Editor's note: Quotes in this article have been lightly edited for length and clarity. You can play the full audio of this interview near the top of this page.

articles.title: 5 things we learned from Michigan's historic voter turnout in 2026 midterm election
articles.description: There were a lot of “firsts” and broken records in the 2026 midterm. Turnout data is incomplete, but the numbers show most Michiganders cast votes in the midterm.
articles.content: There was a short line for voting at this Ypsilanti polling place on the Nov. 3, 2026 election. But turnout still broke records in surrounding Washtenaw County and the state as a whole.(Mercedes Mejia/Michigan Public)There were a lot of “firsts” and broken records in the 2026 election. Turnout data is incomplete, but the numbers definitely show that a larger portion of Michiganders cast votes in the midterm than they usually do.Here’s what we’ve learned so far about how people made themselves heard.Michigan is still breaking turnout records, but not everywhereThis year’s election was loud. More money was spent on advertising than any prior midterm. Debates, particularly in the U.S. Senate race, were intense. Ballot questions at the state and local level offered voters opportunities to make massive changes that would immediately impact their lives.Michigan State University Political Science Professor Corwin Smidt said we’re seeing communities becoming more politically active.“What we know about voting is its habit-forming,” said Smidt, who used to direct the university’s public polling arm. “Once you do it, you're more likely to do it again, and Michigan's had all these competitive elections, and different issues, and as more people sort of participate it sticks with them.”Turnout increased significantly in many places that may not be surprising, such as Wayne, Kent, and Washtenaw counties.Preliminary data also suggests there were large increases in rural Oscoda and Ogemaw counties. But unlike other counties that saw big increases, voters in Oscoda and Ogemaw only slightly shifted toward Democrats compared to the 2024 presidential election, keeping the Republican margin of victory across the top of the ballot strong in both counties.There is an exception: in the U.S. Senate race, preliminary data suggests Ogemaw is the only county that shifted more toward the Republican candidate relative to the 2024 presidential race.However, a comparison to a presidential election year is not enough.Looking at past midterm races in Oscoda, Ogemaw and many other rural counties, U.S. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson actually underperformed compared to past U.S. Senate and gubernatorial candidates from their own party.Benson outperformed fellow 2026 Michigan Democrats in statewide racesThe governor-elect saw more people vote for her than Democratic candidates for U.S. Senate (El-Sayed), attorney general (Eli Savit) and her replacement for secretary of state (Garlin Gilchrist) in this election. She outperformed them in every county, too, according to preliminary results.As political parties pick apart results to argue for or against “centrist” platforms, an overperformance like this is being held up as evidence about where voters stand.In three of the last five midterm elections in Michigan, the winning governor candidate outperformed all other members of their party who were running for statewide office.Benson is responsible for the most recent exception. She outperformed Gov. Gretchen Whitmer by less than 1% when she ran as the incumbent for secretary of state in 2022.The same thing happened to Republican Gov. Rick Snyder in the 2014 midterm, when he was outperformed by Secretary of State Ruth Johnson. But Snyder still did better than the Republican U.S. Senate and attorney general candidates on the ballot.Benson’s overperformance in the 2026 election may partly be explained by people “splitting” their tickets: voting Democrat for governor, then choosing Republicans or third parties for the other races.But overperformance is not a good measurement of ticket splitting on its own. Preliminary data also suggests about 1% of people who turned in ballots skipped the governor’s race. A slightly smaller number of voters skipped the U.S. Senate race.Around twice as many voters skipped the attorney general and secretary of state races.The data doesn’t show how many voters skipped all of these races or just one of them. Sometimes, voters submit ballots that are entirely blank.General elections represent more of Michigan's population, but primaries fall short Not long ago, Michigan’s midterms only saw a small portion of the state go to the polls. About 40% of Michigan’s voting age population participated in the 2010 and 2014 elections.The result: Candidates got votes from about a fifth of the state’s population and still became governors, attorney generals and senators.The record-breaking 4.8 million votes cast in the November 2026 midterm are enough for about 60% of the state’s voting age populace.Some counties saw even higher participation. Leelanau, a county near Traverse City with just over 20,000 residents, saw over 80% of its voting age population turn out.But Nov. 3 wasn’t the only election this year. The August primary election saw a "bruising" competition on the Democratic side for the U.S. Senate seat, between El-Sayed and Congresswoman Haley Stevens.Plus, Democrats and Republicans had open primaries for governor. That last time that happened was 2018.2018 was also the last time the midterm primary saw half as many voters as the general election.“We know when you vote in the primary, you’re very likely to vote again in the general,” Smidt said. “So that’s usually why people focus on it a lot.”But, he said, low participation means primaries “don’t give the full picture.”Plus, research suggests primary voters tend to be the more engaged, partisan and older. Their reasons for choosing one candidate or another may have less to do with a candidate’s platform and more to do with perceptions of electability in the upcoming general.In the U.S. Senate primary, Stevens got almost twice as many Detroit votes as El-Sayed.That led some to question whether El-Sayed had a “Detroit problem”; not that El-Sayed would lose the city, but that he might lose the state if enough Black voters drifted toward Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers or did not turn out.“That narrative didn’t really make sense,” Smidt said, pointing to multiple polls that showed a clear majority of Black voters supporting El-Sayed.In the end, El-Sayed did about as well as any Democrat running for U.S. Senate in the city. Turnout was normal for a midterm; El-Sayed won with a larger percentage of the Detroit vote than Elissa Slotkin had in 2024, as well as a similar percentage as Gary Peters in 2020 and Debbie Stabenow in 2018.Absentee ballots and Election Day polling centers are popular. Early in-person voting? Not so muchAt least 40% of Michiganders turned in a ballot by dropping it off or mailing it in, preliminary data suggests. That can happen on Election Day, but most absentee voters submitted their ballots early.Smidt said early voting changes the dynamics of a campaign. An October or November “surprise” such as Stevens endorsing Rogers at the last minute used to be potentially devastating."How big of a deal can it be,” he said, "if more than half of people have already voted?"Absentee ballots are not the only way to vote early. This is the second statewide election in which state law required early in-person polling centers available to the public across the state. It was opt-in for communities that wanted it in previous years.But preliminary data suggests that a small group of voters took advantage of that option."We're testing the limits of our clerks right now, by having a lot of options," Smidt said. "It's great for the voter. It's hard for the clerks."Even with the options presented by absentee and early voting, preliminary data suggests a huge chunk of voters showed up to vote in person on Election Day."And so maybe this [is a] downplay in early voting, maybe there was some novelty," he said. "But also maybe we're going to have to look at whether we're funding all these different forms of election administration correctly given the level of popularity they might have."A governor-elect who used to be the state's top election official might help, he said.Regardless, Michigan's election system is set to be tested again in 2028, as the state is fifth in line for the Democratic presidential primaries that year.Turnout was a mixed bag for Michigan cities — but one stands outOn Election Day, officials for Michigan’s two largest cities had very different expectations for turnout.Detroit Clerk Janice Winfrey anticipated a record-breaking 40-45% turnout for her city. Grand Rapids Clerk Joel Hondorp expected a “normal” turnout for a midterm.“It doesn’t feel like turnout is extremely high, but it doesn’t feel like it's lower, either," he said on Election Day.Hondorp was more correct.Detroit’s turnout of 39% beat the city’s 2022 total, but fell just shy of the 2018 midterm in percentage (41%). More votes were cast this year, but more people were registered to vote in the city.A similar pattern played out in Grand Rapids, resulting in a nearly 53% turnout this year. But Dearborn smashed its past turnout with nearly 57% of registered voters turning in ballots. That’s a larger percentage than the 2022 and 2018 midterms, as well as the 2024 and 2020 presidential elections.“I think what got them to the polls are candidates who centered the issues of working class families, like many of the American and Muslim American families right here in the city of Dearborn," Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud told NPR.President Donald Trump was credited with “winning” Dearborn in 2024. But of the people who cast ballots, less than half voted for him. Remaining votes were split between third parties and people who skipped that race.Abdul El-Sayed got two times as many votes in this year’s U.S. Senate race.Votebeat's Election Expert Desk contributed to this story.

articles.content: For a long time, SpaceX has been synonymous with the development of newer, larger, and ever-more-reusable rockets. But that began to change over the last decade with the introduction of Starlink, and the change has accelerated during the last 18 months as the company has pivoted to data and artificial intelligence. At last week's UP.Summit conference in Florida, the vice president of launch at SpaceX, Kiko Dontchev, offered some of the most revealing comments to date about the company's changing focus, how it is embracing AI, and why the Falcon 9 rocket—which has dominated global launch for a decade and remains the world's preeminent launch vehicle—is firmly on the road to retirement. "In the last couple years, when I talk about SpaceX, yes, we are a rocket company, but fundamentally we are an infrastructure company at this point," Dontchev said. "We're building infrastructure on the ground and low Earth orbit, soon on the Moon, and obviously eventually Mars."Read full article Comments

articles.title: F1 in Brazil: You’ve got to keep your tires alive
articles.description: A topsy-turvy grid and intermittent rain resulted in a very entertaining race.
articles.content: In sports, a “dead rubber” is a match that takes place after the outcome of the series or championship has already been decided. The people in charge hate this*—if you wrap up a title two-thirds of the way through a season, the viewers evaporate, as there’s nothing left at stake. But anyone who decided to skip this year’s Brazilian Grand Prix this past weekend missed one of the year’s most entertaining races, as a combination of a mixed-up starting order, some very fast drivers at the back, and a wet track that dried and then saw rain again resulted in action aplenty. A peculiarity of F1 is that even if you manage to win a championship, there’s no guarantee you’ll be in a position to defend it. Take McLaren’s Lando Norris, who took the crown in 2025 after a nail-biting fight with his teammate Oscar Piastri and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen. Sadly for Lando, McLaren did not start this year in a position to win races, and even with several upgrades, the team has produced a car that is still very tricky to drive. But this weekend in Brazil, Norris demonstrated the form that earned him the number 1. Rain on Saturday during qualifying helped jumble the usual running order. It was heavy enough that drivers used the wet weather tire with deep treads, which usually generates so much spray that visibility disappears and running has to be suspended. But with fewer cars on track in the later knockout qualifying sessions, this was not a problem for once. More disruption came from grid penalties for Verstappen and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, both of whom needed to use extra power unit components outside of the season’s allowance.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Who’s the Detroit News Boys High School Team of the Week? Vote now!
articles.content: Every week, Michigan high school teams across the state are winning championships, breaking records, reaching milestones and putting together seasons worth celebrating. The Detroit News is recognizing those standout squads as Team of the Week. From nominations submitted by coaches, parents and fans, we’ve selected five boys teams as this week’s finalists. Any boys team, in any sport and from any region of Michigan, is eligible. Now it’s your turn to decide who deserves the honor. Voting is open from 10 a.m. Monday through 5 p.m. Thursday. Readers can vote multiple times, so rally your school community and get everyone involved. The winner will be announced Friday morning in a special Detroit News post celebrating its accomplishments. Who deserves to be named the Detroit News Boys Team of the Week? Cast your vote below. Birmingham Seaholm didn't just repeat as Division 2 boys tennis state champion. It dominated the competition, winning 35 matches at the state finals, the most of any program. Seaholm claimed five flight championships, with all eight flights advancing to at least the semifinals. Senior Kalil Wahab and freshman Hunter Helfman went unbeaten in five matches, winning every one in straight sets. That included a 7-6 (1), 6-4 victory in the No. 1 doubles final. Sophomore Charlie Griffith also came through, winning his second consecutive individual title at No. 3 singles. He battled through a three-set final, 6-2, 5-7, 6-3, and finished the season with a 20-4 record. It was another dominant performance for a program that continues to set the standard in Division 2. Holland Calvary Christian didn't leave much doubt about who belonged at the top of Division 4 boys cross country. The team put all five scorers in the top 15 Saturday at Michigan International Speedway, cruising to its second consecutive state championship with 35 points. No boys team in any division scored better at the state finals. Senior Noah Schipper led the way with a fifth-place finish in 16:03.7. Senior Christian Getz wasn't far behind, taking seventh in 16:06.1. Senior Brody Van Tuinen also delivered, finishing 12th to earn his first All-State honor. With all five scorers in the top 15, Holland Calvary Christian put together one of the day's most impressive performances and defended its state championship in convincing fashion. Troy put together a season nobody else in Michigan boys soccer could match. The team finished 19-0-2, becoming the state's only unbeaten boys soccer program. It capped its historic run with a 2-1 victory over Livonia Stevenson in the Division 1 state championship Saturday at Grand Ledge High School. It was Troy's second state championship and first since 2003. Senior defender Faris Ibrahim and sophomore midfielder Connor Hotts each scored on a set piece in the championship game. Hotts finished the season with 20 goals and 14 assists. Troy also took down Salem, 5-2, in Wednesday's semifinal before closing out its unbeaten season with another championship performance. Warren De La Salle has turned winning Division 2 state championships into an annual tradition. The team captured its third consecutive state title Saturday at Grand Ledge High School, holding off St. Joseph, 3-2, in a back-and-forth championship game. Senior forward Andrew Corder was the difference-maker all weekend. He scored twice in a 3-2 semifinal victory over DeWitt before adding two more goals and an assist against St. Joseph. Senior goalkeeper Dominic Baldarotta also came up big, making several acrobatic catches on long passes into the box as St. Joseph pushed for a late equalizer. The championship was De La Salle's eighth overall, giving the program the third-most state titles of any boys soccer team in Michigan, regardless of division. After going without a district championship since 2002, Jonesville finally broke through Friday, Nov. 6, with a 52-30 victory over former Big 8 rival Union City in the Division 7 playoffs. The win capped a remarkable turnaround for a team that lost four consecutive games early in the season before winning five straight. Senior running back John Milks led the way with 190 yards and three TDs on 26 carries, pushing his season total past 2,300 yards. Senior quarterback Carson Young threw for 114 yards and three TDs, connecting with senior Reece Rundquist for two scores. The defense also delivered three takeaways, highlighted by sophomore Lucas Stanton's 75-yard fumble return for a TD. Stanton added five tackles, while senior Harper Griffiths led the team with nine. President Donald Trump meets with Mayor Zohran Mamdani ahead of the UN General Assembly.
articles.content: On September 21st, 2026, President Donald Trump and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani met ahead of the United Nations (UN) General Assembly to discuss key issues facing the city, such as the cost of living and the Sunnyside Yards housing projects. “I have said time and again that I will work with anyone — no matter what party they belong to, no matter how much we may disagree on other topics — Whoever has the power and the will to lift that weight off New Yorkers’ backs,” said Mayor Mamdani at a press conference at Gracie Mansion. Facilitating discussions on housing proved to be one of the most important factors in improving New Yorker’s lives. “We’ve agreed to set up a new level of that [housing] conversation between our housing and operations team at City Hall and the White House team,” said Mayor Mamdani. According to Mayor Mamdani, 12,000 new homes and 30,000 jobs would be created if the housing projects go into effect at Sunnyside Yards. This could create a new thriving neighborhood for New Yorkers who struggle to find affordable housing. President Trump added, “They’ve been talking about developing [Sunnyside Yards] for 50 years, so maybe they have a shot at doing it.” Both Mayor Mamdani and the president described their last-minute meeting as positive and constructive, with President Trump even hinting that Mayor Mamdani will make a fine mayor. Despite this, President Trump’s appearance at Gracie Mansion raises the question of whether the visit was meant to boost his public perception amid increasing disapproval ratings from the American public. Additionally, Mayor Mamdani still faces tough questions about his campaign promises with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) crackdowns, rising New York Police Department (NYPD) negligence payouts and a housing crisis weighing on everyday life. The timing of their meeting appears to be less than spontaneous. Queens College (QC) Political Science Professor Alexander Reichl said, “They are savvy politicians with sharp eyes on how they can achieve wins and boost their political standing.” He added, “The same might be said of [Mayor] Mamdani. Ultimately, both men see more to gain from a constructive relationship than there is to lose by appearing to negotiate with the enemy.” Since Mayor Mamdani’s inauguration, he and President Trump have met two times, discussing how to make NYC affordable for New Yorkers. “Recent events suggest there are real limits to this alliance — particularly with regard to ICE and immigration. It appears that the mayor will have a tough time getting [President] Trump to back off,” said Reichl. However, these meetings may prove beneficial to improving the city. “Trump is at heart a builder, and Mamdani has been wise to appeal to this impulse,” said Professor Reichl. The recent proposal for Sunnyside Yards housing units could be a shared victory for both Mayor Mamdani and President Trump. Mayor Mamdani can successfully address the NYC housing crisis and President Trump can potentially gain public goodwill from supporting these projects. As Professor Reichl said, “That type of deal may be too enticing for the political rivals to resist!” Your email address will not be published. Notify me of follow-up comments by email.

Commentary: GM’s former factories are attracting data center developers as redevelopment continues
articles.description: General Motors’ historic 2009 bankruptcy was so massive that it’s taken 15 years for a real estate trust to clean up and sell the hundreds of buildings and thousands of acres of land across 14 states that GM left behind. And the work isn’t done yet. Bruce Rasher is RACER Trust’s redevelopment manager. Rasher, who […]
articles.content: Former GM Lansing Plant 6 property. It's among properties being marketed by Revitalizing Auto Communities Environmental Response, or RACER, for industrial uses including for data centers. (RACER photo)General Motors’ historic 2009 bankruptcy was so massive that it’s taken 15 years for a real estate trust to clean up and sell the hundreds of buildings and thousands of acres of land across 14 states that GM left behind. And the work isn’t done yet. Bruce Rasher is RACER Trust’s redevelopment manager. Rasher, who has led the property sales effort since the trust was established by the U.S. Bankruptcy Court in 2011, said the remaining properties should be sold within the next three years. RACER stands for Revitalizing Auto Communities Environmental Response. At its inception, RACER was one of the largest holders of industrial property in the United States. Bruce Rasher – RACER Trust I asked Rasher if he thought it would take so long to close this chapter in what was the biggest industrial bankruptcy in U.S. history, an event that shook the economies of Michigan and much of the manufacturing-dependent Midwest. “I’ve been so focused on the mission I really didn’t think about it,” said Rasher, a former mayor of Marshall. “Some properties take a long time before they sell.” GM’s bankruptcy reorganization was highly controversial because it was financed by a nearly $50 billion taxpayer bailout through the federal Troubled Asset Recovery Program. TARP also saved a dying Chrysler, which filed for bankruptcy a month before GM. The bankruptcy split the automaker into two companies: “new” GM, which continued as an ongoing concern, and “old” GM, which consisted of unwanted property transferred to RACER. A Gallup poll at the time found 51% of Americans opposed the auto bailouts. GM was derisively called “Government Motors” for years. Mitt Romney, a former U.S. Senator from Utah and a Michigan native, famously wrote in the New York Times in 2008 that the federal government had no business bailing out GM and Chrysler. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE But without federal aid, GM and Chrysler might have failed, wiping out more than a million U.S. jobs, according to a forecast by the Center of Automotive Research in Ann Arbor. Racer Trust was allocated $500 million from TARP for the massive environmental cleanup required before many of GM’s former factories and land could be sold. The trust is responsible for monitoring, groundwater treatment and environmental stewardship of some of the more heavily contaminated properties for 100 years, Rasher said. Another $250 million was granted for other costs of selling the properties. Proceeds from the sales go to offset about $100 million in RACER costs that TARP didn’t cover, Rasher said. RACER doesn’t disclose sale prices of its properties. The former Buick City complex in Flint now contains the Flint Commerce Center Building at right and Lear Corporation at left. (RACER photo)The former Buick City complex in Flint now contains the Flint Commerce Center Building at right and Lear Corporation at left. (RACER photo)M1 Concourse racetrack in Pontiac. (RACER photo)M1 Concourse racetrack in Pontiac. (RACER photo) The trust’s work hasn’t undone all the economic carnage inflicted by GM’s bankruptcy on struggling communities like Flint, Saginaw and Pontiac that were GM company towns for decades. GM cut 20,000 jobs, shuttered 14 assembly and parts plants and terminated the franchises of 2,000 dealerships in its bankruptcy reorganization, according to the MotorCities National Heritage Area. But a recent economic impact study commissioned by Racer found that tens of thousands of new jobs and billions of dollars in business investment have been generated at the former GM facilities. Nearly 82,000 permanent direct and indirect jobs with annual payrolls of $7.6 billion have been created at the former GM sites, an annual average of $92,700 per job. The new business investment has generated $63.6 billion in overall economic impact across the 14 states where GM had operations. All the former GM’s 166 buildings—mostly factories, warehouses and offices—and 75% of the nearly 7,000 acres of vacant land have been sold, Rasher said. The buyers represent a mix of industries, creating a much-needed economic diversification in communities that were overly dependent on manufacturing. United Wholesale Mortgage employs 4,300 people at GM’s former sprawling Centerpoint engineering campus in Pontiac, the most of any sites sold by Racer Trust, according to the study. United Wholesale Mortgage in Pontiac. (RACER photo) Most of the more than two dozen remaining properties are being marketed by Racer as potential sites for data centers, warehouses, and solar and battery storage facilities. Among them are former assembly and parts plant locations in Lansing, Saginaw and the Flint area. Rasher said he gets as many as 10 feelers a week from developers inquiring about those properties for possible data centers. “It’s like a gold rush right now,” Rasher told me when I spoke with him on Election Day. That could change with Democrats taking control of the U.S. House and Senate, as well as the Michigan Legislature and governor’s office in the blue tsunami. Strong opposition by voters to data centers needed to power artificial intelligence helped Democrats across the country defeat Republicans in last week’s election. But if the Democrats can work to restore economic policy certainty that businesses crave, the way could be cleared to sell the remaining properties RACER holds. “I truly believe that, based on inquiries from developers, uncertainty about the business climate, high interest rates and tariffs are causing them to hold off,” he said. Rasher said the sale of GM’s former facilities was a team effort involving federal state and local governments and their economic development arms. “I think this is a model for helping communities hurt by severe economic circumstances,” he said.

articles.title: Control Room: A central system to track and stop model workloads across our research infrastructure
articles.description: Learn how OpenAI’s Control Room tracks model workloads across our research infrastructure and can rapidly stop them when safety or security concerns arise.
articles.content: As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed. To solve this, we built Control Room. Control Room is a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise. It connects every research inference workload, including agentic sampling for model training and evaluation, data processing, and more. This works together with our misalignment monitoring systems, and halts model output within 35 seconds of a decision to intervene to stop or pause a job. It has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down. Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest. Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed. Control Room works by integrating a few systems: the workload, the inference engine, and the centralized Control Room service. The workload is the job being run, such as a reinforcement learning experiment, an evaluation, a high-volume sampling or data processing job. We require every research workload that does agentic inference to be associated with an approved safety case. The inference engine, or just engine, is the model itself. You can think of the engine as the brain of the model, running directly on GPUs. A workload normally uses one or more models, which might be running on one or more different inference engines. The same inference engine might be used by more than one different workload. The Control Room service tracks jobs and controls whether they are allowed to continue generating model output. Engines check with the Control Room service before fulfilling a request. If a job has been stopped, the service denies the request, preventing further output. Control Room is integrated in the following way: When starting a new job, the workload code requests a new job_id from Control Room. Whenever the workload needs to sample tokens from a model, it makes a request to an inference engine running that model, passing the job_id. The engine requests permission from Control Room to fulfill that request, passing the job_id along to Control Room. Control Room checks whether that job has been terminated, and if so, it denies the inference request. The engine responds to the workload's inference request with a refusal, stopping further model output from being produced for that job. The process starts with a researcher launching a job—for example, an experiment or an evaluation. Job code (or workload code) is owned and run by researchers. Inference engines might be started as part of this job, or standalone engines which are not associated with any particular job might already be running. The workload code requests a job ID, associating the job with an approved safety case. The job itself makes this request. Control Room records the job and returns its identifier. The workload will attach this same ID to its inference requests. The request includes the job_id. This request is made directly from the workload code and does not pass through Control Room. Before fulfilling the request, the inference engine asks Control Room whether this job is still authorized to run. The job is still authorized, so Control Room grants permission. The inference engine can now fulfill the request. The model generates a response and the engine sends it back to the research job. The job can use that output and continue its work. A person or monitoring system tells Control Room to stop this job. Control Room marks its ID as stopped. The workload code remains running. We do not rely on the workload code to correctly perform a check of whether or not the job is still running. The engine asks Control Room for permission to fulfill the new inference request, passing along the same job ID. When the engine checks permission again, Control Room denies the stopped job. The engine must refuse the inference request. The engine returns a refusal instead of model output. The research process may remain alive, and the engine remains available to other authorized jobs. All of our frontier reinforcement learning jobs run with a monitor. A monitor is another model which inspects everything that the model-being-trained is doing, and raises an alert if it detects a problem. For example, our recent DNS-related incident(opens in a new window) was caught by a monitor. Control Room and our monitoring system are integrated in the following way: If the monitoring system detects a potential issue, depending on the details and severity, the monitoring system may decide to stop the job. In this case, the monitoring system sends a message to Control Room to stop the job, passing the job_id. Control Room records that the job is terminated. Next time the job having that job_id makes an inference request to sample more tokens from any model running on any engine, the request will be denied, stopping further model output. The maximum time between the moment when Control Room receives an instruction to stop a job, and the moment when further progress is no longer possible, is 35 seconds. The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly. Workloads, including experiments, evaluation jobs, etc., are normally owned and operated by researchers or teams of researchers. As a result, workload code changes often, and is not an ideal place to implement critical load-bearing safety protections. Because of this, our implementation is designed to be resilient to buggy or broken workload code. We achieve this by implementing the termination mechanism in the inference layer. Workload code is highly-varied and decentralized. In contrast, there are only a very small number of inference code paths in use across all of OpenAI research, and their deployments are much more centralized and uniform. This means that the inference layer can serve as a bottleneck, where we can get strong guarantees that all model inference running in research is subject to Control Room authorization checks on every inference request. We additionally run continual agentic and programmatic sweeps to check that users are not accidentally or maliciously launching rogue engine implementations with Control Room unimplemented or disabled. Finally, our system “fails closed”, meaning that the Control Room integration in the engines is configured in such a way that if the Control Room service goes down, either due to a system error or because it is disabled for any other reason, including tampering by a bad actor, then all inference requests will be denied until Control Room resumes normal operation. Fail-closed is rolled out now to all frontier model research workloads, and will finish rolling out across all remaining research workloads over the next few days. Control Room is just one part of our holistic approach to safe frontier model training and deployment. We’ll continue to strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches. If you want to help build systems for the safe and secure development and deployment of AGI, we're hiring!

articles.title: Michigan coach Kyle Whittingham fires embattled offensive coordinator Jason Beck
articles.description: Kyle Whittingham has made his first major move as Michigan’s coach, firing embattled offensive coordinator Jason Beck.
articles.content: Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham glances at the scoreboard against Michigan State in the fourth quarter of an NCAA college football game, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026, in Ann Arbor, Mich. (AP Photo/Lon Horwedel)(Lon Horwedel/AP Photo/Lon Horwedel / FR170538 AP)Kyle Whittingham has made his first major move as Michigan's coach, firing embattled offensive coordinator Jason Beck.“The results have not matched our desired outcome, and I felt that a change in leadership was required for our offense,” Whittingham said in a statement Sunday night. “We need to put our offensive players and the entire team in the best possible position to be successful."Whittingham named Jim Harding as interim offensive coordinator for the rest of the season. Harding is the team's offensive line coach and assistant head coach. He worked with Whittingham for 12 seasons at Utah, including two years as co-offensive coordinator.The Wolverines (5-4, 2-4 Big Ten) started the season ranked No. 16 in the AP Top 25 and have fallen short of expectations with one of the nation's worst offenses, shaky special teams and a defense that has been solid at times.Michigan might fall short of earning a bowl bid as underdogs at No. 18 Oregon (6-3, 3-2) on Saturday, at home against No. 4 UCLA and against rival and 21st-ranked Ohio State on the road.The Wolverines barely avoided being shut out for the first time since 2014 against rival Michigan State, scoring with 1:35 left in a 15-6 loss after being favored to win by two touchdowns.Michigan was been held scoreless in the first half three times in a season for the first time since 1979.Under Beck, the Wolverines were ranked No. 132 out of 138 FBS teams in total offense, No. 126 in scoring, No. 125 in passing offense and No. 109 in rushing offense.Beck was Whittingham's offensive coordinator at Utah last season, helping the team rank No. 2 in rushing, No. 4 in total offense and No. 5 in scoring offense. He was New Mexico's offensive coordinator in 2024.“We appreciate the hard work and effort that Jason has dedicated to the program,” Whittingham said. “Jason is a great man and coach, and unfortunately, it did not work out the way that we wanted it to at Michigan. We wish Jason and his family nothing but the best in the future.”After a 20-14 loss to Minnesota last month, when quarterback Bryce Underwood did not play well one week after making many positive plays in a loss to Iowa, tight end Zach Marshall criticized Beck in group text messages that were leaked on social media.Marshall publicly apologized, but he did not play in the following game against Penn State due to a noninjury situation, according to Whittingham.Michigan's quarterback situation that Beck managed was closely watched with a former No. 1 recruit getting benched in favor of a backup with a familiar name.Underwood was taken out of the game against Penn State after the team was held scoreless in a first half for the first of three straight home games. Tommy Carr, whose grandfathers are College Hall of Famers and brother is Notre Dame's quarterback, successfully filled in for Underwood in a comeback win against the Nittany Lions.Carr struggled against the Spartans, but Whittingham said the offensive coaches wanted to stick with him and the head coach said he agreed with their call.No matter who has taken snaps this season, Michigan has failed to consistently make plays on offense and it cost Beck his job.

What is an API endpoint? A guide to connected software
articles.description: Learn what an API endpoint is, how requests and responses work, common HTTP methods, and how to test and secure endpoints, with ElevenAPI examples.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. An API (Application Programming Interface) endpoint is the specific URL where an API receives requests and sends back responses. API endpoints serve as the exact web address where an application connects to a server to request data or run a command. While traditional architectures are still in use, modern applications rely on REST APIs to handle HTTP requests across diverse services. This guide explains how endpoints process requests, how to format your calls, and how to maintain API endpoint security in production environments. We’ll also show you how to connect your systems cleanly using ElevenAPI, and ship production-ready audio workflows. An API endpoint is a digital location that an API uses to receive requests and return responses. Client applications use a specific URL tied to this endpoint to access server resources. Every endpoint route handles a distinct interaction by pairing an HTTP method with a resource path. The client sends a request to that route, and the server processes the data before sending a response with a status code. For example, when an application requests user metadata or submits a data payload, it sends an HTTP request to a designated endpoint URL hosted on the API server. While the terms API, API endpoint, and URL are frequently used together, they represent distinct components of software architecture. An API provides the complete software interface that sets the rules and protocols for two applications to communicate. Meanwhile, an API endpoint serves as a specific digital entry point on a server that the apps use for two-way communication. Finally, a URL is the complete written web address string that client applications use to locate and connect to that endpoint over the network. The main differences between API, endpoints, and URLs include: API endpoints use a structured request-and-response cycle between client applications and servers, which typically follows these steps: REST API endpoints use standard HTTP methods to define the actions clients execute on a server resource. GET requests read data and make no changes to backend resources. In contrast, POST requests write data by submitting new data to create resources or trigger server-side actions. Additionally, developers use PUT or PATCH requests to modify existing records, and DELETE to remove specific resources from the database. In ElevenAPI, integrations mostly rely on GET and POST requests, alongside streaming and WebSocket endpoints for real-time audio. GET endpoints retrieve available voice and model metadata, while POST endpoints execute generation tasks, such as running Text to Speech synthesis. Examining real-world requests in ElevenAPI illustrates how API endpoints function in production environments. With ElevenAPI, each endpoint route maps to specific HTTP methods that perform certain tasks, such as fetching system metadata or generating audio. Client applications send GET requests to retrieve information and POST requests to submit data and execute processing tasks. Here’s how these core routes work in production. GET https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/models retrieves a list of available voice synthesis models and their capabilities. This request requires the xi-api-key HTTP header for authentication but does not require a request body. The server processes the query and returns a JSON payload containing model details. POST https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech/{voice_id} sends payload data to the server to generate audio. Your application sends a JSON body containing parameters, such as text and model_id to execute Text to Speech synthesis. The endpoint processes these parameters and streams formatted audio back to your application. Read more in the Text to Speech API reference. Development teams choose from seven common API architectures, and make decisions based on their data transfer needs. Building web integrations that need stateless, standardized HTTP communication using structured JSON or XML data formats Enterprise apps demand strict security protocols, formal messaging contracts, and XML-based data exchange Client apps need to query precise data fields in a single request to avoid overfetching or underfetching data Client apps execute specific functions or processes directly on a remote server with minimal network overhead Connecting high-performance microservices that require low-latency communication and binary serialization Building interactive apps that require persistent, two-way connections for real-time data streaming and instant response Connecting web browsers and client applications to server-side resources over standard HTTP and HTTPS protocols ElevenAPI blends several architectural styles into a single platform to maximize efficiency and minimize latency. Typically, it uses REST for standard requests and WebSocket protocols for real-time audio streaming. Using design best practices keeps API endpoints stable, maintainable, and resilient even when underlying platforms change and use cases scale. ElevenAPI uses clean REST rules to simplify integration for engineering teams, such as: Testing API endpoints early confirms authentication and validates network connectivity before developers write application logic. Send a request to GET https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/models (or run curl https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/models) using the xi-api-key HTTP header to validate credentials, verify network access, and return available models. Then, monitor live traffic and watch for HTTP 429 error responses. Engineering teams track metrics to spot unexpected usage spikes and adjust outbound request rates accordingly.
