articles.title: Detroit City Council to choose 5 honorary street signs from 20 nominees
articles.description: One council member is proposing a one-year moratorium on new applications in 2027 to consider amendments to the secondary street sign process.
articles.content: Detroit Free Press is a partner and shares a reporter with BridgeDetroit. Stories shared are not under a paywall. Detroit Free Press Every year, family, friends and admirers of notable Detroiters make a case for street signs displaying their names, but only five applications make the cut. Detroit City Council is slated to make those decisions on Tuesday, Nov. 10. Council will choose from 20 applicants, many of which rolled over from previous years. There are three new nominations this year: Melvin Franklin, Luther “Badman” Keith and Tyrone Winfrey, Sr. Blue secondary street signs serve as an honorary recognition and are placed above or below a street’s official sign. Installations will begin later this month. The city initially received 22 applications, but at the Oct. 23 planning and economic development committee meeting, Lisa DiChiera, deputy director of the Historic Designation Advisory Board, said one withdrew. Another, Henry “Blaze” Marzette, a police officer turned drug dealer who controlled much of the trade in Detroit, was pulled from consideration by the committee at the October meeting. View the full list online or on the council’s Oct. 23 committee agenda. More information on nominations is available on the city’s website. Applications that do not receive the votes can be rolled over and heard in the following years up to five times. However, District 4 Council Member Latisha Johnson is proposing a one-year moratorium on new applications in 2027 to provide the city a chance to amend the process for a more streamlined approach. Johnson said it is difficult to manage a heaping stack of applications, which includes new applicants and those rolled over from previous years. If approved, the moratorium would prevent new applications in 2027 but council could continue with the existing rollover applications, Johnson said, who requested a resolution to be drafted. That request has been referred to the city’s planning and economic development committee for its meeting Thursday, Nov. 12. “I personally would like to see more of our residents being recognized for the work they do in the neighborhoods. It seems to have become a popularity contest,” Johnson said. Historic Preservation Planner Janice Tillmon previously asked City Council to consider changes, including limiting applications and raising the cap on annual secondary street signs. Tillmon researched how other cities identify residents and found Detroit is the only one to allow rollover applications and has a low cap on the number of winners allowed. Musician and founder of Motown group Melvin Franklin was a founding member of legendary group The Temptations. Signed to Motown in 1961, The Temptations earned multiple Grammy awards and were inducted in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1989. Franklin’s granddaughter, Detroit resident Nakira Jordan, said she is proud to share Franklin’s legacy — and she wants Detroit to feel the same. Jordan highlighted the importance of celebrating and honoring “the people who made Motown’s legendary” right here at home. “The world remembers his (Franklin’s) voice,” Jordan said. “Our family carries his name, and the street sign will help Detroit preserve his legacy.” Franklin attended Northwestern High School and lived on Clairmount Avenue, where a sign honoring him is proposed. He and his family gathered neighbors and Motown artists in his home and cooked many meals for guests. “Detroit gave the world a soundtrack,” said Franklin’s other granddaughter, Michigan state Rep. Morgan Foreman. “Our grandfather helped create that sound, and his legacy deserves to be remembered right here at home.” Newspaper’s first Black sportswriter and activist Luther Keith was an award-winning journalist for The Detroit News for 35 years and was the publication’s first Black sportswriter, state capitol reporter and editor, specifically an assistant city editor. Keith was also the founding director for Wayne State University’s Journalism Institute for Media Diversity and mentored Black journalists. Luther Keith, a fierce community advocate, journalist and musician died Wednesday March 5, 2025. He was 74. Credit: Khary Frazier He founded ARISE Detroit! after leaving The Detroit News in 2005 and led the organization for 18 years, where he advocated for volunteerism, particularly during the annual Neighborhoods Day in early August when residents host scores of community events including. The nonprofit aims to address issues surrounding illiteracy, high school dropout rates, crime and youth violence, drug abuse and more. Attorney Erin Keith, Keith’s daughter, told the planning committee of her father’s accomplishments and love for the city. To post her father’s sign at the intersection of Livernois Avenue and Eight Mile Road would be perfect, she said, as it is near Baker’s Keyboard Lounge, the venue Keith played the night before he died. Keith was also a blues musician who wrote his own songs, produced albums and often performed at Baker’s Keyboard Lounge under the name Luther “Badman” Keith. “He loved this city with all his heart, and I always jokingly said my father belonged to me and my mother and the family, but he really belonged to this city. And I continue to share him with everyone I know, everywhere I go.” An advocate for education Tyrone Winfrey Sr., was a longtime education and youth advocate who dedicated much of his life and career to helping young Detroiters go to college. In addition to years spent in admissions and counseling at Michigan State University and University of Michigan, Winfrey previously was a Detroit Board of Education board member and president. He later served as the first chief of staff and senior administrator for the Education Achievement Authority of Michigan, a state-run organization that runs poor performing schools in Detroit. Tyrone Winfrey, executive director of community affairs for the Detroit Public Schools Community District, beside his wife, Detroit City Clerk Janice Winfrey. Tyrone, 63, died on Saturday, Nov. 5, 2022. Courtesy of Chrystal Wilson / DPSCD Winfrey was the husband of Detroit City Clerk Janice Winfrey, who spoke about her late husband’s legacy during the Oct. 23 meeting. “Tyrone gave his life to the children of this city,” Janice Winfrey said. “His lifelong passion was to ensure that all of our children had an opportunity to higher education. Not just the ones from Cass Renaissance and King, but (that) all the children of the city of Detroit had an opportunity to higher education, and we’re just so grateful that you all thought enough of his work to recognize it.” Tyrone Winfrey served as the director of community affairs at DPSCD from 2017 until he died in 2022. The Detroit Public Schools Community District awarded him with a Lifetime of Excellence Tribute in 2021. He attended Hampton Elementary School, Cass Tech High School and later Wayne State University for graduate studies. The sign honoring his name would be posted near Indiana Avenue where he grew up in northwest Detroit. Rollover nominees There are 17 candidates for secondary street signs who were previously nominated. They are: George Clinton, Barbara Rose-Collins, George Cook, Jr., the Rev. Dr. Clarence Crews, Sr., Gabriel Fred Crutcher, Dr. Haifa Fakhouri, Ernest Harden, Jr., Ronald J. Hewitt, John Lee Hooker, Dick “Night Train” Lane, Daniel J. Loepp, the Rev. Dr. John Payne, Jalen Rose, John Sinclair, Tony Spina, Andrew Starks, Martha Jean “The Queen” Steinberg.

articles.title: New grocery co-ops can take over a decade to stabilize. Can Detroit’s push through the hard first years?
articles.description: After a public fundraising plea, Detroit People’s Food Co-Op has drawn overwhelming support from residents and local organizations. Co-ops across the Midwest say building deep community roots is key to surviving the difficult early years.
articles.content: This story also appeared in Next City This story was produced with Next City as part of its Local Reporting Hub, with funding from the Kresge Foundation. When Detroit People’s Food Co-Op asked the community for help keeping its doors open in September, the response came from across the city: churches organized shopping days, a local nonprofit awarded a historic grant and a group of Black women rallied to become member-owners. The outpouring of support has offered a lifeline to the grocery cooperative, which opened its Woodward Avenue storefront on May 1, 2024, after years of fundraising. Despite a strong opening, the store’s recent financial struggles reflect a challenge facing food co-ops across the country: building a community-owned grocery store is one thing. Financial sustainability is a tougher battle. Anthony Goodwin, who serves as chief executive officer of Development Co+operative at the National Co+op Grocers, told BridgeDetroit that it can take between 10 and 12 years for a start-up co-op to become financially sustainable. “During this extended timeline, the market conditions that originally prompted the co-op’s formation may change significantly,” Goodwin said. “(And) achieving financial viability as a single-store operator is increasingly difficult in today’s competitive grocery environment.” Malik Yakini, former Executive Director of the Detroit Black Community Food Security Network. Credit: Quinn Banks, BridgeDetroit Detroit People’s Food Co-Op needs to generate at least $73,000 a week in order to sustain operations, food sovereignty activist and Detroit Black Community Sovereignty Network board co-op board appointee Malik Yakini told BridgeDetroit. But the co-op’s sales dropped below that benchmark over the summer due to dangerous air quality during Canadian wildfires and heat waves, which forced people to stay indoors. Financial struggles like Detroit People’s Food Co-Op is experiencing are referred to as post-open stabilization struggles, said JQ Hannah, executive director of the Food Co-Op Initiative, a national nonprofit that assists communities seeking to create grocery co-ops. “To have cash flow problems at this stage is really not uncommon,” Hannah said. “It’s a real opportunity to galvanize the community to invest in something that they can believe in, and I believe Detroit is making that case very well.” The Detroit People’s Food Co-op launched its fundraising drive on Sept. 7, titling it the “Mframadan Campaign.” Mframadan is a Ghanaian word that translates to “a house built to withstand windy and treacherous conditions,” according to the campaign, which runs through Nov. 30. At its inception, the co-op established a clear mission to improve Detroiters’ access to fresh food with a business model that allows shoppers to be part of the ownership structure and have a voice in their community. Megan Royal (left) and Trudy Satterwhite (right) shop down the aisle during the October 10, 2026, Detroit People’s Food Co-Op’s Black Girl Cash Mob. Credit: Quinn Banks, BridgeDetroit Experts told BridgeDetroit that many residents don’t understand how a food co-op differs from a corporate grocery store, which can make its prices seem higher than they are and results in fewer people becoming member-owners. “Most people don’t understand that prices are set to be fair to workers and producers, as well as cheap for customers,” said Molly Anderson, program director in Food Studies at Vermont’s Middlebury College. “They are thinking of it as a ‘regular’ grocery store, but it’s so much more than that.” Detroit People’s Co-op uses an open store model, where anyone can shop. Those who choose to become member-owners pay a one-time $200 member-owner fee, which can be paid in installments. Member-owners receive periodic discounts on select items and have voting rights at the co-op’s board meetings, where policies are set. When speaking with new customers and recruiting them to join the co-op, Yakini said he has found that many feel strongly about shelf prices being too high. This is especially apparent as grocery prices have increased 33% since 2019, according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data analyzed by the Associated Press. For co-ops, Yakini said, it is important for affordability to be weighed against the value of creating an institution that centralizes power in the hands of residents over corporations. “Our value proposition has much more to do with community empowerment,” Yakini told BridgeDetroit, “supporting a vibrant, non-extractive local economy, creating a democratic institution, and modeling how we can exhibit control over the food system that provides our food.” Torie Anderson-Lloyd, organizer of Detroit People’s Food Co-Op’s Black Girl Cash Mob, checks out her items during the event on October 10, 2026. Credit: Quinn Banks, BridgeDetroit Legacy co-ops advice Across Michigan’s two peninsulas, there are 11 grocery cooperatives, not including Detroit’s. The majority of them were founded during a national boom in co-ops during the 1960s and 1970s. Hannah said Michigan’s co-ops were part of the country’s second wave of grocery cooperatives following a large burst in the 1940s when the Great Depression motivated communities to move away from corporate structures. “We lost most of those, but not all of them,” Hannah said, referring to the handful of surviving Depression-era cooperatives across New England. “Then the 1960s and ‘70s launched the natural food co-op movement that most people think of today.” Michigan’s oldest co-op, Oryana Community Co-op in Traverse City, started in 1973 as a buyer’s club, a small group of residents who organized to purchase directly from wholesalers. Today, it operates three storefronts. Cody Sovis, marketing manager for Oryana, said that a secret to sustaining a grocery co-op for decades is using the co-op as the starting ground for establishing roots in a community. From engaging community members with events and educational programming to incorporating local brands on shelves, a co-op needs, “an engaged base of customer ownership that is willing to stick with us no matter what.” “We invest a lot of time and energy in supporting local brands and young brands because we know that when we support them, then they support us,” Sovis said. “It creates a circular relationship that we are all invested in the shared success of.” Ypsilanti Food Co-Op, which opened in 1975 as a small storefront, has now expanded to include a full-service bakery, retail space and in-store eating area. Corinne Sikorski has served as the co-op’s general manager since 1981, seeing the store through decades of changes. Sikorski said it’s vital not to conflate the financial bottom line with the cooperative’s mission. Community members shop during Detroit People’s Food Co-Op’s Black Girl Cash Mob on October 10, 2026. Credit: Quinn Banks, BridgeDetroit “Their bottom line [as corporate grocers] is to make money for stockholders, and so our mission, even when we’re losing money, is still to make sure that we are serving our community with good food,” Sikorski told BridgeDetroit. “Staying focused on that good quality food has been important to keeping what we are alive.” When higher bulk grocery prices nationwide, combined with fluctuating tariffs and high diesel prices, translates to higher shelf prices, Sikorski said the trick is substituting higher-end organic foods with more affordable natural alternatives. “Our community wouldn’t have a grocery store if we hadn’t chosen to be there and stay there,” Sikorski said. “We want to serve, be part of the community that we’re in, and that makes it so the people want to support us and keep us there.” Outside of the East Coast, the Midwest has the second-most dense grocery cooperative scene. In Minnesota, 45 grocery co-ops operate across the state, with 26 registered with the National Co+Op Grocers, a coalition of national grocery co-ops. Wisconsin has 16 rural and urban grocery co-ops, followed by seven in Illinois that are registered with the National Co+Op Grocers. Hannah said her organization has found that in recent years, urban, rural and historically redlined cities have increased their interest in forming food co-ops as a way to improve access. “Together, remote rural and the Black-led, historically redlined urban communities are now 50% of the 120 communities currently organizing food co-ops across the country,” Hannah said. In Madison, Wisconsin, just over an hour west of Milwaukee, Willy Street Food Co-Op Marketing and Communications Director Brendon Smith told BridgeDetroit that the store has found great success in leveraging its location in a college town while also serving an urban, inner-city community. State Representative for Michigan’s 16th House District, Stephanie Young, takes a selfie with other patrons at Detroit People’s Food Co-Op’s Black Girl Cash Mob on October 10, 2026. Credit: Quinn Banks, BridgeDetroit “We really had to find that balance between change and consistency,” Smith said. “If you change too much, you run the risk of alienating people who have been with the co-op for a long time. Conversely, if you don’t, then there is always competition ready to swoop in and try to do what you’re doing better or cheaper or faster.” A similar strategy is being utilized by Chicago’s Wild Onion Co-Op, President of the Co-Op’s Board of Directors Chad Curry told BridgeDetroit. Flexibility is the best tool to have for a co-op situated between Northwestern University and Rogers Park, the city’s most racially and ethnically diverse neighborhood. “We don’t have the corporate budgetary assistance that traditional grocery (stores) have, so we have to be creative in the way that we take care of problems,” Curry said. “The margins for co-ops are very tight, and it’s important to educate the community so customers understand that it is a form of activism.” Wild Onion’s story closely mirrors that of the Detroit People’s Food Co-op, with the store opening in 2024 after a decade of pushing to create greater access to fresh produce. Curry said it is this strong community foundation that has kept the store afloat in times of struggle. “This type of grocery store is an act of resistance,” he said. “Co-ops are really a place for you to understand your food and be part of a different kind of future.” Dereka McClay checks an item during the October 10, 2026 Detroit People’s Food Co-Op’s Black Girl Cash Mob. Credit: Quinn Banks, BridgeDetroit Community to the rescue Detroit People’s Food Co-Op announced on Oct. 18 that the store generated its highest weekly sales since the grand opening, bringing in nearly $98,000 between Sept. 28 through Oct. 4, a 60% increase from last year. The co-op’s grand opening week saw $111,000 in sales. Since launching the fundraising initiative, President of the co-op’s Board of Directors Lanay Gilbert-Williams has welcomed 260 new member-owners since launching the fundraising campaign on Sept. 8. The difference between co-ops that survive and those that fail lies in their ability to plan quickly around changing conditions, Hannah noted. “You need a good plan,” Hannah said. “And that is what makes me excited about Detroit (People’s Food Co-Op) because they have a multi-point plan that they’re speaking to very clearly in a way that I have seen historically lead to success.” In order to ensure cash flow problems do not arise during a future drop in sales, Yakini said that the cooperative has implemented community feedback in “a full operational reset in the store.” “We are retraining staff, restocking the store, thoroughly cleaning, stressing better customer service,” he said. “We are doing all of these things so that people have a positive experience in the store and want to come back.” Carmia Larkins helps Barbara Jones (right) check out her groceries on October 10, 2026. Credit: Quinn Banks, BridgeDetroit Just over one month since launching the campaign, Yakini said Detroit People’s is on

States push short-term insurance as healthcare costs climb
articles.description: Earlier this year, Madison Harden-Stein and her colleagues at the Georgetown University Center on Health Insurance Reforms posed as consumers interested in buying insurance as part of a secret shopper study. They found that insurance brokers and sales representatives often pushed short-term health insurance plans with limited coverage, and used misleading and inaccurate information to […]
articles.content: Elvia Macedo, a Medi-Cal patient, gets a check-up with Dr. Oscar Casillas at Martin Luther King Jr. Community Hospital in Los Angeles in 2022. Some conservative states are promoting short-term health plans for people who have been priced out of Obamacare or who stand to lose their Medicaid coverage in the coming year due to federal changes. (Photo by Pablo Unzueta for CalMatters)Earlier this year, Madison Harden-Stein and her colleagues at the Georgetown University Center on Health Insurance Reforms posed as consumers interested in buying insurance as part of a secret shopper study. They found that insurance brokers and sales representatives often pushed short-term health insurance plans with limited coverage, and used misleading and inaccurate information to make them more appealing. The deceptive sales tactics made it difficult to make an informed decision about what they’d be signing up for. “It was very confusing to understand what they were even marketing,” said Harden-Stein, an assistant research professor. But as insurance costs skyrocket for many, consumers could see more such plans in the coming year. Conservative states are making it easier for insurance giants to sell cheap, short-term healthcare plans with limited coverage — potentially sticking buyers with thousands of dollars in unexpected medical bills. The push follows a spike in Obamacare premiums after Republicans allowed federal subsidies to expire at the end of last year. Meanwhile, millions of people stand to lose Medicaid coverage in the coming year due to federal changes. Some Republican state and federal officials are pitching the plans as a cheaper alternative to the comprehensive coverage sold on the marketplaces created under the Affordable Care Act. Earlier this year, Mississippi Insurance Commissioner Mike Chaney announced he wanted to make short-term plans more accessible by offering them through a state-operated customer portal. “The goal here is to give Mississippi consumers more choices,” Chaney said in a September statement. “We should not assume that every Mississippian has the same health insurance needs,” he said. “Some people need comprehensive coverage with broad benefits and protections. Others may need a lower-cost option to bridge a temporary gap in coverage.” But critics call them “junk plans.” They say shoppers may be drawn in by low premiums and copayments without fully understanding that they lack the consumer protections people have come to expect since the Affordable Care Act. The 2010 law created regulated health insurance markets and banned insurers from denying coverage, dropping policies, or charging higher rates to people with preexisting health conditions. Short-term, limited duration health plans have been around for decades, intended as stopgap insurance for people between jobs or who are waiting for their employer-sponsored insurance to kick in. The plans usually have cheaper premiums and copayments, but cover fewer services. They don’t have to cover maternity care, mental health treatment or prescription drugs. And insurers are allowed to drop a person’s coverage due to preexisting conditions, or limit the amount paid out per service. They can charge higher premiums for certain people. Research has found some plans charge women up to 19% more than men for the same coverage, which isn’t allowed under ACA-compliant plans. Under these types of plans, people with chronic conditions like diabetes or high blood pressure, or who are pregnant, can’t get coverage. Restrictions on the plans have seesawed as the Obama and Biden administrations limited the plans to just a few months’ duration and the Trump administration relaxed those rules. Most recently, the Trump administration announced in August 2025 it would not enforce Biden-era rules that limited the duration of short-term plans to a few months, and encouraged states to do the same. Shortly after, states including Arkansas and Oklahoma said they would allow insurers to sell short-term plans that last less than a year, and allow them to be renewed up to three years, greatly extending the “short-term” nature of the plans. Consumer advocates say brokers and insurance agents have used misleading or outright false information to entice consumers into purchasing the plans, which later surprised them with thousands of dollars in medical bills. And while these plans can be lucrative for insurers, critics warn they will drive up costs for everyone else. Jennifer Snow, the national director of government relations and policy at the National Alliance on Mental Illness, said someone like her 18-year-old son, who does not have complex health needs, could be considered an ideal candidate for short-term insurance. But “you need those healthier people in the overall market to balance out the risk of people who need a lot more healthcare in a given year.” said Snow, who is also a consumer representative with the National Association of Insurance Commissioners. Health insurance works by spreading healthcare expenses across a large group. If insurers divert healthier people into cheaper, short-term plans, that leaves sicker people who need more expensive care in the risk pool for the comprehensive plans, leading insurers to raise those rates to cover those costs. And, she said, short-term plans rarely cover mental health care, even though about half of people will have a mental health condition over their lifetime — coverage for which usually isn’t included in short-term plans. “At the end of the day, we are all human,” she said, “and we have healthcare needs that are going to be unpredictable.” Better than nothing? Insurance giant UnitedHealthcare will begin offering a handful of short-term plans through Mississippi’s state-run portal by early next year. Those plans could benefit some of the 200,000 Mississippians who left the ACA marketplace in the past year, said Chaney, the insurance commissioner. But that exodus from the ACA marketplace is largely the result of recent federal action. Last year, the ACA saw its highest-ever enrollment of 24 million people, thanks to enhanced premium tax credits made available by the American Rescue Plan Act in 2021 and later extended through the end of 2025 by the Inflation Reduction Act. Those subsidies significantly lowered the cost of Obamacare coverage — making it free or nearly free for some people with low incomes. But they were designed as a temporary pandemic-era measure, and the GOP-controlled Congress allowed them to expire at the end of last year. As a result, premiums jumped. Then marketplace enrollment dropped by 13%, according to federal data, indicating rates were no longer affordable for many. For example, a 60-year-old couple with an annual income of $85,000 suddenly faced annual premiums of $22,600 this year, instead of the roughly $7,225 they paid with enhanced premium tax credits, according to an analysis from the Bipartisan Policy Center. Already the share of uninsured, working-age adults is growing. Eleven percent of adults ages 19-64 now have no insurance, up from 8.9 percent just two years ago, according to a new analysis from the Commonwealth Fund, a health policy nonprofit. Given these realities, some insurance is better than none at all, Chaney and other officials have said. Short-term plans are currently sold in 36 states, according to the most recent analysis from KFF, a nonprofit health policy and research organization. Five states ban them: California, Illinois, Massachusetts, New Jersey and New York. Nine other states, plus the District of Columbia, require they adhere to stricter consumer protection requirements, and no short-term plans are currently available in those states. But in the states that allow them, more officials are exploring ways to expand access. Tennessee lets insurers offer short-term plans on its state ACA marketplace, with some minimum coverage requirements. States including Alabama, Florida, Missouri and Ohio have passed laws in recent years that allow farm bureau health plans, similar to short-term insurance. Experts expect cheaper ACA-alternative plans will proliferate, as the feds continue loosening restrictions. ‘Skeevy marketing’ After a year-long investigation into short-term plans, a congressional committee released a report in 2020. It found that most insurers yanked coverage if they determined an enrollee had a prior health condition or risk factors they should have disclosed when applying for the plan, and some insurers denied claims for people who developed previously undiagnosed medical conditions after enrollment. Some states have tighter rules around deceptive marketing practices, said Harden-Stein. “But it’s a bit of a whack-a-mole situation,” she said. “You can take down one group that has these skeevy marketing tactics, but they might pop up again under another business name. That’s what makes the regulation of this difficult” without stricter federal rules like those in the ACA. Short-term plans are lucrative for insurance companies, because by staying outside of ACA rules, they can pick and choose whom they insure and avoid roadblocks to denying coverage. And while federal law generally allows insurers to only keep about 15-20 cents of every premium dollar collected for ACA-compliant plans, short-term plans have no such restrictions, meaning insurers can keep more of an enrollee’s monthly premiums and pay less toward medical claims. As healthcare costs rise and with little appetite at the federal level to increase financial help paying for it, experts expect to see short-term plans proliferate in the coming years as states relax their rules and more people settle for “better than nothing” health insurance. But cheaper doesn’t necessarily mean more affordable, Harden-Stein cautioned. “It may not necessarily be the affordable option in the long run because it doesn’t offer that comprehensive coverage.” Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org. Emergency order for West Michigan coal plant set to expire again
articles.description: The Trump administration's Department of Energy has issued new emergency orders every 90 days since it initially forced the coal-fired plant to stay open last year.
articles.content: Consumers plans to decommission the J.H. Campbell coal-fired power plant this year.(Consumers Energy)The emergency order keeping a West Michigan coal-fired power plant open is set to expire this Saturday. The Trump administration has repeatedly issued new orders to extend the life of the plant since May of last year, when the J.H. Campbell plant was originally scheduled to close.The Trump administration’s Department of Energy has claimed the nation is under an energy emergency and can’t afford to let the plant close.But environmental and other community groups argued there is no emergency.Sergio Cira Reyes is climate justice catalyst with Urban Core Collective, which has fought to overturn the orders. He says Consumers Energy, local energy regulators, and others in the community, carefully planned for the plant to close in 2025.“And so there’s already experts in community — locally, at the state level and regionally — that have made assessments,” Cira Reyes said. “And they know what they’re doing.”A federal judge agreed, and vacated the Energy Department's initial emergency order in September. That ruling is now being appealed. The department has issued multiple emergency orders keeping other coal plants open as well.The Michigan Attorney General’s Office said in September that keeping the J.H. Campbell plant open has cost an additional $295 million, a cost that could get passed on to electric customers in the state.The Michigan plant is one of several in the country that the Trump administration has ordered to keep operating. Cira Reyes said customers are already facing bills that are too high.“Michigan families can’t afford to pay this added cost of this stubborn Department of Energy’s stance to essentially do a favor for the coal industry and order these different coal plants across the country to stay open,” Cira Reyes said.

Michigan voters support more education funding, but how to pay for it is complicated
articles.description: Jen Stroven, an organizer for Kalamazoo’s Yes For Families campaign, knew what she was up against: ‘Affordability, affordability, affordability.’ Asking voters to raise their own taxes to lower child care costs, expand access, and raise teacher wages may have seemed like a tall order at a time when the increased cost of living is a […]
articles.content: Getty ImagesJen Stroven, an organizer for Kalamazoo’s Yes For Families campaign, knew what she was up against: ‘Affordability, affordability, affordability.’ Asking voters to raise their own taxes to lower child care costs, expand access, and raise teacher wages may have seemed like a tall order at a time when the increased cost of living is a top issue on voters’ minds. But Stroven was confident the 0.5-mill property tax proposal would pass and she was right. In August, 63% of voters in Kalamazoo County approved the eight-year initiative that will add an average of $50 a month to their property tax bills. Stroven said that even for those voters who didn’t have young kids, they were able to see the economic benefit for communities and businesses that are losing workers because of lack of affordable childcare. She said they also understood how far-reaching the impact could be from the benefits to families to childcare workers, to the kids themselves. “It seemed for most folks to be a worthwhile investment,” Stroven said. The success of the Kalamazoo millage may come at a particularly cash-strapped time for voters but its passage is part of a larger trend both statewide and nationally of a shift in thinking from childcare and early childhood education as a personal responsibility to a public good. Kent County approved an early childhood millage in 2018; Leelanau County followed in 2019. If voters can coalesce around early childhood education as a social good, whether or not funding for K-12 education can receive similar support is a little more complicated. Jen Stroven from the Kalamazoo Yes for Families Campaign. (Photo provided) The legacy of Proposal A For better or worse, K-12 educational funding in Michigan changed dramatically in 1994. Before, each school district relied heavily on local property taxes for funding. Unsurprisingly this led to massive inequities: Cities with a lot of property wealth could easily fund high teacher salaries, extensive programming and small class sizes with even smaller tax rates, while districts with low property values and rural communities were underfunded. In late 1993, the state Legislature removed the local property tax system, followed several months later by the voter-approved Proposal A constitutional amendment restructuring how Michigan funds K-12 public school operations. Since then, the Legislature distributes the exact same amount for each student in all schools through the School Aid Fund. Revenue for the fund comes mostly from sales taxes with small portions of revenue from income and property taxes. Inequities still exist: Districts can pass voter-approved millages for capital expenses, such as school bonds and sinking funds to build new buildings or improve old ones. This means that some districts have state-of-the-art school buildings while students in other districts are stuck in crumbling schools. David Arsen | Michigan State University But all Michigan districts are legally restricted from asking voters to fund operational expenses like hiring more teachers, increasing salaries or even basics like paying a building’s utility bills. This funding paradox can create an incongruent situation like what’s currently playing out in Ann Arbor: a budget crisis with teacher layoffs while new school buildings are erected from a 2018 millage. On one hand, the Proposal A funding model has created more solidarity among districts, said David Arsen, a Michigan State University professor who specializes in education policy and school finance. But the downside, he says, is that communities lose the ability to respond locally to their own needs even if voters would be willing to tax themselves as they were in Kalamazoo. Why are schools still underfunded? In July, Michigan lawmakers celebrated a per-pupil funding increase from $10,050 to $10,300, along with other notable educational investments from the School Aid Fund, including an expansion of the Great Start Readiness Program to fund PreK for All and free school meals. Still, school funding hasn’t kept up with inflation and the changing economy. A recent poll commissioned by the K-12 Alliance of Michigan found that half of surveyed voters said that their local school districts have funding shortages for the resources they need. Not keeping up with inflation While $10,300 per student may sound like a lot, that number hasn’t kept pace with inflation according to research from the Education Policy Innovation Collaborative at MSU. When adjusted for inflation, Michigan now spends less on school operations than it did decades ago. In 2002, the School Aid Fund provided an inflation-adjusted average of $13,858 per student. Decreased enrollment As a result of declining birth rates, population loss and other factors, public school enrollment in Michigan has declined by nearly 20%, or more than 335,000 students, since 2002. Tying funding to the number of students means that when enrollment drops, money disappears, even if costs increase. Schools have many fixed costs that can’t fluctuate with enrollment. A loss of even 20 students across all grade levels means a district loses hundreds of thousands of dollars while its operational costs, such as heating and cooling, running bus routes and paying school nurses, remain fixed or even increase with inflation. Compounding enrollment losses over several years force districts to cut essential staff and increase class sizes just to keep their budget balanced, even as per-pupil funding numbers are increased. The problem with sales tax Arsen explains that because the state sales tax is the primary source of revenue for the School Aid Fund, the education system loses out when there is a shift in consumer behavior and the tax code doesn’t keep up. “The sales tax, which is the main source of revenue to the school aid fund, is based on the goods economy. There are a whole host of things in services that are not taxed. And so as the economy itself shifts from goods-producing to more services, that source of income doesn’t keep pace,” Arsen said. Where is the money going to come from? The good news for schools is that voters generally agree that funding education should be a priority, and as supporters of the Kalamazoo millage demonstrated — a case can be made that well-educated kids are essential for the future of the state. However, figuring out where the money will come from remains a challenge. “We can get consensus in Michigan on equitable and adequate funding. What we have not been able to do yet is get agreement on where the revenues will come in order to fund that,” Arsen said. Molly Sweeney, organizing director of 482Forward, a member of the Invest in MI Kids ballot proposal coalition tells reporters the group plans to begin circulating petitions. July 31, 2025 | Photo By Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance The 2025 Invest in MI Kids campaign was an attempt at a solution. The campaign aimed to get a constitutional amendment on the 2026 ballot to place a 5% surcharge on single filers earning more than $500,000 and joint filers earning over $1 million. The initiative would have raised between $1.5 and $2 billion annually to lower student-to-teacher ratios, expand technical education and improve teacher retention. The campaign faced several obstacles, including pushback and procedural delays along with a high signature threshold. Though the campaign collected more than 250,000 signatures, it fell short of the goal and suspended operations in March, saying it would look toward the 2028 election cycle instead. Despite not making this year’s ballot, campaign manager Jessica Newman, co-director of the Michigan Education Justice Coalition, still thinks there’s a path to future success. Jess Newman with Invest in MI Kids (Photo provided) “This is a state that is ready to tax the rich, it’s ready to fund our public goods and services, and I wouldn’t take our failure to get on the ballot as evidence of that at all,” she said. Newman is not alone in that belief. Stroven and Arsen agreed that education funding is increasingly a bipartisan issue in Michigan. As Invest in MI Kids looks to the 2028 ballot, the campaign is now considering several other funding options beyond an increased income tax on high earners. Funding options that the campaign proposed in a survey to past canvassers include repealing data center property and sales tax exemptions, raising the corporate income tax rate, introducing a wealth proceeds tax, introducing a digital advertising tax and extending the sales tax to include services. Disclosure: The author was a volunteer signature collector for the campaign in 2025. Voters in Kalamazoo and other counties approved taxes to pay for childcare. If Invest in MI Kids manages to get a proposal on the ballot next year, will Michiganders vote to fund education statewide? Public opinion seems to indicate they might. According to the EPIC survey, 65% of voters support an increase in education spending and put it on the top of their list of priorities, above even healthcare and fixing the roads. Newman remains hopeful. “I don’t have kids, but I understand that public schools are a public good that help every single person in the community.” Support for this reporting came from The Better Life Lab at New America.

Abdul El-Sayed says Democrats will work with Trump if 'he wants to act serious'
articles.source: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content: The Michigan senator-elect called the president "an unserious fool." Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed said Sunday that Democrats will work with President Donald Trump to help the American people if "he wants to act serious," but if the president instead chooses "foolishness," the incoming senator said he will not find a willing partner in Congress. "Let's talk about how he is an unserious fool. Think about this war in Iran that every single president had resisted fighting because, of course, it was a dumb idea," El-Sayed told ABC "This Week" in an exclusive interview. "Let's talk about the foolishness of a tariff war with Canada. ... Let's talk about the foolishness of gutting Medicaid to pass tax cuts for the richest people in America." "So look, if he wants to act serious, we are happy to work alongside him to actually address these issues," El-Sayed continued. "He is the president of the United States. But if he wants to continue to fool, he will hire people like Stephen Miller to run the White House, and he gets to choose where he goes next." President Trump on Friday said White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller would assume the role of chief of staff effective Monday, replacing Susie Wiles. With his victory in Michigan's Senate race last Tuesday, El-Sayed is set to make history as the nation's first Muslim senator. During his campaign, El-Sayed said he focused his message on three issues: "to get money out of politics, put money in your pocket and pass Medicare for all." But the issue that most defined both the contentious and close primary campaign against fellow Democrat Haley Stevens and the general election campaign against former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers was U.S. support for Israel. El-Sayed has been a staunch critic of the Israeli government and U.S. military aid to Israel. Asked on "This Week" if he's heard from his Republican opponent, El-Sayed said, "Not that I know of. I think he had a flight to catch to Florida." Despite differences and his criticism of Trump, El-Sayed did say he would be willing to work with the president if it would help "advance the goals I ran on, to get money out of politics, put money in pockets, pass Medicare for All." "I've said this, if he wants to pass Trump care for all, which will guarantee health care to everyone and put his name on it like he's putting his name on everything, I'm game,” El-Sayed said. Karl also pressed El-Sayed on his past criticism of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. El-Sayed said that he and Schumer “figured out how to work together” during the campaign but he did not pledge to support a Schumer bid to become majority leader. “The question to me is, who wants to be the leader who's going to make sure that we deliver on the mandate that we just got? I want to see who else is in the running,” El-Sayed said. El-Sayed voiced support for Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who has not publicly announced intention to become majority leader. El-Sayed stressed that he is looking for a leader “who is ready to take action on day one,” adding that he has “not been impressed by what we've been able to do.” “I want leadership who is going to deliver on the goal of getting money out of politics, put money in pockets, passed Medicare for all. As you know, a vote is a choice between two or more options. I don't know what those options are, but I am committed to making sure that we can deliver on the goals that we need, and we need action now,” El-Sayed said. El-Sayed also reflected on his own journey to becoming Michigan’s next senator, again recounting a story from 2007 where he gave a speech to his graduating college class, and the commencement speaker, former President Bill Clinton, told him to run for office. El-Sayed said he initially dismissed the former president. “I laughed in his face. I said, ‘Mr. President, I don't know if you saw my name. It's got 11 letters in it. People like me don't get to run for office.’” El-Sayed said it was watching President Barack Obama get elected the following year that opened the path for him to run for office. “[President Clinton] saw something in me I'd never seen in myself. And President Obama showed me something in me I'd never seen in myself. And 19 years later, I'm grateful to be the senator-elect from the state of Michigan,” said El-Sayed. 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

He fought France's far right for half a century. Now Mélenchon eyes a 2027 runoff with Le Pen
articles.description: He fought France's far right for half a century. Now Mélenchon eyes a 2027 runoff with Le Pen AP News Opinion | France’s cost-of-living trap The Washington Post Mélenchon's foreign policy proposals would weaken France Le Monde.fr French presidential hopeful Melenchon pledges economic stimulus, renews NATO exit call Reuters ‘Radical’ or ‘hero’?: France debates leftist candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon Al Jazeera
articles.content: LE BOURGET, France (AP) — Young supporters wore his name on their backs like a soccer star’s, above the number 27. They sang about brass bands and revolution. Many had spent the fall protesting or blockading their schools. Then in walked Jean-Luc Mélenchon: 75 years old, on his fourth presidential run and old enough to be their grandfather. “I have only one sensible thing to propose,” he told 20,000 supporters in a vast hall north of Paris on Saturday. “Everything must change.” The septuagenarian may never get another chance. Three presidential bids have ended short of the runoff. In 2022, just 421,308 votes kept him out. Now, riding a surge in support, he is eyeing a winner-take-all showdown with far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen. The bespectacled, booming and seemingly tireless leftist wants more than the presidency. He wants to rewrite the rules of the French republic — invoking the unfinished promise of the Revolution of 1789. A place in the May 2 runoff could prove a cruel prize. If Le Pen beats him, the anti-capitalist who has spent half a century fighting the far right could help give it what it has never won: the Elysee Palace — and command of France’s nuclear arsenal. Victory could send shock waves across the Atlantic. Trump would still be in the White House. Russia is waging war in Ukraine. Yet Mélenchon wants to pull the EU’s only nuclear-armed power out of NATO, starting with its military command. His debt plans could also put France on a collision course with Europe’s central bank, rattling markets. His detractors see that as the greater danger. They accuse him of stoking unrest and antisemitism, scorning the police and the press, and going soft on Moscow — charges he rejects. Born in Tangier, Morocco, in 1951, the showman was a Trotskyist student, then a Socialist for three decades, rising to become a senator and junior minister. In 2008, he walked out to build his own movement. Even his rallies have a name: the “Mélenshow.” On Saturday, cameras swept over the crowd on cables while a film followed a woman through life’s struggles. One by one, his lieutenants stepped forward with solutions. It was a campaign rally staged as a government in waiting. Modesty is not his style. Backstage, behind a black curtain, he paused to listen to the roar. “Enjoy it,” he told French media. “It’s not often in a lifetime that you see something like this.” He then recalled a 1972 rally when Socialist François Mitterrand and Communist Georges Marchais shared the stage. But this time, Mélenchon boasted, “I’m doing this all by myself!” He even sniffed at former Socialist President François Hollande, who rallied in the same hall on his way to power: “They only filled a third of the room,” he said. To some, the boasts had a Trumpian ring: The U.S. president, too, brags about the size of his crowds — and once declared, “I alone can fix it.” One far-right mayor has called Mélenchon “the Donald Trump of the left.” When police searched his party’s offices in 2018, he bellowed at them: “I am the Republic!” He was later convicted over the confrontation. A 2025 investigative book described a leader who demands blind devotion and treats doubters as traitors. His 2027 bet is on the young and the suburbs. Le Bourget lies in Seine-Saint-Denis, mainland France’s poorest department. To the far right, it symbolizes crime and failed immigration. To Mélenchon — a white veteran of the old Left — it represents the future: a younger, more diverse “New France” whose votes could carry him to power. The hall fell silent in memory of Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old Frenchman of African descent shot dead last month in what the government called a racist terror attack. Since September, a high school protest movement over crumbling schools and teacher shortages has swept France. Police have made thousands of arrests. Mélenchon embraced it from the start. “Don’t touch our young people,” he warned the government. “We are the future, and he listens to us,” said Jamal Santos, 22, a student whose group joined the protests. Last month, cost-of-living protests turned to looting and arson in more than 20 cities. Rioters torched the 19th-century City Hall in Limoges. Le Pen accused his party of plunging France into chaos. Mélenchon blamed police tactics and denied his party organized the protests. France’s old political order is coming apart. The Socialists and conservative Republicans, who traded power for decades, won just 6.5% of the first-round presidential vote between them in 2022. Now a Le Pen-Mélenchon runoff could leave both parties watching from the sidelines as two movements that have never governed France battle for the presidency. Mélenchon is racing to bank that energy before mainstream rivals regroup. Center-right former Prime Minister Édouard Philippe is also vying to face Le Pen. If the center unites, or voters rally to block a runoff between the extremes, second place could slip away. Mélenchon’s program, over 1,000 points long, reads like a blueprint for another country. It would lower the voting age to 16, bring back retirement at 60, make the rich pay more and impose a moratorium on artificial intelligence. At its heart is a new constitution to replace the Fifth Republic that Charles de Gaulle founded in 1958. He would have a special assembly of citizens, excluding current lawmakers, write a new constitution for voters to approve. And between elections, ordinary French people could gather signatures to force votes to overturn laws, change the constitution or even oust a sitting president. “We are no longer in 1958,” said Hicham En-Naji, 27. Few French politicians inspire such devotion, or such fury. He has made Gaza a rallying cry for the young, insisting Saturday that “genocide must be called genocide.” Activists who accuse him of fanning antisemitism, a charge he denies, disrupted the rally with whistles. “Some commentators are advising me to tone things down,” he said. “I won’t do that.” He closed by turning a well-known 2017 gaffe by President Emmanuel Macron about “people who are nothing” into a line from the “Internationale,” the historic anthem of communists and socialists worldwide. “Macron told you that you are nothing,” he said. “So let us be everything!” The hall answered, singing “La Marseillaise.” Whether the teenagers in No. 27 jerseys remember him as the man who finally carried his revolution into the Elysee Palace, or the one who held its door open for the far right, may come down to the one thing he refuses to do: soften. Associated Press journalist Jade Le Deley contributed to this report.

articles.title: A pastor at a Beijing underground church has been arrested, his wife says
articles.content: TAIPEI, Taiwan (AP) — A pastor of a house church in Beijing has been arrested, his wife told The Associated Press this week, as China intensifies its crackdown on unregistered churches. Pastor Xianfeng Edward Cui, who founded Beijing Jiaquan Church, was arrested on Oct. 23 on charges of fraud, said his wife, Jin Young Gu, who lives outside of China. Cui was first detained on Sept. 4 as part of a raid on his church that involved around 100 police officers, Gu said. Gu said the fraud allegations are related to church members’ offerings. Such charges are likely related to the fact that the church is unregistered. Police in Beijing’s Shijingshan district did not respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press. The Chinese Foreign Ministry did not answer questions about the pastor sent via a messaging app. Cui’s arrest is the latest case in Chinese President Xi Jinping’s long-running campaign to tighten control over religion to ensure all groups of faith abide by Communist Party rule. In one of the biggest crackdowns on religious activity in recent years, authorities in October 2025 arrested 30 leaders of Zion Church, one of the country’s largest underground church networks, following overnight raids in several cities. Among those arrested was church founder Jin Mingri. He was freed in July following a personal request by U.S. President Donald Trump to Xi during Trump’s visit to Beijing. Beijing Jiaquan Church was founded in 2006 and had grown in size as an unregistered congregation, Gu said. By 2019, authorities sealed off the group’s worship facility in Beijing, forcing the congregation to meet in smaller groups and at different locations, Gu said. In 2023, authorities interrupted a Sunday church class to warn Gu and Cui that their church had become too large, Gu said. “They told him that he should lead only one church with fewer than 100 people,” Gu said. “This was a direct warning from the authorities concerning the size and organization of our church.” Gu, a Korean national, said she’s been denied a visa since 2023 to return to China as a family member.
